oneLiner: Three killer DDx — ACS, PE, aortic dissection — must be excluded before discharge. Risk-stratify with HEART score; image based on clinical suspicion.
framing: One of the highest-volume ED chief complaints. Roughly 10-15% have acute coronary syndrome; the remainder split between musculoskeletal, GI, anxiety, pleural, and the rare-but-deadly aortic dissection and tension pneumothorax.
keyHistory: Character (crushing / pleuritic / tearing / burning) and radiation (jaw / arm / back / shoulder)
Onset (sudden vs gradual), duration, provocation/relief, time course
Cardiac risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, family history, prior MI)
PE risk factors (immobility, recent surgery, malignancy, OCP / pregnancy, prior VTE)
Aortic dissection risk factors (Marfan, bicuspid valve, hypertension, cocaine use, pregnancy)
GI features (worse lying, related to food, regurgitation)
keyExam: Vitals — HR, BP both arms, RR, SpO₂, temp
Cardiovascular — heart sounds, murmurs, JVP, peripheral pulses (asymmetry), peripheral oedema
Respiratory — breath sounds, percussion, focal findings
Chest wall reproducibility (lowers but does not exclude ACS)

differential.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI / NSTEMI / unstable angina)
differential.pointers: Pressure / crushing pain ± radiation; risk factors; new ECG changes; troponin rise.
differential.investigation: 12-lead ECG within 10 min; serial troponin (hs-cTn 0-1 h or 0-3 h); HEART score; bedside echo.

differential.pointers: Pleuritic pain + dyspnoea + tachycardia; VTE risk factors; clear chest with hypoxia.
differential.investigation: Wells / Geneva score; D-dimer if PERC fails; CTPA if Wells > 4 or D-dimer positive; ECHO for RV strain.

differential.pointers: Sudden tearing pain radiating to back; pulse deficit; new diastolic murmur; widened mediastinum on CXR; SBP differential > 20 mmHg between arms.
differential.investigation: CT angiogram aorta (gold standard); TOE if unstable; D-dimer high sensitivity but not specific.

differential.pointers: Sudden pleuritic pain + dyspnoea + tracheal deviation + hyperresonance + absent breath sounds; shock if tension.
differential.investigation: Bedside ultrasound (faster than CXR if tension); immediate needle decompression / chest drain if tension.

differential.pointers: Sudden chest pain after vomiting; subcutaneous emphysema; pleural effusion.
differential.investigation: CT with oral contrast; surgical emergency.

differential.pointers: Pleuritic, worse lying, relieved by sitting forward; recent viral illness; diffuse ST elevation + PR depression.
differential.investigation: ECG, troponin, echo, CRP/ESR; MRI if myocarditis suspected.

differential.pointers: Reproducible on palpation; trauma history; positional; no risk factors.
Burning, related to food, regurgitation, response to PPI / antacids.
differential.investigation: Trial PPI; gastroscopy if alarm features.

differential.pointers: Younger, no risk factors, hyperventilation, perioral paraesthesia. Diagnosis of exclusion in any new-onset chest pain.

redFlags: New ECG ischaemic changes (ST elevation/depression, T-wave inversion, new LBBB)
Tearing back pain with pulse deficit
initialInvestigations: Troponin (serial — repeat per local hs-cTn protocol)
FBC, U&E, glucose; D-dimer if PE / dissection considered AND high-sensitivity scoring rule supports
Bedside echo if available (RV strain / pericardial effusion / regional wall motion)
disposition: Admit any patient with ACS, PE, dissection, pneumothorax, oesophageal rupture, sustained haemodynamic instability or hypoxia. HEART score 0-3 with negative serial troponin + normal ECG may be safe for outpatient follow-up with GP review in 48-72 h and safety-net advice (return if pain returns, worsens, or new symptoms emerge).

references.label: Six AJ et al. Chest pain in the emergency room — value of the HEART score. Neth Heart J 2008.
ESC 2020 Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes.

oneLiner: Differential is wide — work systematically: airway / heart / lungs / blood / brain / body. PE, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema, acute asthma and severe pneumonia are the time-critical exclusions.
framing: Most common acute respiratory presentations in adults: acute exacerbation of asthma / COPD, pneumonia, acute pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism. Sudden onset + pleuritic = PE or pneumothorax. Onset over hours-to-days + sputum / fever = pneumonia. Onset over days + orthopnoea + leg swelling = heart failure.
keyHistory: Provoking factors (exertion, allergen, cold air, infection, pregnancy)
Associated chest pain (cardiac vs pleuritic vs musculoskeletal)
Cough (productive, blood-stained), fever, weight loss, sweats
Orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, peripheral oedema
VTE risk factors (immobility, recent surgery, malignancy)
keyExam: Vitals + SpO₂ (room air and supplemented); RR is the most under-recorded vital
Cyanosis, tracheal position, accessory muscle use, tripoding
Breath sounds (wheeze, crackles bilateral / focal, absent), percussion
JVP, heart sounds, peripheral oedema, leg swelling

differential.pointers: Bilateral basal crackles, raised JVP, gallop rhythm, peripheral oedema, history of HF / ACS / arrhythmia.
differential.investigation: BNP/NT-proBNP, ECG, CXR, bedside echo, troponin.

differential.pointers: Sudden onset, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia disproportionate to clear chest, VTE risk factors.
differential.investigation: Wells score; D-dimer if PERC fails; CTPA.

differential.pointers: Wheeze, prolonged expiration, prior diagnosis, triggers identified.
differential.investigation: Peak flow / FEV1, ABG if severe, CXR to exclude pneumothorax / consolidation.

differential.pointers: Fever, productive cough, focal crackles or bronchial breathing, CRP elevated.
differential.investigation: CXR, CRP, FBC, U&E, blood and sputum cultures, urinary Legionella/pneumococcal antigens.

differential.pointers: Sudden pleuritic pain, tracheal deviation, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, haemodynamic compromise.
differential.investigation: Bedside ultrasound > CXR; immediate needle decompression if tension.

differential.pointers: Sudden onset minutes after exposure; urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis — DO NOT delay adrenaline.

differential.diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of pulmonary fibrosis / ILD
differential.pointers: Known ILD or new bilateral fine crackles + clubbing; progressive dyspnoea over weeks.
Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath (DKA), tinnitus (salicylates), abdominal pain.
differential.investigation: Glucose, ketones, ABG, lactate, salicylate level if clinical concern.

differential.pointers: Pallor, tachycardia, postural drop, melaena / haematuria / vaginal bleeding.
differential.investigation: FBC, group and screen, CT to localise bleed if suspected.

redFlags: SpO₂ < 92% on air, or < 88% in known COPD on room air
Unable to speak in full sentences
initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, CRP, troponin if cardiac picture
BNP / NT-proBNP if heart failure differential
D-dimer if PE possible AND PERC criteria fail
disposition: Admit any patient with hypoxia, marked tachypnoea, haemodynamic instability, raised lactate, or known progressive disease. Acute asthma: discharge when peak flow > 75% predicted, SpO₂ > 94% air, able to manage at home, with rescue pack + 24-h GP follow-up.

references.label: NICE NG191 — COVID-19 rapid guideline: managing the long-term effects of COVID-19.
BTS / SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma.

oneLiner: Site + onset + character locate the cause. Must-not-miss: ruptured AAA, mesenteric ischaemia, ectopic pregnancy, perforation, sepsis. β-hCG in any female of reproductive age presenting with abdominal pain.
framing: One of the broadest differentials in medicine. History + exam direct investigations more than the other way around. The classic catastrophic causes (AAA rupture, mesenteric ischaemia, ectopic) are missed when the picture is atypical.
keyHistory: Site of pain (epigastric / RUQ / LUQ / RLQ / LLQ / suprapubic / generalised / radiating)
Onset (sudden — perforation, AAA, ovarian torsion, embolic mesenteric; vs gradual — appendicitis, diverticulitis, cholecystitis)
Character (colicky vs constant; relieved by anything)
Associated nausea, vomiting (bilious? blood?), bowel habit change, melaena, haematochezia
LMP (any female 12-55); contraceptive use; pregnancy possibility
Cardiovascular risk factors (mesenteric ischaemia in AF, recent embolic event)
keyExam: Vitals: tachycardia, hypotension (perforation, ruptured AAA, sepsis)
Inspection: distension, scars, hernias, bruising (Cullen/Grey-Turner in pancreatitis/AAA)
Palpation: localised tenderness, peritonism (rebound, guarding, rigidity), Murphy's sign, McBurney's tenderness, expansile mass (AAA)
PR / PV if indicated (PR bleeding, gynae source); β-hCG in any female of reproductive age

differential.pointers: Sudden severe abdominal/back pain in patient > 60, hypotension, pulsatile expansile mass, vascular risk factors. Misdiagnosed as renal colic in 30%.
differential.investigation: Bedside ultrasound (FAST + abdominal aorta diameter); CT angiogram if stable. EMERGENCY vascular consult.

differential.pointers: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam; AF / recent embolic event / vascular disease; bloody diarrhoea (late); high lactate.
differential.investigation: Lactate, CT angiogram mesenteric vessels. Surgical / interventional emergency.

differential.pointers: Female of reproductive age, lower abdominal pain ± shoulder-tip (diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum), PV bleeding, syncope.
differential.investigation: Serum β-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound. EMERGENCY gynae.

differential.pointers: Sudden generalised pain → peritonism → board-like rigidity; sepsis features; free air on imaging.
differential.investigation: Erect CXR (free air); CT abdomen if equivocal. Urgent surgical.

differential.pointers: Periumbilical pain migrating to RIF; anorexia, low-grade fever; RIF tenderness, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign. Alvarado score.
Epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; alcohol or gallstones; lipase ≥ 3× ULN. Severity by Glasgow / APACHE-II.
differential.investigation: Lipase / amylase, LFTs, CRP, calcium, glucose, ABG, ultrasound for gallstones.

differential.pointers: RUQ pain, Murphy's positive (cholecystitis); fever + jaundice + RUQ pain (Charcot's triad — cholangitis).
differential.investigation: Ultrasound, LFTs, FBC, CRP, blood cultures. ERCP urgent if cholangitis.

differential.pointers: LLQ pain, fever, elderly, raised inflammatory markers. CT for complications (abscess, perforation).
differential.investigation: CT abdomen with contrast; FBC, CRP, blood cultures if sepsis.

differential.pointers: Loin to groin pain in waves; haematuria; restless patient (vs lying still in peritonism).
differential.investigation: Urinalysis, CT KUB, U&E. CAUTION — AAA mimics this in elderly.

differential.pointers: Colicky central pain, vomiting (bilious early in SBO), abdominal distension, absolute constipation late; previous surgery.
differential.investigation: AXR (distended small bowel loops), CT (level, transition point, cause).

differential.diagnosis: Gynae causes (ovarian cyst rupture/torsion, PID, endometriosis)
differential.pointers: Sudden severe pain (torsion / cyst rupture); fever + cervical motion tenderness (PID); cyclical (endometriosis).
differential.investigation: TVUS, β-hCG, STI screen, gynae review.

differential.pointers: Diabetic, elderly, female — atypical ACS presentations; epigastric pain mimicking dyspepsia.
differential.investigation: ECG, troponin in any older patient with epigastric pain.

redFlags: Severe pain out of proportion to exam (mesenteric ischaemia)
Positive β-hCG with abdominal pain — exclude ectopic
initialInvestigations: β-hCG in any female of reproductive age
FBC, U&E, LFTs, lipase, CRP, lactate, glucose, group and screen
Bedside ultrasound (FAST, biliary, aortic) — extends physical examination
CT abdomen with contrast — gold standard for most acute abdomen scenarios
disposition: Admit any patient with peritonism, haemodynamic instability, intractable pain, vomiting precluding oral intake, raised lactate, or where surgical/gynae intervention may be needed. Acute appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, SBO → surgical admission. Discharge with safety-netting if benign cause identified and pain controlled.

references.label: Royal College of Surgeons. Emergency Surgery Standards for unscheduled care.
ACR Appropriateness Criteria — Right Lower Quadrant Pain.

oneLiner: Most are primary (migraine, tension); the must-not-miss secondary causes are SAH, meningitis, GCA, raised ICP (mass / abscess / venous thrombosis), and CO poisoning. Thunderclap onset = SAH until proven otherwise.
framing: Headache is one of the most common presentations and one of the most diagnostically delicate. The diagnosis hinges on careful history + focused exam, NOT routine imaging.
keyHistory: Onset (thunderclap < 1 min to peak = SAH until proven otherwise; gradual over days = mass / venous thrombosis / GCA in elderly)
Worst-ever / first-ever quality (suspicious for SAH or other secondary)
Triggers (Valsalva, exercise, sex, position — raised ICP)
Time of day (worse on waking = raised ICP)
Associated features: visual changes, focal neurology, confusion, neck stiffness, fever, jaw claudication (GCA), vomiting
Pregnancy / postpartum (eclampsia, cerebral venous thrombosis, PRES)
Carbon monoxide exposure (winter, faulty heating, multiple household members affected)
keyExam: Vitals incl. temp, BP both arms
GCS, full neurological exam (cranial nerves, limbs, reflexes, cerebellar)

differential.pointers: Thunderclap onset, worst ever, neck stiffness, decreased consciousness, focal signs.
differential.investigation: Non-contrast CT brain within 6 h (sensitivity > 98%); lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT negative and > 6 h, OR if equivocal.

differential.pointers: Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status, petechial rash (meningococcal).
differential.investigation: Blood cultures + lumbar puncture (with CT first if focal signs / immunocompromise / reduced GCS); empirical antibiotics within 1 h of suspicion — do NOT delay for LP.

differential.pointers: Age > 50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual disturbance, ESR > 50, PMR features.
differential.investigation: ESR, CRP, temporal artery biopsy. START high-dose prednisolone (40-60 mg) IMMEDIATELY if visual symptoms — do not wait for biopsy; visual loss is permanent.

differential.diagnosis: Raised intracranial pressure (mass, abscess, IIH, venous thrombosis)
differential.pointers: Worse on waking, worse with Valsalva, projectile vomiting, focal signs, papilloedema. CVT in pregnancy / OCP / dehydration.
differential.investigation: MRI brain (with MRV for CVT); CT venogram if MRV unavailable.

differential.pointers: Winter, faulty heating, multiple household members affected. Cherry-red skin LATE / unreliable. Symptoms improve away from source.
differential.investigation: ABG with co-oximetry (COHb); ECG for ischaemia. Hyperbaric O₂ if severe / pregnant / cardiac signs.

differential.pointers: Unilateral throbbing, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, aura (visual scintillation), prior similar episodes.
differential.investigation: Clinical. Image if first attack > 50, focal signs, atypical features.

differential.pointers: Band-like, bilateral, mild-moderate, no nausea/photophobia, related to stress/posture.
Strictly unilateral periorbital, severe (suicide headache), autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, conjunctival injection, Horner's), clustering in time.
Facial pain worse on bending forward, nasal congestion, fever, purulent discharge.
differential.investigation: Clinical; CT only if complications suspected.

differential.pointers: Daily / near-daily headache, regular use of analgesics (paracetamol > 15 days/month, triptans > 10 days/month).
Severe headache + SBP > 180 + papilloedema / focal neurology / chest pain / pulmonary oedema.
differential.investigation: BP, ECG, troponin, U&E, urine for haematuria/proteinuria, CT brain if neurology. IV antihypertensive in resus.

redFlags: Headache worse on waking + vomiting (raised ICP)
Postpartum or pregnant patient (eclampsia, CVT, PRES)
initialInvestigations: Non-contrast CT brain if any red flag
Lumbar puncture (xanthochromia for SAH; cell count + protein + glucose + culture for meningitis) after CT clear
BP both arms in elderly (rule out dissection presenting as headache)
disposition: Admit any red-flag headache pending investigation. Discharge with safety-netting if primary headache identified, well, normal exam, with GP follow-up. Provide written safety-net advice.

references.label: NICE CG150 — Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management.
Connolly ES Jr et al. AHA / ASA guidelines for the management of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.

oneLiner: Apply NICE traffic-light system. Red = immediate intervention, amber = senior review, green = home with safety-net. Always check for meningococcal rash, encephalopathy, dehydration, respiratory distress, UTI in any febrile child without obvious focus.
framing: Most febrile children have self-limiting viral illness. The challenge is identifying the small fraction with serious bacterial infection (SBI) or invasive meningococcal disease before they decompensate. NICE NG143 traffic-light system is the standard UK approach; WHO IMCI applies in LMIC settings.
keyHistory: Duration and pattern of fever (response to antipyretics is NOT a reliable marker of bacterial vs viral)
Focal symptoms (cough, ear pain, rash, dysuria, diarrhoea, joint swelling)
Activity / responsiveness — parental concern is a sensitive indicator
Recent travel, sick contacts, immunisations (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, MMR)
Antibiotic use in last 2 weeks (may mask classical signs)
Immunocompromise (sickle cell, splenectomy, oncology, primary immunodeficiency)
Age (< 3 months — much higher SBI risk regardless of presentation)
keyExam: Vitals: HR, RR, BP, SpO₂, temp, capillary refill (age-band specific)
Hydration: skin turgor, fontanelle, mucous membranes, urine output
Skin: rash (non-blanching purpura = emergency), petechiae, mottling
Respiratory: nasal flaring, recessions, grunting, accessory muscles
Throat (Strep, EBV); ears (otitis media); meningism (Brudzinski's, neck stiffness, full fontanelle)

differential.pointers: Coryza, sore throat, cough, low-grade fever; well between fevers; preserved feeding.
Ear pulling, distress, bulging red tympanic membrane.
ANY febrile infant < 3 months OR febrile child with no clear focus needs urine sample (clean-catch / catheter / SPA per age and clinical state).
Tachypnoea (WHO age-band cut-offs), focal crackles, intercostal recessions, low SpO₂.
differential.investigation: Clinical ± CXR if uncertain, FBC, CRP.

differential.pointers: Non-blanching purpura, mottling, leg pain, cold extremities (early), then shock, decreased GCS, neck stiffness, photophobia.
differential.investigation: Bedside glucose; IV access; antibiotic FIRST (ceftriaxone) before LP; PCR; LP after stabilisation if no contraindication.

differential.pointers: Altered mental status, seizures, focal neurology, behavioural change.
differential.investigation: Bedside glucose; FBC, U&E, ammonia, blood gas; IV aciclovir + ceftriaxone if suspected; LP + MRI when stable.

differential.pointers: Lethargy, poor feeding, mottled, prolonged CRT > 3 s, tachycardia, hypotension late.
differential.investigation: Septic screen: blood cultures, FBC, CRP, lactate, urine, ± CSF; antibiotics within 1 h.

differential.pointers: ≥ 5 days fever + 4 of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucosal changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphic rash, peripheral changes (oedema/desquamation), cervical lymphadenopathy.
RIF tenderness, peritonism, fever, atypical in young children.
Limp, refusal to weight-bear, joint swelling, fever.
differential.investigation: X-ray (often normal early), MRI, FBC, CRP, blood cultures, joint aspiration.

redFlags: No response to social cues; appears ill to a healthcare professional
Age < 3 months with any fever (≥ 38°C rectal)
initialInvestigations: Urine dip / culture in any infant < 3 months with fever, OR child without focus
Bedside glucose if poor feeding / altered mental status
FBC, CRP, blood cultures if traffic-light amber/red
LP if meningitis / encephalitis suspected (after antibiotics, after stabilisation)
disposition: RED (NICE traffic-light): immediate IV access + senior review + investigations + empiric antibiotics + transfer for paediatric assessment. AMBER: senior review; consider observation, watch for progression. GREEN: home with written safety-net advice, parental return criteria (fever > 48 h, new rash, behavioural change, poor feeding, breathing changes), and GP follow-up.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management.
WHO IMCI guidelines (LMIC contexts).

oneLiner: Most is mechanical low-back pain (red-flag-free); the must-not-miss are cauda equina, spinal infection, malignancy, fracture, AAA, and aortic dissection. Cauda equina symptoms = same-day MRI.
framing: Up to 90% of acute low back pain is non-specific and self-limits within 6 weeks. Imaging unnecessary unless red flags. The diagnostic task is to recognise the 1-2% with sinister cause early enough to prevent permanent neurological injury or to identify a vascular catastrophe.
keyHistory: Onset (sudden — fracture, AAA; gradual — discogenic, infection, malignancy)
Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, bowel disturbance, sexual dysfunction (cauda equina)
Weight loss, night pain, night sweats, history of cancer (metastatic disease)
Fever, IV drug use, recent infection, immunocompromise (spinal infection / epidural abscess)
Steroid use, age > 70, osteoporosis history (vertebral fracture)
Cardiovascular risk factors, sudden tearing pain to back (AAA, dissection)
keyExam: Palpation of spinous processes (tenderness suggests fracture, infection, malignancy)
Neurological exam of lower limbs (power, reflexes, sensation in dermatomes L2-S1)
Straight leg raise, cross straight leg raise
PR exam if cauda equina suspected (anal tone, perianal sensation)
Abdominal palpation for AAA (pulsatile expansile mass)

differential.pointers: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention (post-void residual > 200 mL), faecal incontinence, lax anal tone.
differential.investigation: Urgent (within hours) MRI spine. Neurosurgical emergency — operative decompression within 24-48 h preserves function.

differential.diagnosis: Spinal epidural abscess / discitis / vertebral osteomyelitis
differential.pointers: Severe localised pain, fever, neurological deficit, IV drug user, immunocompromised, recent bacteraemia. CRP elevated.
differential.investigation: MRI spine with contrast; blood cultures; FBC, CRP, ESR. URGENT spinal surgery / ID.

differential.pointers: Sudden onset, history of trauma (even minor), steroid use, age > 70, prior fracture, tenderness over spinous process.
differential.investigation: X-ray spine; MRI if neurological deficit / pathological suspected.

differential.pointers: Cancer history, progressive thoracic / lumbar pain, neurological deficit, sphincter disturbance.
differential.investigation: Urgent whole-spine MRI; dexamethasone 16 mg IV stat; oncology / spinal surgery.

differential.pointers: Sudden severe back / loin / abdominal pain in patient > 60, vascular risk factors; can mimic renal colic. Hypotension late.
differential.investigation: Bedside ultrasound abdominal aorta; CT angiogram. Vascular emergency.

differential.pointers: Sudden tearing chest + interscapular back pain; pulse deficit; new aortic regurgitation; widened mediastinum; SBP differential between arms.
Onset with movement, no neurological signs, normal exam, no red flags. Lumbar paraspinal spasm.
differential.investigation: None routinely; reassurance + early mobilisation + simple analgesia.

differential.pointers: Sciatica (L5/S1 distribution most common), positive straight leg raise, dermatomal sensory loss, motor weakness in single nerve root.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis; MRI if persistent > 6 weeks despite conservative or if progressive neurological deficit.

differential.pointers: Loin pain, fever (pyelo), haematuria (colic), nausea, vomiting.
differential.investigation: Urinalysis, U&E, CT KUB for stones, blood cultures + antibiotics for pyelo.

redFlags: Cauda equina symptoms (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary / bowel dysfunction)
Progressive neurological deficit (weakness, sensory loss in dermatomal distribution)
Fever / IV drug use / immunocompromise + back pain (spinal infection)
Weight loss / night pain / history of cancer (metastatic disease)
Trauma in osteoporotic patient / chronic steroid user
Sudden tearing back pain in patient with vascular risk factors (AAA / dissection)
initialInvestigations: Bladder scan / post-void residual if cauda equina suspected (> 200 mL is suspicious)
FBC, U&E, CRP, ESR if infection / malignancy suspected
Urgent MRI spine (same day) if cauda equina, spinal infection, or metastatic cord compression suspected
Bedside ultrasound abdominal aorta in any > 60 with sudden back / abdominal pain
disposition: Cauda equina → emergency neurosurgical referral + MRI same day. Spinal infection / metastatic compression → admission + urgent specialty. Mechanical low back pain with no red flags → simple analgesia, early mobilisation, NICE-style safety-net advice, GP follow-up if not resolving in 6 weeks.

references.label: NICE NG59 — Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s.
Greenhalgh S et al. Red flags for cauda equina syndrome. Manual Ther 2018.

chiefComplaint: Adult syncope / transient loss of consciousness
oneLiner: Distinguish reflex (vasovagal), orthostatic, cardiac, neurological. Cardiac syncope has high mortality — exertional / unprovoked / with abnormal ECG = admit. The Canadian Syncope Risk Score risk-stratifies ED disposition.
framing: Lifetime incidence ~ 35%. Most episodes are benign vasovagal; the diagnostic priority is excluding cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, structural disease, PE) which carries a 1-year mortality up to 30%.
keyHistory: Prodrome (warm, lightheaded, nausea, sweating — vasovagal; vs nothing — cardiac)
Position at onset (standing / lying / changing position)
Trigger (cough, micturition, prolonged standing, emotion, exertion)
Duration of LOC, post-event confusion (suggestive of seizure)
Associated chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea, neurological symptoms
Cardiac history, family history of sudden death, medications (QT-prolonging, antihypertensives)
Recent volume loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, blood loss)
keyExam: Vitals incl. postural BP (lying and standing 1 + 3 min)
Cardiovascular — heart sounds (aortic stenosis murmur), gallop, JVP, peripheral pulses, peripheral oedema

differential.pointers: Prodrome (lightheaded, nausea, sweating); trigger (emotion, pain, prolonged standing, micturition, cough); quick recovery; younger.
On standing; medication-induced (antihypertensives, diuretics, vasodilators); volume depletion; autonomic failure (Parkinson's, diabetes).

differential.diagnosis: Cardiac arrhythmia (brady — sinus, AV block; tachy — VT, SVT)
differential.pointers: No / minimal warning, exertional, in lying position, palpitations preceding, family history of sudden death.
differential.investigation: 12-lead ECG + telemetry; Holter if intermittent; loop recorder if intermittent and unexplained; ICD assessment if structural heart disease.

differential.diagnosis: Structural cardiac disease (aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ARVC, anomalous coronary)
differential.pointers: Exertional syncope, ejection systolic murmur, family history of sudden death.
Syncope with persistent hypoxia / RV strain on ECG / hypotension; VTE risk factors.
Tearing pain, pulse deficit, neurological signs.
Thunderclap headache, residual neurological signs, neck stiffness.
Diabetic on insulin / sulfonylurea; recent missed meal; rapid recovery with glucose.
differential.investigation: Bedside glucose at scene + on arrival.

differential.pointers: Tongue biting (lateral), incontinence, prolonged post-ictal confusion, witnessed tonic-clonic movement.
differential.investigation: Clinical; EEG / MRI brain if first seizure.

differential.pointers: Melaena, anaemia, anticoagulant use, prior PUD.
differential.investigation: Hb, group + screen, PR exam, OGD.

differential.pointers: Hypotension + abdominal pain; female of reproductive age with positive β-hCG.

redFlags: Family history of sudden cardiac death < 40
Abnormal ECG (long QT, Brugada, WPW, AV block, LVH, bradycardia)
initialInvestigations: β-hCG in any female of reproductive age
Bedside echo if structural disease / PE suspected
CT head if neurological signs or sudden severe headache
disposition: ADMIT: any high-risk feature (Canadian Syncope Risk Score). DISCHARGE: low-risk vasovagal with normal vitals, normal ECG, no red flags, safe to manage at home with written safety-net advice. INTERMEDIATE: observation unit / monitored bed for 6-24 h with telemetry.

references.label: Brignole M et al. 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope.
Thiruganasambandamoorthy V et al. Canadian Syncope Risk Score. CMAJ 2016.

oneLiner: Use a structured approach: AEIOUTIPS (Alcohol, Endocrine/Encephalopathy, Insulin, Opiates/Overdose, Uraemia, Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric/Poison, Stroke/Seizure/SAH). Glucose, oxygen, naloxone, thiamine — the 'coma cocktail'.
framing: Common presentation; the differential is vast and the order of investigation matters. Treatable + reversible causes first (glucose, opioid, thiamine), then structural, then metabolic. In older adults, delirium is often the FIRST sign of acute illness (UTI, pneumonia, AKI, MI).
keyHistory: Time course (sudden = vascular / hypoglycaemia / overdose; over hours = sepsis / hypoxia; over days = metabolic, delirium)
Recent illness, fever, focal symptoms (UTI in elderly common)
Alcohol or drug use; access to medications (overdose)
Trauma history (subdural, especially elderly on anticoagulants)
keyExam: ABC + vitals + SpO₂ + temp + bedside glucose
GCS or AVPU; pupillary response (pinpoint = opioid / pontine; mid-position fixed = midbrain; one dilated = uncal herniation)
Look for trauma signs (battle's, raccoon eyes, haemotympanum)

differential.pointers: Diabetes treated with insulin / sulfonylurea; missed meal; sweating, tremor, then confusion / coma.
Respiratory disease, COPD with type 2 failure, narcosis.
Miosis, bradypnoea, low GCS, track marks.
Sudden focal neurology; thunderclap headache (SAH); risk factors.
differential.investigation: Non-contrast CT brain; consider thrombolysis / thrombectomy.

differential.pointers: Trauma (even minor in elderly anticoagulated); thunderclap headache; declining GCS.
Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, focal seizures, immunocompromise.
differential.investigation: Antibiotics + aciclovir empirically before LP; CT then LP.

differential.pointers: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, raised lactate. Delirium often the only sign in elderly.
differential.investigation: Sepsis screen, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h.

differential.pointers: Chronic liver disease, asterixis, fetor hepaticus, raised ammonia, precipitated by GI bleed / infection / constipation / sedatives.
differential.investigation: Ammonia, LFTs, treat precipitant + lactulose + rifaximin.

differential.pointers: Known CKD or AKI, raised urea, asterixis, myoclonus.
Alcoholic / malnourished / hyperemesis / post-bariatric; triad confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia (often incomplete).
differential.investigation: TREAT EMPIRICALLY with IV thiamine (Pabrinex) for any alcoholic / malnourished with altered mental status; do not wait for confirmation.

differential.pointers: Specific toxidrome patterns; medication history.
Polyuria, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath (DKA); marked hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolar (HHS).
Confusion, seizures at Na < 120; thiazide use, SIADH, hypovolaemia, congestive failure.
differential.investigation: Na, paired serum + urine osmolality + urine Na.

differential.pointers: Witnessed seizure or unexplained confusion in known epilepsy.
differential.investigation: EEG if no improvement; consider benzodiazepine trial.

differential.pointers: Fluctuating, often worse at night; UTI, pneumonia, AKI, constipation, pain, polypharmacy.
differential.investigation: Look for precipitants — septic screen, urine, CXR, U&E, calcium, B12, TFT, drugs.

redFlags: Anticoagulant use + altered mental status (intracranial bleed)
initialInvestigations: Bedside glucose, GCS, SpO₂, vitals, temperature
ECG, FBC, U&E, LFTs, Ca, Mg, glucose, TFTs, CRP, lactate, ABG
Toxicology screen + paracetamol + salicylate + ethanol + ammonia + osmolality
CT brain if focal signs / declining GCS / trauma / on anticoagulant
LP if CNS infection suspected (after CT clear)
disposition: Admit. Coma cocktail empirically when relevant: oxygen, glucose, naloxone, thiamine. Address airway + ABC first. Resus / HDU level if GCS ≤ 8, refractory hypotension, status epilepticus, or unstable physiology. Senior + ICU input early.

references.label: NICE CG103 — Delirium: diagnosis, prevention and management.

oneLiner: Upper GI bleed until proven otherwise. Resuscitate first, score with Glasgow-Blatchford, endoscopy within 24 h (or sooner if unstable variceal).
framing: Mortality 5-10%, higher in variceal bleed and elderly comorbid patients. ABC first; transfusion targets restrictive (Hb 70 g/L) in non-massive bleed.
keyHistory: Volume and frequency of haematemesis (coffee-ground vs fresh blood)
Prior peptic ulcer, varices, liver disease, alcohol use
keyExam: Signs of chronic liver disease (jaundice, spider naevi, ascites, caput medusae, asterixis)

differential.pointers: NSAID/aspirin use, H. pylori, epigastric pain.
Chronic liver disease, ascites, jaundice.
differential.investigation: Urgent OGD; terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics; band ligation.

differential.pointers: Retching/vomiting then haematemesis; usually self-limits.
Reflux symptoms, NSAID, alcohol.
Weight loss, dysphagia, anaemia, age > 55.
Prior aortic graft; massive haemorrhage.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, coagulation, group and crossmatch
IV access x2 wide-bore, fluid resuscitation, transfusion to Hb > 70 g/L
OGD within 24 h (sooner if unstable or variceal)
disposition: Admit all. Resus / HDU if unstable. Glasgow-Blatchford 0 with normal Hb and no comorbidity may be considered for outpatient endoscopy per local protocol.

references.label: NICE CG141 — Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s.
BSG guidelines on management of acute upper GI bleeding.

oneLiner: Black tarry stool = upper GI bleed (usually). Resuscitate, score with Glasgow-Blatchford, endoscope within 24 h.
framing: Melaena implies blood transit ≥ 4 h, usually proximal to ligament of Treitz. Brisk lower GI bleed can also produce melaena. Mortality similar to overt haematemesis.
keyExam: PR exam — confirm true melaena (sticky, foul-smelling, black)

differential.pointers: NSAIDs, H. pylori, epigastric pain.
Liver disease, portal hypertension.
Weight loss, anaemia, age > 55.

differential.diagnosis: Brisk lower GI bleed (e.g. right colon)
differential.pointers: Negative OGD; haemodynamically significant.
Drug history; PR — not true melaena.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E (urea-creatinine ratio raised in UGIB), LFTs, coagulation, crossmatch
Colonoscopy / CT angiogram if OGD negative
disposition: Admit. Resus level if unstable. Glasgow-Blatchford 0 may be outpatient OGD.

references.label: NICE CG141 — Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

oneLiner: Distinguish from haematemesis and posterior epistaxis. Causes range from bronchitis to lung cancer to PE to TB; massive haemoptysis (> 200 mL in 24 h) is an airway emergency.
framing: TB endemic regions, malignancy in smokers > 40, bronchiectasis in chronic cough. Massive haemoptysis often arises from bronchial circulation; mortality from asphyxia.
keyHistory: Volume estimate (teaspoon vs cupful) and duration
Fever, weight loss, night sweats (TB, malignancy)
keyExam: Mouth and nasopharynx (rule out epistaxis source)
Respiratory exam — focal crackles, wheeze, consolidation
Cardiovascular — for mitral stenosis murmur, RV heave

differential.pointers: Cough, sputum, blood-streaked.
Chronic cough > 2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats, endemic region.
differential.investigation: CXR, sputum AFB / GeneXpert, HIV test.

differential.pointers: Smoker > 40, weight loss, persistent cough, clubbing.
Pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, VTE risk factors.
Chronic productive cough, recurrent infections.
Mid-diastolic murmur, RHF.
Pulmonary-renal syndrome, haematuria.

redFlags: Massive haemoptysis (> 200 mL/24 h or > 100 mL single episode)
initialInvestigations: Vitals, SpO₂, FBC, coagulation, group and screen
CTPA if PE suspected; CT chest with contrast otherwise
Sputum for AFB / GeneXpert / culture if TB suspected
Bronchoscopy if persistent or localisation needed
disposition: Massive haemoptysis → resus, position bleeding lung down, IR / thoracic surgery, intubation if airway compromise. Mild haemoptysis → CT chest, outpatient bronchoscopy if persistent. Isolate suspected TB.

references.label: BTS guideline for the investigation and management of haemoptysis.
WHO TB guidelines (sputum-positive haemoptysis).

oneLiner: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, with inattention. Always reversible cause: drugs, infection, metabolic, structural, withdrawal. Use 4AT or CAM.
framing: Affects up to 30% of medical inpatients > 65. Mortality 25-33%. Often the first sign of physical illness in older adults.
keyHistory: Time course (acute / subacute), fluctuation, time of day

differential.pointers: Most common precipitant in elderly.
Recent change or initiation.
Tremor, sweating, tachycardia, autonomic; history.
Lab abnormalities.
Resp disease, COPD.
Focal signs, head injury, falls on anticoagulant.
Easily missed reversible precipitants.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, Ca, Mg, CRP, TFT, B12, folate, glucose
CT brain if focal signs, fall, anticoagulant, declining GCS
disposition: Identify and treat precipitant; supportive care (orientation, hydration, mobilisation, sleep, pain). Avoid antipsychotics except for severe distress / risk. Admit until precipitant addressed.

references.label: NICE CG103 — Delirium: diagnosis, prevention and management.
SIGN 157 — Risk reduction and management of delirium.

oneLiner: Classical FUO: temperature > 38.3°C lasting > 3 weeks, no diagnosis after appropriate workup. Differential dominated by infection, malignancy, autoimmune.
framing: Durack-Street classification: classical, nosocomial, immunodeficient, HIV-associated. ~50% infection, 20% malignancy, 15% autoimmune, 15% miscellaneous or undiagnosed.
keyExam: Full systems exam (skin, lymph nodes, joints, heart, abdomen)
Stigmata of endocarditis (splinter haemorrhages, Janeway, Osler)

differential.pointers: New murmur, embolic phenomena, prosthetic valve, IVDU.
differential.investigation: Blood cultures x3 from separate sites; TTE then TOE.

differential.pointers: Endemic exposure, weight loss, HIV.
differential.investigation: CXR, sputum AFB, IGRA, CT, biopsy.

differential.pointers: Localising sign, prior surgery.
B-symptoms, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly.
differential.investigation: FBC, LDH, CT, lymph node biopsy.

differential.pointers: Hypernephroma, hepatoma.
Rash, arthralgia, ferritin > 10 000 in Still's; ESR > 50 in GCA.
Risk factors, oral thrush, weight loss.
Recent drug initiation; relative bradycardia.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, ESR, LDH, ferritin, blood film
CT chest/abdo/pelvis if no source after first-line
disposition: Stable ambulatory patients can be worked up as outpatient. Admit if septic, immunocompromised, rapid deterioration, or requiring invasive diagnostics.

references.label: Mulders-Manders C et al. Fever of unknown origin. Lancet 2015.
BMJ Best Practice — Fever of unknown origin.

oneLiner: Most viral and self-limiting. Identify dehydration, dysentery (bloody + fever), C. difficile risk, returning traveller, immunocompromised. Most do not need stool cultures.
framing: Acute diarrhoea < 14 days, mostly viral. Investigate if blood/mucus, persistent fever > 38.5, severe dehydration, recent antibiotics, immunocompromised, food handler / healthcare worker, traveller.
keyExam: Hydration: mucous membranes, skin turgor, urine output

differential.pointers: Watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low-grade fever, self-limits 1-3 days.

differential.diagnosis: Bacterial gastroenteritis (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli)
differential.pointers: Bloody diarrhoea, high fever, severe pain.
differential.investigation: Stool culture if bloody / severe / immunocompromised; avoid antibiotics in shiga-toxin E. coli.

differential.pointers: Recent antibiotics, hospital exposure, foul-smelling stool.
differential.investigation: Stool C. diff toxin/PCR; CT if severe.

differential.pointers: Recent travel, freshwater exposure.
Bloody diarrhoea > 4 weeks, weight loss, mucous discharge.
Older, vascular disease, sudden abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea.
Chronic diarrhoea + HIV.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, CRP, lactate if severe
Stool culture, O&P, C. diff toxin if indicated
AXR / CT if peritonism or toxic megacolon suspected
disposition: Mild: oral rehydration + safety-net. Moderate: IV fluids, observation. Admit if shock, bloody + septic, toxic megacolon, immunocompromised, pregnant, severe electrolyte derangement.

references.label: NICE CKS — Gastroenteritis.
IDSA 2017 guidelines for infectious diarrhoea.

oneLiner: Diarrhoea > 4 weeks. Distinguish inflammatory vs malabsorptive vs secretory vs functional. Red flags = colorectal cancer workup.
framing: Most are functional (IBS) in younger; in older, malignancy, IBD, microscopic colitis, coeliac, chronic pancreatitis, drug-induced.
keyHistory: Family history of IBD / coeliac / colorectal cancer

differential.pointers: Rome criteria; no red flags; abdominal pain relieved by defecation.
differential.investigation: Clinical after exclusion of organic causes.

differential.pointers: Bloody mucous diarrhoea, weight loss, extraintestinal features.
Age > 50, change in bowel habit > 6 weeks, PR bleeding, iron deficiency.
Steatorrhoea, weight loss, anaemia, dermatitis herpetiformis.
differential.investigation: Anti-tTG IgA + total IgA; duodenal biopsy.

differential.pointers: Watery diarrhoea, older women, autoimmune association, normal colonoscopy macroscopically.
Steatorrhoea, weight loss, alcohol, prior pancreatitis.
Weight loss, tremor, palpitations.
Post-cholecystectomy, terminal ileal disease.

redFlags: Age > 50 with new bowel habit change
Family history of colorectal cancer / IBD
initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, ferritin, B12, folate
Stool culture, O&P, C. diff if exposure
Colonoscopy with biopsies if any red flag
disposition: Outpatient workup. Refer to gastroenterology if red flags, suspected IBD, suspected malignancy.

references.label: BSG guidelines on the management of chronic diarrhoea.
NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral.

oneLiner: Identify dehydration, intracranial cause (raised ICP), GI obstruction, metabolic emergency (DKA, AKI, hypercalcaemia), pregnancy, drug-induced, surgical abdomen.
framing: Vomiting is a non-specific symptom with a broad differential. Bilious vomiting suggests obstruction distal to ampulla; faeculent vomiting suggests distal small bowel obstruction or gastrocolic fistula.
keyExam: Abdomen — distension, scars, hernias, peritonism, bowel sounds

differential.pointers: Diarrhoea, contacts, self-limiting.
Bilious / faeculent vomiting, distension, prior surgery, absolute constipation.
Headache worse on waking, projectile vomiting, neurology.
Diabetic, polyuria, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing.
Positive β-hCG, ketonuria, weight loss.
Epigastric pain radiating to back.
Older, diabetic, atypical presentation.
Medication history.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, lipase, CRP, ketones
disposition: IV fluids, antiemetic. Admit if dehydrated, surgical cause, metabolic emergency, severe electrolyte derangement, pregnancy with ketonuria.

references.label: NICE CKS — Nausea and vomiting.

oneLiner: Pre-hepatic (haemolysis) / hepatic / post-hepatic (obstruction). Painless jaundice + weight loss in older = pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise. Jaundice + fever + RUQ pain = cholangitis.
framing: Visible when bilirubin > 35-50 μmol/L. Differential split by conjugated vs unconjugated; LFT pattern (hepatocellular vs cholestatic) directs workup.
keyHistory: Alcohol intake, drug history (paracetamol, anti-TB, statins, amoxicillin-clavulanate)
Risk factors for hepatitis (IVDU, sexual, travel, blood products)
keyExam: Signs of CLD (palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, caput, ascites, splenomegaly)

differential.pointers: RUQ pain, fever, jaundice (Charcot's triad).
Painless jaundice + weight loss, palpable gallbladder.
Prodrome, transaminitis (ALT > 1000).
differential.investigation: Hep A IgM, HBsAg, anti-HCV, hep E IgM.

differential.pointers: Heavy alcohol use, tender hepatomegaly, AST:ALT > 2.
Paracetamol overdose, anti-TB, antibiotics.
Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, raised LDH, low haptoglobin.
differential.investigation: FBC, reticulocytes, blood film, DAT, LDH, haptoglobin.

differential.pointers: Young women (AIH), pruritus + alkaline phosphatase (PBC), IBD association (PSC).
Asymptomatic unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with fasting/illness.

redFlags: Painless jaundice + weight loss + palpable gallbladder
initialInvestigations: LFTs (conjugated vs unconjugated; hepatocellular vs cholestatic pattern)
MRCP for biliary obstruction; ERCP if therapeutic
disposition: Admit if cholangitis, acute liver failure, paracetamol overdose, severe alcoholic hepatitis, decompensated cirrhosis. Outpatient workup for stable jaundice with non-emergent imaging.

references.label: BSG guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests.
NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer recognition (pancreatic).

oneLiner: Septic arthritis is the must-not-miss — joint aspiration is mandatory. Gout, pseudogout, trauma, reactive arthritis are differential but cannot be assumed without aspirate.
framing: Acute hot swollen joint = septic until proven otherwise. Mortality 5-15% if missed; permanent joint destruction within days. Crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout) can coexist with sepsis.
keyHistory: Speed of onset (hours = crystal, sepsis, trauma; days = inflammatory)
Risk factors for sepsis (IVDU, immunosuppression, diabetes)
keyExam: Range of movement (markedly reduced in sepsis)

differential.pointers: Hot, red, exquisitely tender, severely restricted movement, fever; Staph aureus most common; gonococcal in young sexually active.
differential.investigation: Urgent joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics — Gram stain, culture, cell count (> 50 000 WCC suggestive); blood cultures.

differential.pointers: 1st MTP (podagra), foot, ankle, knee; rapid onset overnight; prior episodes; tophi; diuretics.
differential.investigation: Aspirate — negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals. Cannot exclude sepsis without culture.

differential.pointers: Knee, wrist; older; chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.
differential.investigation: Aspirate — positively birefringent rhomboid calcium pyrophosphate crystals.

differential.pointers: Preceding GI / GU infection 1-4 weeks earlier; conjunctivitis, urethritis (Reiter's triad).
Trauma, anticoagulant use, haemophilia.
Tick exposure, prior erythema migrans, knee involvement.

initialInvestigations: URGENT joint aspiration (BEFORE antibiotics) for Gram stain, culture, cell count, crystals
Blood cultures, FBC, U&E, CRP, ESR, urate, glucose
Empirical IV antibiotics covering Staph aureus pending culture if sepsis likely
disposition: Admit any acute hot joint pending aspirate. Suspected sepsis → urgent orthopaedic washout. Crystal arthritis with confirmed diagnosis, no sepsis features → outpatient treatment with NSAID / colchicine / steroids.

references.label: BSR / BHPR guideline for management of the hot swollen joint.
EULAR 2016 recommendations on the management of gout.

oneLiner: Multiple swollen joints. Distinguish inflammatory (RA, SLE, viral, reactive) from non-inflammatory (OA flare). Pattern (symmetrical small joint vs migratory vs additive) directs differential.
framing: Early inflammatory arthritis (RA) requires urgent referral — DMARD within 12 weeks prevents erosions. Migratory arthritis suggests rheumatic fever, gonococcal, Lyme. Symmetric small joint = RA / viral.
keyHistory: Duration of morning stiffness (> 30 min = inflammatory)
Rash, mouth ulcers, hair loss, photosensitivity
keyExam: Symmetrical small joints (MCP, PIP, wrist) — RA

differential.pointers: Symmetric small joint, morning stiffness > 1 h, RF + anti-CCP.
differential.investigation: RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP, hand X-rays. Refer rheumatology within 6 weeks.

differential.diagnosis: Viral arthritis (parvovirus, chikungunya, hepatitis B/C, EBV, rubella)
differential.pointers: Prodromal viral illness, self-limiting weeks; symmetric small joint.
Young women, malar rash, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, cytopenia, renal.
Psoriasis, nail pitting, dactylitis, DIP involvement.
Post-GI/GU infection 1-4 weeks earlier, asymmetric large joint, enthesitis.
Young sexually active, migratory, tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions.
differential.investigation: Joint aspirate, urethral/cervical NAAT, blood cultures.

differential.pointers: Recent strep throat, migratory large joint, carditis, chorea, rash.
differential.investigation: ASO, anti-DNase B, ECG, echo (Jones criteria).

initialInvestigations: Viral serology if acute prodromal illness
Joint aspirate if any joint hot/effusion
disposition: Urgent rheumatology referral for suspected early inflammatory arthritis (< 6 weeks). Septic / gonococcal / SLE flare → admit. NSAID + analgesia + safety-net pending review.

references.label: NICE NG100 — Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management.
EULAR recommendations for the management of early arthritis.

oneLiner: Sudden painless monocular loss → vascular (CRAO, CRVO, ischaemic optic neuropathy, GCA, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment). Painful loss → optic neuritis, acute angle closure, GCA. Time-critical.
framing: CRAO has a treatment window of hours. GCA causes permanent blindness if steroids delayed. Acute angle closure is irreversible if unrelieved.
keyHistory: Pain (painless vascular vs painful optic neuritis / glaucoma)
Field defect (curtain — RD; central — macular / optic nerve; altitudinal — AION)
Headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness (GCA, age > 50)
keyExam: Fundoscopy (cherry-red spot CRAO; haemorrhages CRVO; pale disc AION; detached retina)
Slit lamp (red eye, cell, hypopyon, fixed mid-dilated pupil — AAC)

differential.pointers: Sudden painless severe monocular loss; cherry-red spot; pale retina; RAPD.
differential.investigation: Same-day ophthalmology + stroke pathway (TIA equivalent). Consider ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis as bridge.

differential.diagnosis: Giant cell arteritis with arteritic AION
differential.pointers: Age > 50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, ESR > 50, pale swollen disc.
differential.investigation: ESR, CRP, IV methylprednisolone IMMEDIATELY; temporal artery biopsy / US.

differential.pointers: Sudden painless loss; flame haemorrhages and disc oedema ('blood and thunder').
differential.investigation: Ophthalmology; vascular risk factor management; anti-VEGF for macular oedema.

differential.pointers: Flashes + floaters → curtain over vision; myopia, trauma.
Diabetic retinopathy, sudden floaters and reduced vision.
Painful red eye, halos around lights, nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, high IOP.
differential.investigation: IOP; emergency ophthalmology — acetazolamide IV, topical pilocarpine, beta-blocker, laser iridotomy.

differential.pointers: Younger, painful eye movement, central scotoma, dyschromatopsia; MS association.
Binocular field loss, preserved pupillary reflex.

redFlags: Painful red eye with halos and nausea (AAC)
initialInvestigations: Visual acuity, pupillary response, fields, fundoscopy
CT/MRI brain if cortical / chiasmal pattern
disposition: Same-day ophthalmology for any sudden vision loss. Treat GCA with high-dose steroid before biopsy if visual symptoms. AAC → emergency ophthalmology + IOP-lowering. CRAO → stroke pathway.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists guidance on acute vision loss.
BSR GCA guidelines 2020.

oneLiner: Most are benign (conjunctivitis, subconjunctival haemorrhage). Sight-threatening = acute angle closure, anterior uveitis, scleritis, keratitis, endophthalmitis. Pain + photophobia + reduced acuity = refer.
framing: Distinguish benign from sight-threatening by pain, vision, photophobia, pupil, ciliary flush. Contact lens wearer with red eye = bacterial keratitis until proven otherwise.
keyHistory: Pain (mild gritty = conjunctivitis; deep severe = uveitis, scleritis, AAC)
Discharge (purulent — bacterial; watery — viral; itchy — allergic)
keyExam: Pattern of redness (diffuse — conjunctivitis; ciliary flush — uveitis, keratitis; sectoral — episcleritis)
Pupil (fixed mid-dilated AAC; constricted irregular uveitis)

differential.pointers: Watery discharge, recent URTI, pre-auricular node, highly contagious.
Purulent discharge, eyelids stuck.
Itchy, watery, bilateral, atopy.
Severe pain, halos, nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, high IOP, hazy cornea.
Photophobia, ciliary flush, constricted irregular pupil, cells in anterior chamber.
Contact lens wearer, severe pain, photophobia, corneal opacity, hypopyon.
Dendritic ulcer on fluorescein, reduced corneal sensation.
Deep boring pain wakes from sleep, blue-violet hue, associated systemic disease.
differential.investigation: Systemic workup (RA, vasculitis, IBD); systemic NSAIDs / steroids.

differential.pointers: Painless, well-demarcated bright red patch, no vision change.

initialInvestigations: Visual acuity, slit lamp, fluorescein, IOP
Refer ophthalmology if any red flag
Topical chloramphenicol for uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis
disposition: Benign conjunctivitis → outpatient with safety-net. AAC, keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis → same-day ophthalmology. Chemical injury → irrigate immediately for 30 min before assessment.

references.label: NICE CKS — Red eye.
RCOphth red eye flow charts.

oneLiner: Distinguish peripheral (BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere's) from central (posterior stroke) using HINTS exam in acute vestibular syndrome. Sudden vertigo + neurological signs = posterior stroke until proven otherwise.
framing: Acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo > 24 h) — HINTS exam more sensitive than MRI in first 48 h. Episodic positional = BPPV. Episodic with hearing = Meniere's.
keyHistory: Character (true spinning vs lightheaded vs unsteady)
Duration (seconds — BPPV; minutes-hours — Meniere's, TIA; days — neuritis, stroke)
keyExam: HINTS in acute vestibular syndrome (Head Impulse, Nystagmus pattern, Test of Skew)

differential.pointers: Seconds, positional, fatigable upbeating-torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike.
Acute continuous vertigo days, post-viral, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, normal hearing (neuritis) vs hearing loss (labyrinthitis).
differential.investigation: Clinical + HINTS reassuring (positive head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus, no skew).

differential.pointers: Vascular risk factors, central HINTS (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation), other neurology.
differential.investigation: MRI with DWI; CTA posterior circulation.

differential.pointers: Episodic vertigo 20 min - 24 h with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness.
Episodic vertigo with migraine features; prior migraine history.
Medication history.

redFlags: Other neurological signs (dysarthria, diplopia, dysphagia, ataxia)
initialInvestigations: Bedside neuro exam + HINTS in acute vestibular syndrome
MRI with DWI if central features
disposition: BPPV — Epley + discharge. Vestibular neuritis — antiemetic, vestibular rehab. Central features — admit, MRI, stroke pathway.

references.label: Kattah JC et al. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome. Stroke 2009.
Bhattacharyya N et al. Clinical practice guideline: BPPV (update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017.

oneLiner: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency — treat within 14 days with oral steroids. Pulsatile tinnitus = vascular cause workup.
framing: Sudden SNHL (> 30 dB across 3 frequencies in < 3 days) — most idiopathic, but exclude vascular, infective, autoimmune, vestibular schwannoma. Outcomes better if treated early.
keyExam: Auscultation over neck and ear (pulsatile tinnitus — bruit)

differential.pointers: Sudden unilateral SNHL; exclusion diagnosis.
differential.investigation: Audiometry within days; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 7-14 days; MRI to exclude schwannoma.

differential.pointers: Progressive unilateral SNHL ± tinnitus, vertigo, facial numbness.
Conductive loss, otoscopy.
Recent URTI, conductive loss, effusion behind TM.
Occupational, gradual, bilateral, high-frequency.

differential.diagnosis: Pulsatile tinnitus — vascular (carotid stenosis, dural AVF, glomus tumour, idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
differential.pointers: Synchronous with heartbeat; bruit on auscultation.

disposition: Sudden SNHL — start oral steroids same day and refer ENT within 24-48 h. Asymmetric SNHL — MRI. Pulsatile — vascular imaging.

references.label: ENT UK / RCEM guidance on sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
AAO-HNSF clinical practice guideline — sudden hearing loss (update 2019).

oneLiner: Identify life-threatening (SJS/TEN, DRESS, anaphylaxis with urticaria, meningococcaemia, necrotising fasciitis) early. Mucosal involvement, skin pain, systemic features = red flags.
framing: Most rashes benign and viral / drug. Three life-threatening dermatological emergencies: SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP. Plus systemic infections (meningococcaemia, RMSF, necrotising soft tissue infection).
keyHistory: Recent new medication (1-8 weeks for SJS/TEN/DRESS)

differential.pointers: Drug 1-4 weeks prior (allopurinol, lamotrigine, anti-epileptics, sulfa, NSAIDs); painful red skin, target lesions, mucosal erosions, Nikolsky positive.
differential.investigation: SCORTEN; stop offending drug; transfer to burns / specialist centre; supportive care.

differential.diagnosis: DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
differential.pointers: Drug 2-8 weeks prior; rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hepatitis.
differential.investigation: FBC (eosinophilia), LFTs, U&E; stop drug; oral steroids.

differential.pointers: Sudden urticaria + angioedema + wheeze / hypotension within minutes-hours.
Non-blanching purpura, fever, shock.
differential.investigation: Empirical IV ceftriaxone immediately; blood cultures, PCR.

differential.pointers: Severe pain out of proportion, dusky / purple / bullous skin, systemic toxicity.
differential.investigation: LRINEC; urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum antibiotics.

differential.pointers: Wheals < 24 h, pruritus, food / drug / infection trigger.
Prodrome, generalised maculopapular rash.
New drug, generalised maculopapular, self-limits.
Unilateral, hot, tender, sharply demarcated.

initialInvestigations: Skin biopsy if SJS/TEN, DRESS, vasculitis
disposition: Admit any rash with mucosal involvement, systemic toxicity, suspected SJS/TEN/DRESS, meningococcaemia, necrotising fasciitis. Refer derm urgently.

references.label: BAD guidelines on the management of SJS/TEN.
Husain Z et al. DRESS syndrome. JAAD 2013.

oneLiner: Generalised pruritus without primary rash — exclude systemic cause: cholestasis, uraemia, haematological (lymphoma, polycythaemia), thyroid, HIV, iron deficiency, drug-induced.
framing: Itch without rash > 6 weeks deserves systemic workup. Aquagenic itch — polycythaemia. Nocturnal — lymphoma. Cholestatic — primary biliary cholangitis.
keyHistory: Cholestatic symptoms (jaundice, pale stool, dark urine)

differential.pointers: Cholestatic LFTs.
CKD, dialysis.
Aquagenic itch, plethoric, splenomegaly, raised Hb.
B-symptoms, lymphadenopathy.
Pallor, fatigue.
Thyroid symptoms.
Risk factors, prurigo nodularis.
Medication history.
Older, dry skin; atopy.

initialInvestigations: FBC + film, ESR, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, ferritin, LDH
disposition: Outpatient workup; topical emollients + non-sedating antihistamine for symptomatic relief; address underlying cause.

references.label: BAD guidelines on the management of chronic pruritus.

oneLiner: ALWAYS pathological. Cardiac syncope — aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary, arrhythmia, massive PE — until proven otherwise. Admit, cardiology, echo.
framing: Exertional syncope carries up to 30% one-year cardiac mortality if untreated. Family history of sudden cardiac death age < 40 = inherited cardiomyopathy / channelopathy.
keyHistory: Family history of sudden cardiac death < 40
keyExam: Murmur changes with Valsalva (HCM increases, AS decreases)

differential.pointers: Older, ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids, slow rising pulse.
Young athlete, family history, ejection murmur louder with Valsalva.
differential.investigation: Echo, cardiac MRI, ECG (LVH, Q waves).

differential.pointers: Young, exertional symptoms.
Prior MI, cardiomyopathy.
Family history, exertion (CPVT), abnormal ECG.
Hypoxia, RV strain.

initialInvestigations: Cardiac MRI if HCM / ARVC suspected
disposition: Admit for cardiology workup. Restrict driving and exertion until diagnosis established. ICD assessment if structural cause confirmed.

references.label: ESC 2018 guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope.

oneLiner: Distinguish benign sinus tachycardia / ectopics from pathological arrhythmias (AF, SVT, VT). ECG during symptoms is the diagnostic gold standard; ambulatory ECG if intermittent.
framing: Common ED and primary care presentation. Risk-stratify by structural heart disease, syncope, family history of SCD. Capture rhythm during symptoms if possible.
keyHistory: Onset (sudden — SVT, VT; gradual — sinus, anxiety)
Rate, regularity (regular — SVT, sinus, atrial flutter; irregular — AF, ectopics)

differential.diagnosis: Sinus tachycardia (anxiety, exercise, fever, anaemia, hyperthyroidism, PE)
differential.pointers: Gradual, identifiable trigger.
differential.investigation: FBC, TFTs, CRP, ECG; identify underlying cause.

differential.pointers: Irregularly irregular pulse; older, hypertension, valvular.
differential.investigation: ECG; CHA₂DS₂-VASc; rate / rhythm control + anticoagulation.

differential.pointers: Sudden on/off, regular narrow-complex, young.
differential.investigation: ECG (delta wave WPW); vagal manoeuvres / adenosine; EP referral.

differential.pointers: Broad-complex regular tachycardia, history of structural heart disease, syncope.
differential.investigation: ECG, echo, EP referral; ICD assessment.

differential.pointers: Worse at rest, often benign.
differential.investigation: ECG, Holter; reassure if structurally normal.

differential.pointers: Weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance.
Paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating.

initialInvestigations: Ambulatory ECG (Holter, patch, loop recorder) for intermittent symptoms
disposition: Symptomatic arrhythmia or red flags → admit. Stable benign palpitations → outpatient ambulatory ECG; reassure + lifestyle advice.

references.label: NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management.
ESC 2019 guidelines for the management of SVT.

oneLiner: DVT until proven otherwise. Use Wells score + D-dimer + ultrasound. Differential: cellulitis, ruptured Baker's cyst, calf muscle haematoma, lymphoedema, post-thrombotic syndrome.
framing: Untreated DVT can embolise. Cellulitis is often misdiagnosed as DVT and vice versa. Ruptured Baker's cyst mimics DVT closely.
keyHistory: VTE risk factors (immobility, surgery, malignancy, OCP / HRT / pregnancy, prior VTE, family history)
keyExam: Circumference difference > 3 cm (calf 10 cm below tibial tuberosity)

differential.pointers: Wells score; calf swelling > 3 cm; pitting oedema; collateral veins.
differential.investigation: Wells + D-dimer if Wells ≤ 1; duplex ultrasound.

differential.pointers: Erythema with sharp margins, warmth, fever, entry portal.
Sudden calf pain, bruising posterior leg, prior knee arthritis.
Trauma, sudden tearing pain.
Pitting initially → non-pitting; pelvic / inguinal malignancy or post-surgery.
Tender erythematous palpable vein.
Severe pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, neurovascular compromise.

redFlags: Suspected compartment syndrome (severe pain, tense, neurovascular)
initialInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound proximal venous if Wells ≥ 2 or D-dimer positive
disposition: DVT → anticoagulation (DOAC first line in most). Cellulitis → antibiotics, admission if sepsis. Compartment syndrome → emergency orthopaedics.

references.label: NICE NG158 — Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing.

oneLiner: Differential: heart failure, venous insufficiency, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia (liver), drug-induced (CCB, NSAID), lymphoedema. Assess JVP, urine dipstick, LFT.
framing: Common in older adults. Distinguish systemic (HF, renal, hepatic, drugs) from mechanical (venous insufficiency, lymphoedema). Acute bilateral with breathlessness = heart failure or bilateral DVT.

differential.pointers: Raised JVP, pulmonary crackles, S3 gallop, dyspnoea.
Varicose veins, haemosiderin staining, worse at end of day.
Frothy urine, proteinuria > 3 g, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia.
differential.investigation: Urinalysis, urine PCR, albumin, lipids, renal biopsy.

differential.pointers: Ascites, jaundice, signs of CLD.
Medication history.
COPD, sleep apnoea, raised JVP, RV heave.
Cancer, dilated abdominal veins.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, albumin, BNP, TFTs
ECG, CXR, echo if HF suspected
USS abdomen / CT if hepatic / IVC concern
disposition: Treat underlying cause. Compression therapy and elevation for venous insufficiency. Admit if acute decompensated HF, nephrotic syndrome with complications, anasarca.

references.label: NICE NG106 — Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management.

oneLiner: Testicular torsion until proven otherwise. 6-hour window for testicular salvage. Do NOT delay surgical exploration for imaging if clinical suspicion is high.
framing: Most common in adolescents and young adults, but also occurs in neonates and older men. Torsion of testicular appendage and epididymo-orchitis are the main mimics.

differential.pointers: Sudden severe pain, nausea, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric, age 12-25.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis — urgent surgical exploration; do not delay for Doppler unless equivocal.

differential.pointers: Gradual onset, dysuria, urethral discharge, fever, Prehn positive.
Younger boys, less severe pain, blue dot sign.
Tender irreducible mass, vomiting, obstruction.
Diabetic / immunocompromised, severe pain, crepitus, systemic toxicity.
Painless mass with sudden pain on bleeding.

redFlags: Sudden severe pain in adolescent / young adult
initialInvestigations: Clinical assessment first — urgent urology if torsion suspected
Doppler ultrasound only if equivocal AND will not delay surgery
disposition: Suspected torsion → emergency surgical exploration. Confirmed epididymitis → outpatient antibiotics (cover STI in young, gram-negatives in older). Fournier's → ICU + surgical + broad antibiotics.

references.label: EAU guidelines on urological emergencies.
BAUS guidance on testicular torsion.

oneLiner: Painful inability to void with palpable bladder. Common in older men (BPH) — catheterise + investigate cause. Painless retention with overflow = chronic; assess for AKI.
framing: Acute retention is painful; chronic painless. Decompression haematuria and post-obstructive diuresis common after catheterisation of chronic retention.
keyExam: PR (prostate size, anal tone, perianal sensation)

differential.pointers: Older man, LUTS history, enlarged smooth prostate.
differential.investigation: Bladder scan; catheterise; PSA after acute episode (not during).

differential.pointers: Dysuria, fever, tender prostate.
Back pain, bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, lax anal tone.
Recent drug.
Loaded rectum.
Difficulty catheterising; haematuria; flank pain.

initialInvestigations: Bladder scan + catheterisation (urethral; suprapubic if urethral fails)
PSA only at follow-up, not during acute retention
MRI spine if cauda equina suspected
disposition: Catheterise + TWOC trial. Admit if AKI, sepsis, haemodynamically unstable, cauda equina suspected. Outpatient urology follow-up for BPH workup.

references.label: NICE CG97 — Lower urinary tract symptoms in men.
BAUS guidance on acute urinary retention.

oneLiner: Visible (macroscopic) haematuria in adults > 45 = urological malignancy until proven otherwise. Non-visible needs risk-stratified workup. Painless = malignancy; painful = stone, infection, glomerular.
framing: Bladder cancer detected in ~20% of adults > 60 with visible haematuria. NICE 2-week-wait referral for any visible haematuria > 45 or any unexplained > 60. Glomerular causes important in younger.
keyHistory: Visible (clots — bladder; tea-coloured — glomerular) vs non-visible
Recent infection, sore throat (post-streptococcal GN), IgA nephropathy

differential.pointers: Painless visible haematuria, smoker, age > 50.
Haematuria, flank pain, palpable mass (classic triad, rare).
Dysuria, frequency, fever, flank pain.
Loin to groin pain in waves; restless patient.
Older man, LUTS.
Tea-coloured urine, casts, proteinuria, hypertension, recent infection.
differential.investigation: Urine microscopy (RBC casts), urine PCR, complement, ANCA, anti-GBM, ASO; renal biopsy.

differential.pointers: On warfarin / DOAC; usually still investigate.
differential.investigation: INR; still proceed with urological workup.

initialInvestigations: Urinalysis, urine M,C&S, urine PCR / ACR
Cystoscopy + CT urogram for urological haematuria
Renal biopsy if glomerular pattern (RBC casts, proteinuria)
disposition: 2-week-wait urology referral for visible haematuria > 45 or unexplained > 60. Nephrology referral for glomerular features. UTI / stone treat appropriately.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (urological cancers).

oneLiner: Renal / ureteric colic is most common, but ALWAYS exclude AAA in patients > 60. Pyelonephritis with obstruction is a urological emergency. Tumour, vascular, MSK causes also considered.
framing: 30% of AAA ruptures are misdiagnosed as renal colic — bedside aortic ultrasound in any patient > 60 with flank pain. Pyelonephritis + obstruction = decompression.
keyHistory: Onset, character (colicky waves — stone; constant — pyelo, AAA)

differential.pointers: Age > 60, sudden pain, hypotension, pulsatile expansile mass; classically misdiagnosed as stone.
differential.investigation: Bedside aortic ultrasound; CT angiogram if stable.

differential.pointers: Colicky loin-to-groin pain, restless, haematuria.
Fever, rigors, CVA tenderness, urinary symptoms.
differential.investigation: Urinalysis + culture, blood cultures, USS for obstruction.

differential.pointers: Stone + infection + sepsis = urological emergency.
AF, embolic source, sudden flank pain, raised LDH.
Reproducible on palpation, trauma history.

initialInvestigations: CT KUB (low-dose for stones, with contrast if AAA/infarct suspected)
disposition: AAA → vascular emergency. Pyelonephritis → admit if septic / vomiting / obstruction. Uncomplicated stone < 5 mm → discharge with analgesia + safety-net. Obstruction + infection → urological emergency.

references.label: EAU guidelines on urolithiasis.
NICE NG118 — Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management.

oneLiner: Meningitis until proven otherwise if febrile. Differential: SAH, cervical disc, trauma, retropharyngeal abscess, torticollis. Photophobia + fever + altered mental status = empirical antibiotics within 1 h.
framing: Meningitis has a narrow time window — antibiotics within 1 h of suspicion. SAH presents with thunderclap headache and may have neck stiffness from meningism. Trauma must be excluded before manipulation.

differential.pointers: Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status.
differential.investigation: Blood cultures + LP (after CT if focal / immunocompromised); empirical IV ceftriaxone + aciclovir within 1 h.

differential.pointers: Thunderclap headache.
differential.investigation: Non-contrast CT brain ± LP for xanthochromia.

differential.pointers: Trauma; immobilise.
Recent ENT infection, drooling, trismus, neck swelling.
differential.investigation: CT neck with contrast; ENT emergency.

differential.pointers: Radicular pain, no systemic features.
Recent drug, sustained abnormal posture.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, CRP, coagulation, blood cultures
LP if meningitis (after CT clear) — do not delay antibiotics
CT neck if deep space infection suspected
disposition: Admit. Meningitis → empirical antibiotics + LP. SAH → neurosurgery. Trauma → spine team. Retropharyngeal abscess → ENT emergency.

references.label: NICE NG240 — Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease: recognition, diagnosis and management.

oneLiner: Most are viral URTI. Identify pneumonia (tachypnoea + recession), asthma (wheeze + variability), foreign body (sudden onset + unilateral signs), pertussis (paroxysmal + whoop), TB (chronic > 2 weeks).
framing: Tachypnoea is the most sensitive sign of pneumonia in children (WHO age-band cut-offs). Sudden choking + unilateral wheeze = foreign body until proven otherwise.
keyExam: Auscultation — wheeze, crackles (focal vs bilateral), reduced air entry

differential.pointers: Coryza, low-grade fever, self-limits.
Tachypnoea (WHO cut-off), focal crackles, recession, fever.
differential.investigation: Clinical ± CXR if uncertain; FBC, CRP if unwell.

differential.pointers: Wheeze, atopy, recurrent episodes, family history.
Sudden choking + unilateral wheeze / reduced air entry; toddler.
Paroxysmal cough + inspiratory whoop + post-tussive vomiting; under-vaccinated.
Chronic cough > 2 weeks, weight loss, contact history.
differential.investigation: CXR, gastric aspirates / induced sputum, Mantoux, IGRA.

differential.pointers: Coryza, wheeze, crackles, RSV season.

initialInvestigations: CXR if focal signs or uncertain
disposition: Admit if respiratory distress, hypoxia, poor feeding, age < 3 months with significant cough, suspected FB / pertussis / TB / severe pneumonia. Most viral URTI managed at home with safety-netting.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s.
BTS guideline on community-acquired pneumonia in children.

oneLiner: Inspiratory stridor = upper airway. Croup most common; do NOT examine throat if suspecting epiglottitis / bacterial tracheitis / foreign body — call senior + anaesthetics. Anaphylaxis = adrenaline IM.
framing: Upper airway emergency. Keep child calm, avoid distress, do not lie flat. Definitive airway management in theatre if epiglottitis / bacterial tracheitis suspected.
keyHistory: Onset (sudden — FB, anaphylaxis; over hours — croup, bacterial tracheitis)
keyExam: Voice character (muffled — epiglottitis; barking — croup; hoarse — laryngeal)
Do NOT inspect throat if epiglottitis suspected

differential.pointers: 6 months - 6 years, barking cough, hoarse, low-grade fever; Westley score.
differential.investigation: Clinical; oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; nebulised adrenaline if severe.

differential.pointers: Toxic, drooling, tripoding, muffled voice, no cough; under-vaccinated.
differential.investigation: Keep calm, anaesthetic + ENT; IV ceftriaxone after airway secured.

differential.pointers: Toxic, high fever, no response to croup treatment, purulent secretions.
differential.investigation: Bronchoscopy + IV antibiotics; often needs intubation.

differential.pointers: Sudden choking; toddler; intermittent stridor.
Rapid onset, urticaria, angioedema, hypotension; food / drug trigger.
Neck stiffness, dysphagia, fever; younger children.

redFlags: Failure to respond to croup therapy
initialInvestigations: Anaesthetics + ENT in theatre if airway threat
disposition: Mild croup → oral dexamethasone, home. Moderate-severe croup → nebulised adrenaline + dex + observation. Suspected epiglottitis / bacterial tracheitis → theatre with senior anaesthetist + ENT. Anaphylaxis → adrenaline IM + admission.

references.label: NICE CKS — Croup.
APLS / RCPCH paediatric airway emergency guidance.

oneLiner: Bronchiolitis < 1 yr; viral-induced wheeze / asthma > 1 yr. Anaphylaxis and foreign body must be excluded. Silent chest = pre-arrest.
framing: Bronchiolitis in infants — supportive care; bronchodilators not routinely effective. Asthma / viral wheeze — bronchodilator + steroid for severe. Sudden unilateral wheeze = foreign body.

differential.pointers: Infant, coryza, wheeze, crackles, poor feeding, RSV season.
differential.investigation: Clinical; supportive care; oxygen, NG feeding if needed.

differential.pointers: > 1 year, recurrent episodes, atopy.
differential.investigation: PEFR if able; bronchodilator + oral steroid.

differential.pointers: Sudden onset with allergen, urticaria, hypotension.
Sudden onset + unilateral wheeze + choking history.
Congenital heart disease, hepatomegaly, gallop.

initialInvestigations: PEFR if able and old enough
CXR if focal signs / unusual / first episode
Bronchiolitis — supportive care, NPA only if clinically useful
disposition: Mild — discharge with bronchodilator advice + safety-net. Moderate-severe — admit; severe / silent chest → resus + senior + PICU. FB suspected → bronchoscopy.

references.label: NICE NG9 — Bronchiolitis in children.
BTS / SIGN British asthma guideline.

oneLiner: Recognise early — RR, recession, grunting, accessory muscles, SpO₂. Differential by age: bronchiolitis (infant), pneumonia, asthma, foreign body, anaphylaxis, cardiac failure, sepsis, DKA.
framing: Children compensate well, then decompensate suddenly. Bradycardia + bradypnoea + exhaustion = pre-arrest.
keyExam: Work of breathing — recession, flaring, grunting

differential.pointers: Infant with coryza, wheeze, crackles.
Fever, focal signs.
Wheeze, prior history.
Sudden, unilateral.
Sudden + allergen + urticaria.
Cyanotic / acyanotic CHD, hepatomegaly, gallop.
Fever, mottled, prolonged CRT.
Kussmaul breathing, polyuria, dehydration.
Neonatal / infant, vomiting, lethargy.

initialInvestigations: Vitals by age + SpO₂ + bedside glucose
FBC, CRP, blood cultures, lactate, ABG / VBG
disposition: Resuscitation first — airway, oxygen, IV access, fluid if shock. Identify and treat underlying cause. PICU early if severe.

references.label: APLS — Advanced Paediatric Life Support.

oneLiner: Most viral gastroenteritis. Must-not-miss: intussusception (under 2), pyloric stenosis (4-8 weeks), bowel obstruction, raised ICP, DKA, sepsis. Bilious vomiting in infant = malrotation until proven otherwise.
framing: Age-related differential: neonate (sepsis, GI atresia, malrotation, inborn errors); infant (reflux, pyloric stenosis, intussusception); child (gastroenteritis, UTI, raised ICP, DKA).
keyExam: Abdomen — distension, masses (sausage in intussusception, olive in pyloric stenosis), peritonism

differential.pointers: Diarrhoea, contacts, self-limits.
