4-8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry after feeds, olive in epigastrium, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis.
6 months - 2 years, intermittent severe pain (drawing up legs), redcurrant jelly stool, sausage-shaped mass.
Neonate / infant with bilious vomiting; surgical emergency.
differential.investigation: Upper GI contrast study; urgent surgical.

differential.pointers: Fever, vomiting can be only symptom in infants.
Morning vomiting, headache, neurology, bulging fontanelle.
Polyuria, dehydration, Kussmaul.
Lethargy, fever, vomiting in infant.
Infant, posseting, otherwise well, gaining weight.

initialInvestigations: Abdominal USS if intussusception / pyloric stenosis
Upper GI contrast study if bilious vomiting infant
disposition: Mild gastroenteritis → ORS + safety-net. Severe dehydration → IV fluids + admission. Suspected surgical / malrotation / DKA / sepsis / raised ICP → urgent specialty.

references.label: NICE CG84 — Diarrhoea and vomiting in children.

oneLiner: Most viral and self-limits. Assess hydration carefully (NICE / WHO IMCI). ORS first-line; IV if shock or failed oral; investigate if bloody / persistent / immunocompromised.
framing: Worldwide a leading cause of under-5 mortality. Plan A (no dehydration), B (some), C (severe with shock) per IMCI. Continue feeding; zinc supplementation; avoid antiemetics under 5 except ondansetron in specific contexts.
keyExam: Hydration (sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, skin turgor, CRT, fontanelle, urine output, mental status)

differential.pointers: Watery diarrhoea, vomiting, contacts.
differential.investigation: Clinical; stool PCR if outbreak / immunocompromised.

differential.diagnosis: Bacterial gastroenteritis (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli)
differential.pointers: Bloody mucous stool, fever, abdominal pain.
differential.investigation: Stool culture; avoid antibiotics in suspected EHEC (HUS risk).

differential.pointers: Bloody diarrhoea then anaemia, AKI, thrombocytopenia.
differential.investigation: FBC, blood film, U&E, LDH, urinalysis.

differential.pointers: Intermittent severe pain, redcurrant jelly.
Polyuria, Kussmaul.
Chronic diarrhoea, faltering growth.
Infant, bloody mucous stool, vomiting, eczema.

redFlags: Severe dehydration (sunken fontanelle, no tears, lethargy)
Persistent vomiting unable to tolerate oral
initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LDH, urinalysis if HUS suspected
Stool culture if bloody / persistent / outbreak / immunocompromised
disposition: No dehydration → ORS + continue feeding + safety-net. Some dehydration → ORS in ED with observation. Severe / shock / failed oral → IV fluids + admission.

references.label: NICE CG84 — Diarrhoea and vomiting in children under 5.
WHO IMCI guidelines.

oneLiner: Broad differential by age. Must-not-miss: intussusception, malrotation with volvulus, appendicitis, testicular torsion, DKA, HSP, pneumonia (referred pain). Children often present atypically.
framing: Appendicitis is the most common surgical cause in children > 4. Always examine the testes in boys. Consider DKA in any unwell child with abdominal pain.
keyHistory: Site, character, migration (periumbilical → RIF in appendicitis)
keyExam: Skin (HSP purpura on buttocks / lower limbs)

differential.pointers: RIF tenderness, migration, fever, anorexia.
Recent URTI, RIF tenderness, fever — mimics appendicitis.
Diarrhoea, vomiting.
Fever, dysuria, abdominal pain in young.
6 months - 2 years, intermittent severe pain, redcurrant jelly.
Bilious vomiting, neonate / infant.
Adolescent boy with abdominal pain — examine testes.
Polyuria, vomiting, Kussmaul.
Palpable purpura on buttocks/legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, haematuria.
Fever, cough, tachypnoea.
Hard stool palpable, infrequent bowel motions.

redFlags: Severe pain with normal exam (early appendicitis)
initialInvestigations: Surgical review if surgical cause suspected
disposition: Surgical / DKA / torsion → admit urgent specialty. Mild gastroenteritis / constipation → discharge with safety-net. Uncertain → observation period.

references.label: RCPCH care pathway for abdominal pain in children.

oneLiner: Non-blanching purpura = meningococcaemia / HSP / HUS / ITP / leukaemia until proven otherwise. Recognise measles, Kawasaki, SJS/TEN, eczema herpeticum, scabies, urticaria.
framing: The glass test (non-blanching) is the key first step. Petechiae from coughing / vomiting (above clavicles) in a well child is benign; widespread purpura is not.

differential.pointers: Fever + non-blanching purpura + mottling + shock.
differential.investigation: Empirical IV ceftriaxone before LP; PCR; blood cultures.

differential.pointers: Palpable purpura on buttocks/legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, haematuria.
Bloody diarrhoea then anaemia + AKI + thrombocytopenia.
Well child, isolated thrombocytopenia, post-viral.
Pallor, fatigue, bruising, lymphadenopathy.
Coryza, conjunctivitis, cough, Koplik spots, maculopapular rash starting on face.
Fever ≥ 5 days + 4 of 5 criteria (conjunctivitis, lips/oral, polymorphic rash, peripheral changes, cervical LN).
Vesicles or maculopapular, well child.
Wheals, itching, allergic/post-viral.
Recent drug, painful skin, mucosal erosions.

redFlags: Non-blanching purpura (esp. widespread, below nipple line)
initialInvestigations: FBC, blood film, coagulation, U&E, CRP
disposition: Meningococcal suspicion → IV antibiotics + admit + ICU. HSP / ITP → admit if complications. Well child viral exanthem → home + safety-net. Kawasaki → admit + cardiology.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s.
RCPCH Kawasaki disease guidance.

oneLiner: Septic arthritis must be excluded (Kocher criteria). Differential by age: under 3 = septic arthritis, NAI, transient synovitis (rare under 3); 3-10 = transient synovitis, Perthes; 10-15 = SUFE, osteomyelitis.
framing: Always consider non-accidental injury (especially under 3 with limp). Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE) in obese adolescent — examine the hip via knee pain.
keyHistory: Knee pain (referred from hip — Perthes, SUFE)
keyExam: Range of movement (especially internal rotation hip)

differential.pointers: Kocher (non-weight-bearing, fever > 38.5, WCC > 12, ESR > 40); refusal to move joint, erythema.
differential.investigation: Joint aspirate URGENT; FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures.

differential.pointers: Focal bone tenderness, fever, raised inflammatory markers.
Age 3-10, post-viral, afebrile, weight-bearing possible, normal inflammatory markers.
Age 4-8, gradual hip pain, limp, knee pain, restricted internal rotation.
Age 10-15, obese, hip / knee pain, externally rotated, restricted internal rotation.
differential.investigation: X-ray AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis.

differential.pointers: History of injury; ALWAYS consider NAI if story inconsistent.
Systemic symptoms, bone pain night, pallor, lymphadenopathy.
Persistent > 6 weeks, multiple joints, morning stiffness.

initialInvestigations: FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures (if Kocher criteria suggestive)
X-ray (AP + frog-leg lateral pelvis for hip)
Joint aspirate if septic arthritis suspected
disposition: Septic arthritis / osteomyelitis → admit + orthopaedics + IV antibiotics. SUFE → admit, non-weight-bearing, orthopaedic surgery. Transient synovitis → outpatient, safety-net. NAI concerns → safeguarding pathway.

references.label: RCEM guidance on the limping child.
Kocher MS et al. Differentiating septic arthritis from transient synovitis. JBJS 1999.

oneLiner: Most are primary (migraine, tension). Red flags for secondary: morning headache + vomiting, worsening over weeks, new focal neurology, age < 6, behavioural change. Same workup logic as adults but lower threshold to image.
framing: Brain tumour HeadSmart symptoms: persistent headache, vomiting, visual change, balance / coordination, behavioural change, abnormal head position, abnormal growth.

differential.pointers: Episodic, bifrontal (more often bilateral in children), nausea, photophobia, family history.
Band-like, mild-moderate, stress-related.
Morning headache + vomiting, focal neurology, behavioural change, papilloedema.
Obese adolescent, visual disturbance, papilloedema.
differential.investigation: MRI / MRV, LP with opening pressure.

differential.pointers: Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia.
Worse after school, frontal.
Recent URTI, facial pain.

disposition: Red flags → urgent MRI + paediatric neurology. Primary headache → reassurance + analgesia + headache diary + GP follow-up.

references.label: HeadSmart — Be Brain Tumour Aware.
NICE CG150 — Headaches in over 12s.

oneLiner: Febrile seizure (6 months - 5 years, simple vs complex) is benign. First unprovoked seizure needs neurology workup. Status epilepticus = > 5 min — emergency.
framing: Most paediatric seizures are febrile (3% incidence). Simple febrile seizure: < 15 min, generalised, no recurrence in 24 h. Complex: focal, > 15 min, recurrent — needs investigation.
keyExam: Skin (neurocutaneous markers — café au lait, ash-leaf)

differential.pointers: 6 months - 5 years, fever, generalised, < 15 min, no recurrence in 24 h, normal recovery.
differential.investigation: Identify infection source; usually no further imaging / EEG.

differential.pointers: Focal, > 15 min, recurrent in 24 h.
differential.investigation: Consider neuroimaging + EEG + LP if other concerns.

differential.pointers: Fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness, focal seizure.
Fasting, diabetic, sepsis, inborn error.
Vomiting, dehydration, infant water intoxication.
Infant with unexplained seizure — always consider NAI.
differential.investigation: CT brain, retinal exam, skeletal survey.

differential.pointers: No provoking factor.
Access to drugs.

references.label: NICE NG217 — Epilepsies in children, young people and adults.
APLS / RCPCH status epilepticus guidance.

oneLiner: Neonatal jaundice in first 24 h = always pathological (haemolysis, sepsis). Prolonged > 14 days (term) / 21 days (preterm) = biliary atresia must be excluded. Older infant / child = hepatitis, malaria, drugs.
framing: Neonatal jaundice physiology vs pathology hinges on timing. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (> 25 μmol/L OR > 20% total) is always pathological — biliary atresia must be diagnosed by 6-8 weeks for Kasai success.
keyExam: Encephalopathy (bilirubin encephalopathy — high pitched cry, lethargy)

differential.pointers: Day 2-14, unconjugated, well infant, breastfed.
differential.investigation: Plot bilirubin on age-specific chart; phototherapy per threshold.

differential.pointers: < 24 h jaundice, anaemia, rapid rise.
Lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pale stools, dark urine, > 14 days.
differential.investigation: Split bilirubin; USS, HIDA scan; Kasai by 8 weeks.

differential.pointers: Prolonged unconjugated jaundice, otherwise well, breastfed.
Prodrome, transaminitis.
Fever, exposure, splenomegaly, anaemia.
Prolonged jaundice, lethargy, hypotonia.

disposition: Phototherapy per chart; exchange transfusion if very high. Suspected biliary atresia → urgent hepatology. Sepsis → admit + antibiotics.

references.label: NICE CG98 — Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days.

oneLiner: In an infant a non-specific but ominous sign. Causes: sepsis, congenital heart disease, metabolic, GI (reflux, pyloric stenosis, malrotation), neurological, oral / cleft, social.
framing: Poor feeding + lethargy in an infant < 3 months = sepsis until proven otherwise. Faltering growth requires multidisciplinary assessment.

differential.pointers: Temperature instability, lethargy, poor feeding.
Sweating with feeds, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, murmur, cyanosis.
Vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, acidosis, hyperammonaemia.

Hypotonia, abnormal reflexes.
Visible cleft, latch difficulty.
Observation of feed; HV / SLT input.

disposition: Admit any infant < 3 months with poor feeding for assessment. Identify and treat cause. Feeding support if no organic cause.

references.label: NICE NG75 — Faltering growth in children.

oneLiner: Sustained inconsolable crying needs systematic workup: infection, GI, surgical, ocular, traumatic, NAI. Consider testicular torsion, intussusception, hair tourniquet, corneal abrasion.
framing: Colic is a diagnosis of exclusion. Systematic head-to-toe exam essential — easily missed causes include hair tourniquet on digit / penis, corneal abrasion, otitis, fracture.
keyExam: Full head-to-toe — including ears, throat, fontanelle, fundoscopy
Skin / mucous membranes / digits / penis (hair tourniquet)

differential.pointers: Fever, source on exam.
Intermittent severe crying, drawing up legs.
Tender groin lump.
Swollen scrotum.
Fluorescein staining.
Discoloured digit, look carefully.
Bruising, focal tenderness, atypical history.
Vomiting, bloody mucous stool, eczema.
Rule of 3s (> 3 h/day, > 3 days/week, > 3 weeks); peaks 6 weeks; thriving otherwise.

disposition: Treat identified cause. Inconsolable / unclear cause / red flags → admit for observation + workup. Colic → reassurance + safety-net.

references.label: NICE CKS — Colic, infantile.
RCPCH safeguarding guidance.

oneLiner: Differential narrows — common: viral, tonsillitis, pneumonia, UTI, gastroenteritis. Must-not-miss: meningitis, sepsis, pneumonia with sepsis, appendicitis, Kawasaki / PIMS-TS, osteomyelitis.
framing: NICE traffic-light system still applicable. Older children better at communicating focal symptoms; obtain detailed history. Lower threshold for septic screen if no focus and unwell.

differential.pointers: Coryza, cough, sore throat, myalgia.
Sore throat, tonsillar exudate; FeverPAIN / Centor.
differential.investigation: Clinical; strep swab/RADT if scoring high.

Headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, rash.
Septic features.
Limp, refusal to weight-bear, joint swelling.

differential.pointers: Migrating abdominal pain.
Persistent fever + multisystem features; recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure.
Fever ≥ 5 days + criteria.

initialInvestigations: FBC, CRP, blood cultures if unwell
Echo / inflammatory markers if PIMS-TS / Kawasaki
disposition: Toxic / red flag → admit + septic workup + antibiotics. Identified focus + well → outpatient with safety-net. Persistent fever ≥ 5 days → consider Kawasaki / PIMS-TS.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s.
RCPCH PIMS-TS guidance.

oneLiner: Always assume sepsis or serious illness. Differential: early-onset sepsis (GBS, E. coli, Listeria), late-onset sepsis, congenital heart disease, metabolic, GI, neurological.
framing: Neonates compensate poorly and decompensate quickly. Temperature can be high, low, or normal in sepsis. Empirical antibiotics within 1 h.
keyHistory: Risk factors (PROM, maternal GBS, chorioamnionitis, prematurity)

differential.pointers: Any poor feeding / lethargy in neonate.
differential.investigation: Full septic screen + IV antibiotics within 1 h.

differential.pointers: Cyanosis, shock as duct closes, hepatomegaly, absent femorals, pre/post-ductal SpO₂ differential.
Vomiting, acidosis, hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia.
differential.investigation: Glucose, ammonia, ABG, lactate, urine ketones, organic acids.

differential.pointers: Jittery, lethargy.
Perinatal event, abnormal tone.
Bilious vomiting, distension, bloody stool.
Maternal drug history.

redFlags: Any neonate with poor feeding / lethargy = serious illness suspected
initialInvestigations: Full septic screen (FBC, CRP, blood cultures, urine, LP)
U&E, glucose, ammonia, ABG, lactate, ketones
Empirical IV antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin + gentamicin per local)
disposition: Admit. Septic screen + IV antibiotics within 1 h. Senior + neonatal team. Cardiology / surgical / metabolic as indicated.

references.label: NICE NG195 — Neonatal infection: antibiotics for prevention and treatment.

oneLiner: Always serious. Differential: surfactant deficiency / TTN, congenital pneumonia / sepsis, congenital heart disease, pneumothorax, meconium aspiration, congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
framing: Grunting is end-expiratory closure against a partially closed glottis to maintain FRC — a sign of significant lung disease. Immediate stabilisation: oxygen, CPAP, sepsis workup + antibiotics.
keyExam: Work of breathing — recession, flaring, grunting
Auscultation (bilateral vs focal, scaphoid abdomen — CDH)

differential.pointers: Term, C-section, mild distress resolving < 48 h.
Preterm, progressive distress.
Maternal risk factors.
Meconium-stained liquor, post-term.
Sudden deterioration, transillumination.
Scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in chest, antenatal diagnosis.
Cyanosis not responsive to O₂, pre/post-ductal SpO₂ differential.

differential.diagnosis: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
differential.pointers: Hypoxia, pre/post-ductal differential.

initialInvestigations: Blood gas, FBC, CRP, blood cultures, glucose
disposition: Admit NICU. Stabilise — oxygen, CPAP, intubation as needed; surfactant for RDS; sepsis treatment; cardiac assessment.

references.label: BAPM neonatal respiratory distress guidance.

oneLiner: Jaundice > 14 days term, > 21 days preterm. Must measure conjugated bilirubin — biliary atresia must be diagnosed and Kasai performed by 8 weeks for liver salvage.
framing: Biliary atresia is the time-critical diagnosis — outcomes deteriorate sharply after 60 days. Pale stools + dark urine + persistent jaundice = urgent hepatology workup.

differential.pointers: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pale stools, dark urine.
differential.investigation: Split bilirubin; USS; HIDA scan; liver biopsy; Kasai.

differential.pointers: Unconjugated, thriving, breastfed.

Family history, ethnicity.
Sometimes only sign of UTI in neonate.
Vomiting, lethargy, hypoglycaemia, cataracts.
Abdominal mass, obstructive jaundice.

disposition: Suspected biliary atresia → urgent paediatric hepatology referral within days. Other causes → manage accordingly.

references.label: NICE CG98 — Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days.
BSPGHAN neonatal cholestasis guidance.

oneLiner: Surgical emergency. Malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise — bowel ischaemia within hours. Urgent contrast study and paediatric surgical review.
framing: Green vomit in a neonate is bowel obstruction below the ampulla of Vater. Time critical — small bowel ischaemia from volvulus leads to short gut.

differential.pointers: Sudden bilious vomiting, may be otherwise well early.
differential.investigation: Upper GI contrast study; urgent paediatric surgery.

differential.pointers: Double bubble on AXR; Down syndrome association; antenatal polyhydramnios.
Distended abdomen, bilious vomiting.
Preterm, feed intolerance, distension, bloody stool.
differential.investigation: AXR (pneumatosis); supportive + antibiotics + surgical if perforation.

differential.pointers: Delayed meconium, cystic fibrosis association.
Delayed meconium > 48 h, distension.

redFlags: Any bilious vomiting in a neonate
initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, CRP, blood cultures, coagulation, crossmatch
Upper GI contrast for malrotation (gold standard)
disposition: Admit, NBM, NG, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, paediatric surgical review. Suspected malrotation → emergency theatre.

references.label: BAPS / RCPCH guidance on neonatal bowel obstruction.

oneLiner: APLS / ATLS principles. Children compensate well then decompensate suddenly. Always consider non-accidental injury. Weight-based equipment + drugs. Permissive hypotension is NOT appropriate in children.
framing: Leading cause of death in children. Larger head : body ratio predisposes to head injury. Less subcutaneous fat increases hypothermia. NAI in any child with injury inconsistent with history.
keyExam: Primary survey ABCDE with C-spine immobilisation

differential.pointers: GCS drop, focal signs, vomiting.
differential.investigation: CT head per NICE / PECARN; neurosurgical.

differential.pointers: Mechanism, midline tenderness, neurology.
Chest deformity, reduced breath sounds, hypotension.
Bruising, distension, tenderness.
Mechanism, deformity, pain.
Story inconsistent, multiple ages of injuries, characteristic patterns (rib, metaphyseal corner).

FBC, U&E, glucose, coagulation, crossmatch, VBG, lactate
disposition: Activate paediatric trauma pathway. Transfer to major trauma centre if criteria met. PICU admission. Safeguarding for NAI concerns.

references.label: RCPCH / APLS major trauma in children.
NICE NG39 — Major trauma: assessment and initial management.

oneLiner: Ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Differential: miscarriage (threatened / inevitable / missed), ectopic, molar, implantation, cervical lesion. β-hCG + transvaginal ultrasound.
framing: Up to 20% of clinically recognised pregnancies miscarry; ectopic affects ~1% of pregnancies but accounts for significant maternal mortality if missed. Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) needs serial β-hCG.
keyHistory: Volume of bleeding, clots, tissue passed
IVF, prior ectopic, PID, tubal surgery (ectopic risk)
keyExam: Speculum exam (cervix open / closed; tissue at os)

differential.pointers: Unilateral pain, shoulder tip pain (haemoperitoneum), syncope, adnexal mass.
differential.investigation: Serum β-hCG + transvaginal US; intervention if rupture.

differential.pointers: Bleeding with closed cervix, viable pregnancy on scan.
Open cervix, products visible.
No fetal heart on scan despite expected size.
differential.investigation: TVUS; repeat in 7-10 days to confirm.

differential.pointers: Hyperemesis, very high β-hCG, snowstorm appearance on US.
differential.investigation: US; histology; gestational trophoblastic disease follow-up.

differential.pointers: Post-coital bleeding; speculum exam.

disposition: Suspected ruptured ectopic → emergency gynaecology / theatre. Stable bleeding → EPAU. Rh-negative → anti-D per local protocol.

references.label: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management.

oneLiner: Less common than first/third trimester. Differential: late miscarriage, placental abnormality, cervical insufficiency, infection, trauma. Senior obstetric review.
framing: Bleeding 13-24 weeks. Cervical insufficiency presents as painless second-trimester loss. Placenta praevia may bleed earlier than third trimester.
keyExam: Abdominal — tenderness, uterine tone, fetal heart
Speculum (avoid digital exam if praevia possible until US)

differential.pointers: Cramping, cervical change.
Painless bleeding; prior C-section.
differential.investigation: US; do not do PV exam until US.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 27 — Placenta praevia and accreta.

oneLiner: Placenta praevia, abruption, vasa praevia, uterine rupture. Maternal and fetal emergency. NO digital vaginal exam until placenta praevia excluded.
framing: Antepartum haemorrhage affects 3-5% of pregnancies. Praevia is painless bleeding; abruption is painful + concealed bleeding possible. Vasa praevia is fetal bleeding with rapid demise on ARM.
keyExam: Vitals — be aware of pregnancy physiological changes
Abdominal — tenderness, hard / tense uterus (abruption), fetal heart
Speculum (do NOT do digital exam until praevia excluded)

differential.pointers: Painless bleeding, malpresentation, prior C-section.

differential.pointers: Painful bleeding + tender hard uterus + fetal distress; concealed bleeding possible.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis; CTG; urgent delivery if compromise.

Mucous plug; contractions.
Post-coital, polyp.

Activate massive haemorrhage protocol if severe
disposition: Obstetric emergency — senior team. Delivery indicated if fetal distress, maternal compromise, or term. Anti-D if Rh-negative.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 63 — Antepartum haemorrhage.

oneLiner: Always exclude pre-eclampsia. Differential also includes cerebral venous thrombosis, PRES, eclampsia, SAH, primary headache. BP + urinalysis + bloods.
framing: Pregnancy increases risk of CVT, PRES, intracranial haemorrhage (especially postpartum). Pre-eclampsia features: BP ≥ 140/90 + proteinuria + symptoms (headache, visual change, epigastric pain).

differential.pointers: BP ≥ 140/90 + proteinuria, headache, visual changes, epigastric pain, low platelets, transaminitis, haemolysis.
differential.investigation: BP, urinalysis, FBC, U&E, LFTs, urate; obstetric review.

differential.pointers: Seizure on background of pre-eclampsia.
Severe progressive headache, focal signs, seizures, pregnancy / postpartum.
Headache + visual change + seizures + hypertension.
Thunderclap headache.
Prior history.

disposition: Pre-eclampsia → admit, BP control (labetalol / nifedipine), magnesium for severe / eclampsia, plan delivery. Other neurological emergencies → admit per cause.

references.label: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management.

oneLiner: Identify chorioamnionitis (with PROM), pyelonephritis, listeriosis, malaria, influenza, COVID. Sepsis in pregnancy mortality high — early antibiotics + obstetric review.
framing: Pregnant women have higher mortality from sepsis. Chorioamnionitis + PROM is an indication for delivery + antibiotics. UTI in pregnancy progresses to pyelonephritis more commonly.
keyExam: Source — chest, abdomen, urinary, ENT, skin

differential.pointers: Fever + uterine tenderness ± PROM + foul vaginal discharge + fetal tachycardia.
Fever + flank pain + dysuria.
Flu-like illness in pregnancy; fetal loss risk.
Travel, paroxysmal fever.
Seasonal; respiratory features.
Pain may be in RUQ / flank as uterus enlarges.

disposition: Admit any pregnant patient with sepsis features. Early broad-spectrum antibiotics. Deliver if chorioamnionitis with viable fetus.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 64a — Bacterial sepsis in pregnancy.

oneLiner: Leading cause of maternal mortality. 4 T's: Tone (atony — most common), Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Use E-MOTIVE bundle (early recognition, uterine massage, oxytocics, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, examination).
framing: Primary PPH within 24 h of delivery, > 500 mL vaginal / > 1000 mL C-section, OR any volume causing instability. Most common cause is uterine atony.
keyHistory: Risk factors (prolonged labour, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, large baby, fibroids, prior PPH, retained products)
keyExam: Fundus tone and height (atonic = soft, high)

differential.pointers: Soft non-contracted fundus; most common cause.
differential.investigation: Uterine massage, oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol; balloon tamponade.

Tears, episiotomy, uterine rupture.
DIC, HELLP, pre-existing bleeding disorder, abruption.
Excessive cord traction; uterus felt at introitus.

Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h

Theatre for examination under anaesthesia, balloon tamponade, B-Lynch, hysterectomy

references.label: WHO E-MOTIVE bundle for PPH (2023).
RCOG Green-top Guideline 52 — Prevention and management of PPH.

oneLiner: Sepsis a leading cause of maternal mortality. Sources: endometritis, wound, mastitis, UTI, VTE-associated, breast abscess, pneumonia. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) most rapidly lethal.
framing: Postpartum sepsis often subtle in early stages — high vigilance. Group A Streptococcus presents with rapid deterioration, severe abdominal pain, foul lochia.

differential.pointers: Uterine tenderness, foul lochia, post-C-section more common.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 64b — Bacterial sepsis following pregnancy.

oneLiner: Acute: ectopic, ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, PID, appendicitis, UTI. Chronic: endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, IBS, pelvic congestion. β-hCG mandatory.
framing: β-hCG in every woman of reproductive age. Ovarian torsion presents with sudden severe unilateral pain ± vomiting — emergency surgical detorsion within 6-8 h to preserve fertility.

Sudden severe unilateral pain, vomiting, palpable mass.
Sudden pain mid-cycle (Mittelschmerz) or postcoital.
Bilateral pain, fever, discharge, cervical motion tenderness, sexually active.

Cyclical pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, infertility.
Known fibroids, pain.

references.label: NICE NG73 — Endometriosis: diagnosis and management.
BASHH PID guidelines.

oneLiner: Absence of menses ≥ 3 cycles in previously menstruating woman. Always β-hCG first. Differential: pregnancy, PCOS, hypothalamic, hyperprolactinaemia, premature ovarian insufficiency, Asherman's.
framing: Pregnancy is the most common cause and must be excluded. Hypothalamic amenorrhoea (low BMI, stress, exercise) is common in younger women. POI < 40 needs hormonal and chromosomal workup.

differential.pointers: Sexually active, positive β-hCG.
Hirsutism, acne, weight gain, polycystic ovaries on US (Rotterdam criteria).

Galactorrhoea, headache, visual change.
Age < 40, hot flushes, vaginal dryness.
Symptoms of hyper/hypothyroidism.
Recent D&C, post-curettage.

MRI pituitary if prolactin > 1000 mU/L or neurology

references.label: NICE CKS — Amenorrhoea.

oneLiner: Triple assessment (clinical + imaging + biopsy) for any persistent breast lump. Refer 2-week-wait for any unexplained lump > 30 or unilateral nipple change. Cyclical mastalgia rarely malignant.
framing: Breast cancer common; early detection saves lives. NICE recommends 2-week-wait referral for: women > 30 with unexplained lump; > 50 with nipple change; skin changes; lump with risk factors.

Palpation systematic quadrants + tail of Spence

Young, smooth, mobile, firm rubbery.

Bilateral, premenstrual.
Localised pain, erythema, fluctuance.

Nipple discharge (single duct, bloody — papilloma).

Skin dimpling, peau d'orange, nipple eczema (Paget's)

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer recognition (breast).

oneLiner: Differential: bacterial vaginosis, candida, trichomonas, STI (chlamydia, gonorrhoea), retained tampon, atrophy. Syndromic management per WHO in many settings; lab-confirmed where available.
framing: Common presentation. STI screening for sexually active; partner notification. PID risk if untreated chlamydia / gonorrhoea.

Mucopurulent cervix, contact bleeding.

Foul discharge, history.
Post-menopausal, dryness, dyspareunia.

Vaginal pH; high vaginal swab if recurrent

references.label: BASHH UK national guidelines on vaginal discharge management.

oneLiner: Assess risk with structured tool (C-SSRS, SAD PERSONS, Beck). Identify intent, plan, means, prior attempts, current state. Admit if active plan / means / intent. Psychiatry liaison early.
framing: Suicide is a leading cause of death in young adults. Risk highest in older men with chronic illness, substance use, recent loss. Means restriction (firearm, medication) reduces suicide deaths.

keyExam: Mental state — appearance, mood, affect, thought content, insight

Medical clearance of overdose (paracetamol, salicylate, ECG)

NICE NG225 — Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022).

oneLiner: Identify reversible medical causes (hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, intoxication, withdrawal, delirium, sepsis, head injury) before assuming psychiatric. De-escalation first; tranquillisation last.
framing: Behavioural emergency is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Reversible medical causes must be excluded. Use least restrictive intervention; tranquillise only if necessary for safety.

Respiratory disease.
Fever, source.
Toxidrome, history.
Tremor, autonomic, history.

references.label: NICE NG10 — Violence and aggression: short-term management.

oneLiner: Diagnosis of exclusion. Must first rule out ACS, PE, hypoglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, substance use, phaeochromocytoma. Then reassure + behavioural support.
framing: Panic attacks may present with chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations — easily mistaken for cardiac. New-onset panic attack > 45 years should prompt medical workup.

differential.pointers: Cardiac risk factors, new-onset, age > 45.
VTE risk factors, hypoxia.

oneLiner: Identify toxidrome (sympathomimetic, opioid, anticholinergic, cholinergic, sedative-hypnotic). Supportive care + antidote where applicable. Check paracetamol + salicylate in any overdose.
framing: Toxidromes guide initial management before levels return. Always consider co-ingestion. Naloxone for opioid; flumazenil only in iatrogenic benzodiazepine OD; activated charcoal within 1 h of ingestion if airway secure.

differential.pointers: Miosis, bradypnoea, low GCS.
Mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation.
differential.investigation: Benzodiazepines, active cooling, IV fluids; ECG (QRS / QT); avoid beta-blockers in cocaine.

differential.pointers: Mydriasis, dry skin, urinary retention, hyperthermia, delirium.
differential.investigation: Supportive; sodium bicarbonate for TCA QRS widening.

differential.pointers: Miosis, salivation, lacrimation, defaecation, urination.
Low GCS, normal pupils, preserved vitals.
Often asymptomatic initially.
differential.investigation: Paracetamol level at 4 h post-ingestion; N-acetylcysteine per nomogram.

differential.pointers: Tinnitus, tachypnoea, mixed acid-base.
differential.investigation: Salicylate level, ABG; urinary alkalinisation; haemodialysis if severe.

redFlags: Wide QRS or QT (TCA, sodium channel)
initialInvestigations: Paracetamol + salicylate level in any overdose
Activated charcoal within 1 h if airway secure
disposition: Observation period based on substance. Antidote where indicated. Psychiatric review if intentional. ICU if airway / haemodynamic / metabolic compromise.

references.label: TOXBASE (NPIS UK).
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies.

oneLiner: Alcohol withdrawal can be fatal (seizures, delirium tremens). Opioid withdrawal is unpleasant but not fatal. Benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause seizures. Use CIWA-Ar (alcohol), COWS (opioid).
framing: Alcohol withdrawal timeline: tremor / anxiety 6-12 h; seizures 12-48 h; delirium tremens 48-72 h. Thiamine BEFORE glucose to prevent Wernicke. Benzodiazepine ladder for symptom control.

differential.pointers: Last drink hours-days ago, tremor, autonomic features, anxiety, hallucinosis, seizures, DT.
differential.investigation: CIWA-Ar; benzodiazepines (diazepam / chlordiazepoxide); IV thiamine BEFORE glucose; consider phenobarbital if refractory.

differential.pointers: Chronic use, tapered abruptly, seizures.
COWS — yawning, rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, piloerection, mydriasis, GI cramps, anxiety; not fatal but unpleasant.
differential.investigation: Symptomatic (loperamide, clonidine, ondansetron); methadone / buprenorphine induction.

differential.pointers: Crash with fatigue, hypersomnia, dysphoria, suicidality.
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; alcoholic / malnourished.

initialInvestigations: IV thiamine prior to / with glucose
disposition: Severe alcohol withdrawal / DT / refractory → admit, possibly ICU. Mild → outpatient with detox plan. Opioid → induction onto methadone / buprenorphine; refer addiction services.

references.label: NICE CG100 — Alcohol-use disorders.
NICE CG52 — Drug misuse in over 16s: opioid detoxification.

oneLiner: A fall is a symptom — identify cause: mechanical, medication (postural hypotension, polypharmacy), syncope, neurological, fragility fracture, NAI. Multifactorial assessment + fall prevention.
framing: 1 in 3 over-65 falls each year. 30% sustain injury. Recurrent falls predict mortality. Assess for cause + injury + future risk + cause of frailty.
keyExam: Vitals + postural BP (lying and standing 1 + 3 min)
Examine for injury, head, hip, ribs

differential.pointers: Drop SBP > 20 / DBP > 10 on standing; multiple antihypertensives.
Trip, slip, no LOC.
LOC, no recall.

differential.diagnosis: Sepsis / acute illness presenting as fall
differential.pointers: Fever, delirium, UTI common precipitant.
Focal neurology.
Pain, inability to weight-bear; can be the cause or the consequence.
differential.investigation: X-ray; CT / MRI if X-ray negative + persistent pain.

differential.pointers: Anticoagulant, fluctuating consciousness, headache.
Inconsistent history, recurrent injuries.

initialInvestigations: CT brain if head injury + anticoagulation / new neurology
disposition: Admit if significant injury, suspected syncope, head injury on anticoagulant, fragility fracture. Falls clinic + OT for community follow-up. Bone health (osteoporosis assessment + DEXA + bisphosphonate).

references.label: NICE CG161 — Falls in older people: assessment after a fall and preventing further falls.

oneLiner: Delirium in older adults often the first sign of underlying acute illness. Identify and treat precipitant. PINCH ME mnemonic: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment.
framing: Delirium occurs in 30% of medical inpatients > 65. Hyperactive (agitated), hypoactive (quiet, often missed), or mixed. Mortality 25-33% during episode.

differential.pointers: Most common precipitant.
Recent change.
Under-recognised; agitation may be only sign.
PR / bladder scan.
Labs.
Focal signs, falls, anticoagulant.
Tremor, autonomic.
Especially in dementia.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, Ca, Mg, glucose, TFTs, B12, folate, CRP
CT brain if focal signs / fall / anticoagulant
disposition: Treat precipitant. Non-pharmacological: orientation, hydration, mobilisation, sleep hygiene, sensory aids. Avoid antipsychotics unless severe distress / safety (caution in dementia / Parkinson's).

references.label: NICE CG103 — Delirium: diagnosis, prevention and management.

oneLiner: Frailty syndrome — non-specific decline often with acute illness, falls, delirium, or polypharmacy. Use Clinical Frailty Scale. Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment improves outcomes.
framing: Frailty is a state of increased vulnerability to stressors. Risk of poor outcome from minor illness, hospital admission. Identify reversible factors.

differential.diagnosis: Acute illness precipitating decline (infection, MI, CCF, AKI)
differential.pointers: Atypical or vague presentation.
differential.investigation: Broad workup — septic screen, ECG, troponin, BNP, U&E, glucose.

differential.pointers: STOPP/START.
MUST score, weight loss.
Anhedonia, social isolation.
Progressive cognitive decline.
Weight loss, anaemia, lymphadenopathy.
Hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, Ca, glucose, TFTs, B12, folate, vitamin D, CRP, ferritin
disposition: Multidisciplinary input — geriatrician, OT, physio, dietitian, social work. Address reversible factors. Advance care planning where appropriate.

references.label: BGS recommendations on the assessment of frailty.

oneLiner: Unexplained weight loss, decreased appetite, malnutrition, dehydration, functional decline. Always exclude malignancy, depression, dementia, chronic disease, social factors.
framing: Failure to thrive in older adults has 4 D's: disease, dementia, depression, drugs. Combination is common. Often presents as gradual decline rather than acute illness.

differential.pointers: Weight loss, anaemia, lymphadenopathy.
differential.investigation: FBC, LDH, ferritin, CT, age-appropriate screening.

differential.pointers: Anhedonia, social withdrawal, hopelessness, GDS.
Cognitive decline, forgetting to eat.
Symptoms of organ failure.
Polypharmacy, anorexogenic drugs.
Inadequate care, financial constraints, caregiver burden.
Choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
Weight loss with normal appetite (thyroid), hyponatraemia (adrenal).

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, calcium, glucose, TFTs, B12, folate, vitamin D, ferritin, LDH, CRP
disposition: Multidisciplinary — geriatrician, dietitian, SLT, psychiatry, OT, social work. Address reversible factors. Safeguarding if abuse suspected.

references.label: BGS guidance on failure to thrive in older adults.

oneLiner: ≥ 5 medications, especially with anticholinergic / sedative burden, increases falls, delirium, hospitalisation. Use STOPP/START. Deprescribe systematically.
framing: Polypharmacy is associated with adverse drug events, falls, cognitive impairment. Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden score predicts cognitive decline. Deprescribing is evidence-based.

differential.pointers: Confusion, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, falls.
Falls, delirium, dependence.
Postural hypotension, falls.
NSAIDs in CKD, dual RAAS, long-acting sulfonylurea, tricyclics.

differential.diagnosis: Missing therapy per START (osteoporosis, statins, vaccines, antiplatelet for vascular disease)
differential.pointers: Untreated indications.

disposition: Structured deprescribing plan with patient + GP. Pharmacist input. Follow-up within weeks to assess withdrawal effects.

references.label: O'Mahony D et al. STOPP/START criteria for potentially inappropriate prescribing in older people (v3, 2023).

oneLiner: > 5% body weight in 6 months. Differential: malignancy, GI (malabsorption, IBD), endocrine (hyperthyroidism, diabetes), psychiatric, chronic infection (TB, HIV), drugs.
framing: Malignancy underlies up to 25% of unintentional weight loss in older adults. Systematic workup; revisit after 6 months if no diagnosis.
keyHistory: Appetite (reduced — anorexia; preserved — malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, diabetes)

differential.pointers: Weight loss + anaemia / pain / B-symptoms.
Preserved appetite, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations.
Polyuria, polydipsia.
Diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, abdominal symptoms.
differential.investigation: Coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin, faecal elastase.

differential.pointers: Night sweats, fevers, risk factors.
Mood symptoms, anorexia.
Polypharmacy, recent additions.
History.

initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, glucose, HbA1c, TFTs, calcium, CRP, ESR, ferritin, LDH
CXR; CT chest/abdo/pelvis if no source
disposition: Targeted referrals (2-week-wait if cancer suspected). Repeat workup at 3-6 months if no diagnosis. Nutritional support.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer recognition.

oneLiner: Drenching sweats are pathological. Differential: lymphoma, TB, endocarditis, HIV, menopause, hyperthyroidism, drugs (SSRI, tamoxifen), withdrawal.
framing: Drenching night sweats (changing clothes / bedding) more concerning. Pattern, associated symptoms, duration direct workup.

differential.pointers: B-symptoms (fever, sweats, weight loss), lymphadenopathy.
Exposure, weight loss, cough.
Risk factors, opportunistic features.
New murmur, embolic phenomena, IVDU, prosthetic.
Age, hot flushes.
Weight loss, tremor.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced (SSRI, SNRI, tamoxifen, opioids, hypoglycaemic agents)
differential.pointers: Medication history.
Alcohol / opioid history.

disposition: Targeted referrals. Empirical menopause management if appropriate. 2-week-wait for suspected lymphoma.

references.label: BMJ Best Practice — Evaluation of night sweats.

oneLiner: Localised reactive (infection) vs persistent / generalised (lymphoma, HIV, TB, sarcoid, autoimmune, drug). Persistent > 2 weeks, > 1 cm, hard / fixed / supraclavicular = biopsy.
framing: Supraclavicular node always pathological — biopsy. Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) classically GI malignancy. Generalised lymphadenopathy needs HIV / lymphoma / autoimmune workup.
keyHistory: Recent infection, travel, animal exposure (cat scratch, toxoplasma)
keyExam: All node areas (cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, inguinal)

differential.pointers: Local source, tender, mobile, resolves.
Persistent painless rubbery firm, B-symptoms.
Hard, fixed, age > 40, especially supraclavicular.
Cold abscess, matted nodes, endemic exposure.
Generalised, recent risk exposure.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, uveitis.
Multisystem features.
Recent drug.

initialInvestigations: FBC, blood film, ESR, LDH, ferritin
Excisional biopsy if persistent (FNA inadequate for lymphoma)
disposition: Suspected malignancy → 2-week-wait. TB / HIV → ID. Sarcoid / autoimmune → respiratory / rheumatology.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer recognition.

oneLiner: Identify source of blood loss vs haemolysis vs marrow failure. Acute symptomatic anaemia → transfusion. Iron-deficiency in older adult mandates GI workup for malignancy.
framing: Symptomatic anaemia presents with fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations, chest pain. Acute large blood loss may show normal Hb initially; serial measurements + clinical assessment.

differential.diagnosis: Iron deficiency anaemia (occult blood loss — GI / menstrual)
differential.pointers: Microcytic, low ferritin, fatigue.
differential.investigation: FBC, ferritin, iron studies; OGD + colonoscopy if no other source.

differential.pointers: Trauma, GI bleed, surgery, anticoagulant.
differential.investigation: Hb may be normal early; group + crossmatch, identify source.

differential.pointers: Jaundice, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, raised reticulocytes.
differential.investigation: FBC, blood film, DAT, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin.

differential.pointers: Pancytopenia, blasts on film.
Macrocytic, neurological symptoms (B12), glossitis.
differential.investigation: B12, folate, MMA, homocysteine; intrinsic factor antibody.

differential.pointers: Normocytic, raised ferritin, chronic illness.

initialInvestigations: Targeted GI workup for iron deficiency
disposition: Symptomatic acute anaemia / Hb < 70 / active bleeding → transfusion + admission. Iron deficiency → OGD + colonoscopy in 2-week-wait if > 50. Pancytopenia → haematology.

references.label: BSH guidelines on the management of iron deficiency in adults.

oneLiner: Distinguish platelet (mucocutaneous bleeding) from coagulation factor (deep haematomas, haemarthroses) defects. Identify ITP, drug-induced, von Willebrand disease, liver disease, vasculitis, malignancy.
framing: Pattern of bleeding directs workup. Lifelong bleeding suggests inherited (vWD, haemophilia); new bleeding tendency suggests acquired (ITP, drug, liver, malignancy).

differential.pointers: Medication history.
differential.investigation: Drug review; INR / anti-Xa for anticoagulants.

differential.pointers: Isolated low platelets, post-viral, well otherwise.
Lifelong easy bruising, menorrhagia, dental/post-surgical bleeding, family history.
Males, joint bleeds, family history.
Multiple coagulation factor deficiency.
Malabsorption, antibiotics.
Sepsis, malignancy, obstetric, bleeding + thrombosis.
Pancytopenia, blasts, fatigue, infection.
Palpable purpura, systemic features.

initialInvestigations: vWF antigen + activity, factor VIII if vWD suspected
disposition: Active bleeding → admit, reverse cause. ITP / vWD / haemophilia / liver coagulopathy → haematology referral. Leukaemia → urgent haematology.

references.label: BSH guidelines on the investigation of a possible bleeding disorder.

oneLiner: Stroke until proven otherwise — activate stroke pathway. Differential: stroke (ischaemic / haemorrhagic), Todd's paresis, hypoglycaemia, migraine with aura, conversion, space-occupying lesion.
framing: Time is brain. Thrombolysis < 4.5 h, thrombectomy < 6-24 h per imaging. Stroke mimics 25% — but treat as stroke until imaged.

differential.pointers: Sudden focal neurology, vascular risk factors, AF.
differential.investigation: Non-contrast CT brain + CTA; thrombolysis / thrombectomy per pathway.

differential.pointers: Headache, vomiting, declining GCS, hypertension.
Diabetic, missed meal.
Witnessed seizure, resolving deficit.
Spreading sensory / visual / motor, headache follows.
Gradual progression, papilloedema.
Inconsistent exam, Hoover's sign positive.

initialInvestigations: MRI if CT non-diagnostic and time permits
disposition: Activate stroke pathway. Thrombolysis / thrombectomy per criteria. Stroke unit admission. Secondary prevention.

references.label: NICE NG128 — Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s.

oneLiner: Spinal cord compression = neurosurgical / oncological emergency. MRI whole spine within hours. Steroids + decompression / radiotherapy. Time to treatment determines neurological outcome.
framing: Metastatic spinal cord compression most common cause in cancer patients. Outcomes deteriorate sharply with delay > 24-48 h. Always image the whole spine — multiple levels common.
keyHistory: Back pain (often precedes neurology by days-weeks)
keyExam: Power, tone, reflexes (UMN signs below lesion, LMN at lesion level)

differential.pointers: Cancer history (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, myeloma, lymphoma); progressive back pain then neurology.
differential.investigation: Urgent whole-spine MRI; dexamethasone 16 mg IV stat; oncology / spinal surgery.

differential.pointers: Fever, severe localised back pain, IVDU, immunocompromise.
differential.investigation: MRI with contrast; blood cultures; surgical drainage + antibiotics.

differential.pointers: Anticoagulant, sudden onset.
Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention.
Sudden onset, anterior cord syndrome (motor + spinothalamic preserved DC).
Subacute onset, sensory level, prior MS / infection.
differential.investigation: MRI, LP, AQP4 / MOG, autoimmune workup.

differential.pointers: Mechanism, immobilise.

disposition: Time-critical emergency. Dexamethasone for malignant compression. Spinal surgery / oncology / neurosurgery as appropriate. Catheterise if retention.

references.label: NICE CG75 — Metastatic spinal cord compression in adults.

oneLiner: Most dysuria is uncomplicated lower UTI, but exclude pyelonephritis/urosepsis, STI (especially in men and the sexually active), and acute retention. Loin pain + fever = upper tract until proven otherwise.
framing: Painful urination is a very high-volume primary-care complaint. In otherwise healthy non-pregnant women, lower UTI is the dominant cause and often needs no culture. In men, the sexually active, the immunocompromised, the pregnant, and those with systemic features, broaden the differential to STI, pyelonephritis and urosepsis.
keyHistory: Onset, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, haematuria, cloudy urine (lower UTI features)
Fever, rigors, loin pain, nausea/vomiting (upper tract / pyelonephritis)
Sexual history, new partner, urethral or vaginal discharge (STI)
Male: flow, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, prostatic symptoms
Recurrent UTI, catheter, recent instrumentation, immunosuppression, diabetes (complicated UTI)
keyExam: Vitals — temperature, HR, BP, RR (sepsis screen)
External genitalia / urethral discharge where relevant

differential.pointers: Fever, rigors, loin pain, costovertebral tenderness, nausea/vomiting; hypotension/tachycardia signal sepsis.
differential.investigation: Urine dip + culture, FBC, U&E, CRP, blood cultures if systemic; sepsis-6 if septic; imaging (US/CT) if obstruction or no response.

differential.pointers: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine, no systemic features.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis in non-pregnant women; urine culture if pregnant, male, recurrent, or treatment failure.

differential.pointers: Urethral/vaginal discharge, new partner, younger; herpes if external vesicles/ulcers.
differential.investigation: NAAT (first-pass urine / swabs); refer to sexual health; consider full STI screen.

differential.pointers: Men, perineal/pelvic pain, fever, tender boggy prostate, voiding symptoms.
differential.investigation: Urine culture; do NOT do vigorous prostatic massage if acute; treat empirically.

differential.pointers: External dysuria, itch, discharge, no frequency/urgency.
differential.investigation: Examination; high vaginal swab if uncertain.

redFlags: Fever, rigors or loin pain (pyelonephritis) → urgent assessment
Sepsis features (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion) → sepsis pathway
Pregnancy with UTI → treat promptly, avoid teratogenic agents
Male UTI or recurrent UTI → investigate underlying cause
Visible haematuria → consider urological referral once infection excluded
initialInvestigations: Urine dipstick (nitrites, leucocytes, blood) and MSU culture where indicated
Pregnancy test in women of reproductive age
FBC, U&E, CRP and blood cultures if systemically unwell
STI NAAT testing if sexual cause suspected
Renal tract ultrasound/CT if obstruction, recurrent or treatment failure
disposition: Uncomplicated lower UTI → empirical antibiotics per local policy + safety-net. Pyelonephritis without sepsis → may treat with oral antibiotics and close follow-up if low risk; admit if systemically unwell, pregnant, vomiting, or obstructed. Suspected urosepsis → admit for IV antibiotics and sepsis management.

references.label: NICE CKS — Urinary tract infection (lower) — women / men; Pyelonephritis (acute).
NICE NG109/NG111 — UTI and pyelonephritis antimicrobial prescribing.

oneLiner: Most sore throats are self-limiting viral pharyngitis. The job is to spot the airway emergencies — epiglottitis/supraglottitis, quinsy and deep-neck-space infection — and to score for streptococcal infection (FeverPAIN/Centor).
framing: An extremely common presentation. Reassure and safety-net the majority, use FeverPAIN or Centor to guide antibiotics, and never miss the rapidly deteriorating airway — a near-normal oropharynx with severe pain, drooling and muffled voice should ring alarm bells for supraglottic infection.
keyHistory: Duration, severity, ability to swallow fluids/saliva (drooling = red flag)
keyExam: Vitals incl. temperature; respiratory effort and stridor
Ability to handle secretions / drooling / tripod posturing
Oropharynx — tonsillar exudate, asymmetry, uvular deviation (quinsy)
Trismus and tender neck masses / lymphadenopathy
AVOID forceful throat examination if epiglottitis suspected

differential.pointers: Severe sore throat with disproportionately normal oropharynx, muffled voice, drooling, dysphagia, fever; stridor is a late, ominous sign.
differential.investigation: Do NOT distress the airway; senior ENT/anaesthetic review; fibreoptic laryngoscopy in controlled setting; manage airway first.

differential.pointers: Severe unilateral pain, trismus, 'hot potato' voice, uvular deviation, peritonsillar swelling.
differential.investigation: Clinical; needle aspiration / incision and drainage by ENT; antibiotics.

differential.pointers: Neck swelling/stiffness, systemic toxicity, unilateral neck/jaw pain; Lemierre's: persistent sepsis after pharyngitis with septic emboli.
differential.investigation: Contrast CT neck; blood cultures; urgent ENT; IV antibiotics.

differential.pointers: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough; higher FeverPAIN/Centor score.
differential.investigation: FeverPAIN or Centor score to guide antibiotics; rapid antigen / throat swab not routinely needed.

differential.pointers: Coryza, cough, hoarseness, low FeverPAIN/Centor; self-limiting.
Adolescents/young adults, marked tonsillar enlargement, fatigue, splenomegaly, posterior cervical nodes.
differential.investigation: FBC (atypical lymphocytes), Monospot/EBV serology; avoid amoxicillin (rash); advise re contact sport if splenomegaly.

redFlags: Stridor, respiratory difficulty or drooling → airway emergency, do not examine throat forcefully
Muffled voice + severe pain + near-normal oropharynx → suspect supraglottic infection
Neck swelling/stiffness with systemic toxicity → deep-neck-space infection
Sore throat on a drug that can cause agranulocytosis (e.g. carbimazole, clozapine) → urgent FBC
initialInvestigations: FeverPAIN or Centor scoring to guide antibiotic decisions
FBC if mononucleosis or drug-induced neutropenia suspected
CT neck and blood cultures if deep-space infection suspected
Throat swab only if specific indication (not routine)
disposition: Self-limiting viral/bacterial sore throat → analgesia, antibiotics only per FeverPAIN/Centor, safety-net. Quinsy → ENT for drainage. Suspected epiglottitis/supraglottitis or deep-neck-space infection → emergency ENT/anaesthetics and admission. Drug-induced neutropenia → stop drug, urgent FBC, admit if neutropenic sepsis.

references.label: NICE NG84 — Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (FeverPAIN/Centor).
ENT UK / RCEM — Acute sore throat and airway red flags.

oneLiner: Most nosebleeds are anterior (Kiesselbach's plexus) and stop with correct first aid. Identify posterior bleeds (older patients, both nostrils/down throat, profuse) and haemodynamic compromise; consider anticoagulation and rare malignancy.
framing: Anterior bleeds account for 90-95% and respond to first aid (firm pressure on the cartilaginous part for 10-15 minutes, leaning forward). Posterior bleeds are more profuse, common in older/anticoagulated patients, and carry airway and haemorrhage risk.
keyHistory: Duration, side(s), volume, clots, blood running down the throat (posterior)
Trauma, nose-picking, recent surgery, foreign body
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets, bleeding disorders, liver disease, alcohol
Hypertension history; recurrent unilateral bleeds (consider tumour)
keyExam: Vitals — HR, BP, signs of hypovolaemia
Anterior rhinoscopy after clot evacuation to identify bleeding point

differential.pointers: Profuse bleeding from both nostrils or down the throat, older patient, failure of anterior measures; risk of aspiration and shock.
differential.investigation: FBC, coagulation, group and save/crossmatch; ENT for posterior packing/balloon; treat shock; admit.

differential.pointers: Visible anterior bleeding point, unilateral, controllable with pressure or cautery.
differential.investigation: Direct visualisation; silver nitrate cautery or anterior packing if needed.

differential.diagnosis: Bleeding due to anticoagulation/antiplatelet or coagulopathy
differential.pointers: On warfarin/DOAC/antiplatelet, liver disease, thrombocytopenia.
differential.investigation: FBC, coagulation, INR; reverse/adjust per local guidance if major bleeding.

differential.pointers: Recurrent unilateral epistaxis, nasal obstruction, facial pain; juvenile angiofibroma in young males.

redFlags: Bleeding down the throat / from both nostrils / not controlled by pressure → posterior bleed, ENT
Anticoagulant-associated major bleeding → reversal per protocol
Recurrent unilateral epistaxis with obstruction → exclude tumour
initialInvestigations: First aid: firm pressure on soft part of nose 10-15 min, lean forward
FBC, coagulation screen, group and save if significant/recurrent or anticoagulated
U&E and crossmatch if major haemorrhage
Consider tranexamic acid for ongoing bleeding per local policy
disposition: Anterior bleed controlled by first aid/cautery → discharge with advice. Failure of anterior measures or posterior bleed → anterior/posterior packing and ENT admission. Haemodynamic instability → resuscitate and admit. Recurrent/unilateral with obstruction → ENT outpatient for tumour exclusion.

references.label: NICE CKS — Epistaxis.
ENT UK — Epistaxis (nosebleeds) guidance.

oneLiner: Most acute cough is self-limiting viral URTI. Exclude pneumonia, PE, heart failure and—when persistent or with red flags—lung cancer/TB. Haemoptysis or weight loss demands urgent workup.
framing: Acute cough (<3 weeks) is usually viral and needs reassurance and safety-netting, not antibiotics. The triage task is identifying lower respiratory tract infection requiring treatment, the deteriorating/hypoxic patient, and red flags pointing to PE, malignancy or TB.
keyHistory: Duration (acute <3 wk / subacute / chronic), sputum, colour, haemoptysis
Weight loss, night sweats, smoking, occupational/TB exposure (cancer/TB)
Choking episode/aspiration risk (foreign body); ACE-inhibitor use
keyExam: Vitals — RR, SpO2, HR, temperature (assess severity)
Respiratory exam — focal crackles/bronchial breathing (consolidation), wheeze, effusion
Signs of heart failure (raised JVP, oedema, gallop)

differential.pointers: Fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, focal signs, raised RR; use CRB-65/CURB-65 for severity.
differential.investigation: Observations, CRB-65/CURB-65, CXR, FBC, U&E, CRP; blood cultures if severe.

differential.pointers: Pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia, haemoptysis, VTE risk; clear chest with hypoxia.
differential.investigation: Wells score, D-dimer if not high probability, CTPA if indicated.

differential.pointers: Persistent cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, age >40 with smoking history, clubbing, supraclavicular nodes.
differential.investigation: Urgent CXR; suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) referral for unexplained haemoptysis or persisting symptoms.

differential.pointers: Orthopnoea, PND, bilateral crackles, oedema, frothy sputum.
Coryza, no focal chest signs, normal vitals, self-limiting.
Cough >3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss, haemoptysis, risk factors/contacts.
differential.investigation: CXR, sputum AFB/culture, consider isolation if active TB suspected.

redFlags: Hypoxia (SpO2 <92% on air) or respiratory distress → urgent assessment
Unexplained weight loss / persistent cough in a smoker → urgent cancer pathway
initialInvestigations: CXR if pneumonia, malignancy, TB or PE suspected, or persistent symptoms
FBC, U&E, CRP if systemically unwell
D-dimer/CTPA per Wells score if PE considered; sputum for TB if indicated
disposition: Viral URTI/acute bronchitis → reassure, safety-net, no routine antibiotics. Pneumonia → treat per severity score; admit if CURB-65 high, hypoxic or septic. PE/malignancy/TB suspicion → appropriate urgent investigation/referral. Heart failure → admit if acutely decompensated.

references.label: NICE NG120 — Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing.
NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (lung).

oneLiner: Not all that wheezes is asthma. Treat acute asthma/COPD exacerbations promptly but consider anaphylaxis, cardiac 'asthma' (pulmonary oedema), inhaled foreign body and central airway obstruction. A silent chest is a life-threatening sign.
framing: Wheeze reflects airflow obstruction. The commonest cause is bronchospasm (asthma/COPD), but the deadly mimics—anaphylaxis, acute left ventricular failure, and mechanical obstruction—must be excluded. Assess severity objectively and watch for exhaustion and silent chest.
keyHistory: Onset and triggers (allergen, exercise, cold, infection, drug/food)
Known asthma/COPD, inhaler use, previous ICU/intubation
Allergic features — urticaria, angioedema, lip/tongue swelling (anaphylaxis)
Orthopnoea, PND, chest pain, cardiac history (cardiac asthma)
Choking episode, sudden onset (foreign body), smoking, hoarseness/stridor (central obstruction)
keyExam: Vitals — RR, SpO2, HR, ability to speak in sentences
Chest — wheeze, air entry, silent chest (severe), crackles (oedema)
Signs of heart failure (raised JVP, oedema), stridor (upper airway)

differential.pointers: Rapid onset after trigger; wheeze with urticaria/angioedema, stridor, hypotension; needs immediate IM adrenaline.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis; IM adrenaline 500 micrograms; ABCDE; mast cell tryptase.

differential.pointers: PEF <50% (severe) / <33%, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, bradycardia, normal/rising CO2.
differential.investigation: PEF, SpO2, ABG if severe; treat with oxygen, nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium, steroids; senior/ICU review.

differential.pointers: Orthopnoea, bilateral crackles, raised JVP, frothy sputum, cardiac history.
differential.investigation: CXR, ECG, troponin, BNP; treat with oxygen, nitrates, diuretics.

differential.pointers: Smoker/known COPD, increased sputum/purulence, breathlessness.
differential.investigation: ABG (CO2 retention), CXR, FBC, CRP; controlled oxygen, bronchodilators, steroids ± antibiotics.

differential.diagnosis: Inhaled foreign body / central airway obstruction
differential.pointers: Sudden onset, monophonic/localised wheeze or stridor, choking history, tumour/goitre.

redFlags: Silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis or altered consciousness → life-threatening, peri-arrest
SpO2 <92% or rising/normal CO2 in acute asthma → critical
Wheeze with angioedema/hypotension after exposure → anaphylaxis, give adrenaline
Stridor or sudden monophonic wheeze → upper-airway/foreign body
Cardiac history with bilateral crackles → pulmonary oedema
initialInvestigations: Observations including SpO2, RR, HR and PEF
ABG if severe or COPD with possible CO2 retention
CXR if pneumonia, pneumothorax, oedema or foreign body considered
ECG, troponin, BNP if cardiac cause suspected
disposition: Anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline, resuscitate, admit for observation. Acute severe/life-threatening asthma or CO2-retaining COPD → admit, consider ICU. Pulmonary oedema → admit and treat. Mild exacerbation responding to treatment → may discharge with steroids/bronchodilators and follow-up.

references.label: BTS/SIGN — British guideline on the management of asthma.
Resuscitation Council UK — Emergency treatment of anaphylactic reactions.

oneLiner: Sudden Airway/Breathing/Circulation compromise with skin/mucosal change after an allergen. The single life-saving action is early IM adrenaline 500 micrograms in the anterolateral thigh — give it before anything else and repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement.
framing: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: sudden onset with rapidly progressing airway, breathing and/or circulation problems, usually with skin/mucosal changes. Common triggers are food, drugs and venom. Adrenaline is the only intervention shown to reduce mortality; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, NOT first-line.
keyHistory: Exposure — food, drug, sting, latex, contrast; timing of onset (usually minutes)
Prior reactions / known allergy / asthma (risk of fatal anaphylaxis)
Symptoms — throat tightness, voice change, breathlessness, dizziness, collapse
Beta-blocker use (may blunt response to adrenaline)
keyExam: Skin/mucosa — urticaria, angioedema, flushing (absent in up to 20%)

differential.pointers: Sudden onset after trigger with ABC compromise ± skin changes; can progress to arrest within minutes.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis; immediate IM adrenaline 500 micrograms; ABCDE; serial mast cell tryptase (baseline, ~1-2 h, >24 h).

differential.pointers: Wheeze and respiratory distress without skin/mucosal change or hypotension; known asthma.
differential.investigation: PEF, SpO2, treat as asthma; overlap with anaphylaxis if allergen exposure.

differential.pointers: Lip/tongue/airway swelling without urticaria or hypotension; ACE-I use or family history.
differential.investigation: Airway assessment; C1 esterase inhibitor if hereditary suspected; stop ACE-I.

differential.pointers: Bradycardia, pallor, rapid recovery when supine, no skin/airway features.

redFlags: Airway swelling, stridor or hoarse voice → imminent airway loss, call for senior/anaesthetic help
Hypotension or collapse → circulatory anaphylaxis, lay flat and raise legs
No improvement after first adrenaline → repeat IM adrenaline at 5 minutes; consider IV adrenaline infusion (specialist)
Biphasic reaction risk → observe after recovery
Known asthma + anaphylaxis → higher fatality risk
initialInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis — do NOT delay adrenaline for tests
IM adrenaline 500 micrograms anterolateral thigh, repeat after 5 min if needed
Mast cell tryptase (serial) to support later diagnosis
ECG and monitoring; refer to allergy clinic after recovery
disposition: All anaphylaxis → resuscitate with adrenaline, oxygen and fluids; admit for observation (biphasic reactions can occur); prescribe adrenaline auto-injectors, provide allergy action plan, and refer to specialist allergy services. Document trigger and avoidance advice.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021).
NICE CG134 — Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment.

oneLiner: A vascular emergency — the 6 Ps (Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishingly cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis). Time-critical: senior vascular referral and IV heparin without delay. Paralysis/fixed mottling suggest irreversible ischaemia.
framing: Sudden arterial occlusion (embolic or thrombotic) threatens the limb within hours. Embolic causes (AF, recent MI) present abruptly in a previously normal limb; thrombotic causes arise on a background of peripheral arterial disease. Paraesthesia and paralysis indicate advanced ischaemia and poorer salvage.
keyHistory: Sudden onset of pain, pallor, coldness, numbness, weakness in a limb
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, aneurysm (embolic source)
keyExam: The 6 Ps — Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Perishingly cold, Paraesthesia, Paralysis
Compare with contralateral limb; assess capillary refill
Palpate and Doppler all pulses; sensory and motor function
Pain on passive movement / tense compartment (compartment syndrome)

differential.pointers: 6 Ps; absent pulses, cold pale limb; paraesthesia/paralysis = threatened/irreversible.
differential.investigation: Urgent vascular review; handheld Doppler; CT angiogram; IV heparin; revascularisation (embolectomy/thrombolysis/bypass).

differential.pointers: Severe pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment; may follow trauma or revascularisation.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis; compartment pressures; emergency fasciotomy.

differential.pointers: Massive DVT can cause a swollen, cyanotic, painful limb (phlegmasia cerulea dolens) threatening viability.
Rest pain, ulceration, gangrene on background of PAD; slower onset.

redFlags: The 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia → emergency vascular referral and IV heparin
Paralysis or fixed mottling → irreversible ischaemia, urgent decision re salvage/amputation
Severe pain on passive movement with tense compartment → compartment syndrome, fasciotomy
Sensory or motor loss → threatened limb, do not delay
initialInvestigations: Handheld arterial Doppler of pedal/limb pulses
IV unfractionated heparin once decision made (per vascular advice)
Bloods — FBC, U&E, coagulation, group and save, CK, lactate
ECG (AF/MI source); CT angiography to define lesion
disposition: Acute limb ischaemia → emergency vascular surgery, anticoagulate, theatre for revascularisation; do not wait for imaging if limb threatened. Irreversible ischaemia → may require amputation. Compartment syndrome → immediate fasciotomy. All require admission under vascular/orthopaedic teams.

references.label: NICE CG147 — Peripheral arterial disease: diagnosis and management.
RCEMLearning — Acute Limb Ischaemia (6 Ps).

oneLiner: A painless intratesticular mass is testicular cancer until proven otherwise. Distinguish from benign extratesticular swellings (hydrocele, epididymal cyst, varicocele) by examination and ultrasound. (For acute painful scrotum, see the acute scrotum pathway.)
framing: Painless scrotal swelling spans benign fluid/cystic causes and the must-not-miss testicular cancer (commonest solid malignancy in young men). The key bedside question is whether the mass arises from the testis (concerning) or is separate/transilluminable (usually benign).
keyHistory: Onset, duration, pain (painless mass raises cancer concern)
Weight loss, back pain, gynaecomastia, breathlessness (metastatic disease)
Risk factors — undescended testis, prior testicular cancer, family history
keyExam: Is the mass intratesticular or separate from the testis?
'Bag of worms' varicocele (left-sided; new right-sided needs renal vein assessment)

differential.pointers: Painless, firm, irregular intratesticular mass that does not transilluminate; young/middle-aged men.
differential.investigation: Urgent scrotal ultrasound; tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH); urology referral; do NOT biopsy through scrotum.

differential.pointers: Painless, transilluminable swelling; new adult hydrocele may overlie a tumour.
differential.investigation: Ultrasound to exclude underlying testicular pathology, especially if rapid or in younger men.

differential.pointers: Separate from testis, transilluminable, smooth.
'Bag of worms', usually left-sided, decompresses lying down; new right-sided / non-decompressing → exclude retroperitoneal mass / renal tumour.
differential.investigation: Ultrasound; abdominal imaging if atypical varicocele.

differential.pointers: Reducible, cough impulse, extends from inguinal region; cannot get above it.
differential.investigation: Clinical; surgical referral; urgent if irreducible/obstructed.

redFlags: Painless firm intratesticular mass → urgent suspected-cancer urology referral
Rapidly enlarging scrotal swelling / new adult hydrocele → ultrasound to exclude tumour
New non-decompressing or right-sided varicocele → exclude retroperitoneal/renal mass
Irreducible, tender hernia → suspect obstruction/strangulation, surgical emergency
initialInvestigations: Serum tumour markers — AFP, beta-hCG, LDH if tumour suspected
Urology referral (suspected-cancer pathway for testicular mass)
Abdominal/chest imaging for staging if malignancy confirmed
disposition: Suspected testicular cancer → urgent urology referral via cancer pathway, ultrasound and markers. Clearly benign cyst/hydrocele/varicocele → reassure; elective referral if symptomatic. Irreducible/obstructed hernia → emergency surgical referral.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (testicular).
BAUS — Scrotal swellings and testicular cancer guidance.

oneLiner: Acute swallowing difficulty: exclude oesophageal food-bolus obstruction (and complete obstruction with inability to swallow saliva), stroke-related aspiration risk, and oesophageal perforation. Progressive dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent cancer workup.
framing: Distinguish oropharyngeal dysphagia (difficulty initiating the swallow, coughing/choking, nasal regurgitation — often neurological) from oesophageal dysphagia (food sticking after swallowing). Acute total obstruction and perforation are emergencies; persistent progressive dysphagia for solids signals malignancy.
keyHistory: Onset (sudden = bolus/stroke), solids vs liquids, progression
Inability to swallow own saliva, drooling (complete obstruction)
Severe chest/back pain after vomiting or instrumentation (perforation)
keyExam: Ability to handle saliva; hydration status
Neurological exam — cranial nerves, swallow/gag, limb signs (stroke)

differential.pointers: Severe chest/back pain, after vomiting or endoscopy, surgical emphysema, tachycardia, sepsis.
differential.investigation: CT with contrast; urgent surgical referral; resuscitate.

differential.pointers: Sudden inability to swallow saliva, drooling, distress; aspiration risk.
differential.investigation: Urgent endoscopy for disimpaction; investigate underlying stricture/eosinophilic oesophagitis.

differential.pointers: Sudden oropharyngeal dysphagia, coughing on swallow, with focal neurology; high aspiration risk.
differential.investigation: Urgent stroke assessment/imaging; NBM and swallow screen; protect airway.

differential.pointers: Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids), weight loss, anaemia, older patient.
differential.investigation: Urgent (2-week-wait) upper GI endoscopy; CT staging if malignancy.

differential.pointers: Dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, chest pain; younger patient.

redFlags: Inability to swallow saliva / drooling → complete obstruction, urgent endoscopy and airway protection
Severe chest/back pain with surgical emphysema or sepsis → oesophageal perforation
Acute dysphagia with focal neurology → stroke, urgent assessment, keep NBM
Progressive dysphagia + weight loss → urgent suspected upper GI cancer referral
initialInvestigations: Assess ability to manage secretions and aspiration risk; keep NBM if unsafe swallow
Urgent endoscopy for food-bolus obstruction or to investigate dysphagia
CT with contrast if perforation suspected
Stroke imaging and swallow screen if neurological cause
FBC and bloods; 2-week-wait referral for progressive solid dysphagia
disposition: Complete obstruction or perforation → emergency endoscopy/surgery and admission. Stroke → stroke unit, NBM until swallow assessed. Progressive dysphagia with weight loss → urgent upper GI endoscopy via cancer pathway. Resolved food bolus → arrange endoscopy to find underlying cause.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (upper GI).
BSG — Guidelines on oesophageal dysphagia and food bolus management.

oneLiner: Usually functional, but exclude bowel obstruction (especially with vomiting, distension, no flatus), colorectal cancer (change in bowel habit, bleeding, weight loss, anaemia), and faecal impaction with overflow in the frail/elderly.
framing: Constipation is common and usually responds to lifestyle measures and laxatives. The triage priorities are spotting mechanical obstruction, identifying red flags for colorectal cancer warranting urgent referral/FIT testing, and recognising faecal impaction with overflow diarrhoea in older patients.
keyHistory: Duration, stool frequency/consistency, straining, incomplete evacuation
Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, mucus, tenesmus (cancer)
Vomiting, abdominal distension, absolute constipation (no flatus) — obstruction
Weight loss, anaemia symptoms, family history of colorectal cancer
Drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, iron), immobility, hypothyroid/hypercalcaemia features
keyExam: Abdominal exam — distension, tenderness, masses, bowel sounds
Digital rectal examination — impaction, mass, blood, tone

differential.pointers: Colicky pain, distension, vomiting, absolute constipation (no flatus), tinkling/absent bowel sounds.
differential.investigation: Abdominal X-ray/CT; bloods (U&E, lactate); NBM, IV fluids, NG tube; surgical referral.

differential.pointers: Persistent change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass.
differential.investigation: FIT testing and 2-week-wait referral per NICE NG12; colonoscopy.

differential.pointers: Elderly/immobile, leakage of loose stool (overflow), palpable hard faeces, full rectum on PR.
differential.investigation: PR exam, abdominal X-ray; disimpaction regimen.

differential.pointers: Low fibre/fluid, inactivity, no red flags; chronic and stable.
Medication review; features of hypothyroidism or hypercalcaemia.
differential.investigation: TFTs, calcium, U&E; review constipating drugs.

redFlags: Vomiting, distension and absolute constipation → bowel obstruction, surgical assessment
Rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia or abdominal/rectal mass → urgent colorectal cancer pathway / FIT
New change in bowel habit in older adults → investigate, do not assume benign
Overflow diarrhoea in the frail elderly → faecal impaction
initialInvestigations: FIT testing and 2-week-wait referral if cancer red flags
disposition: Functional constipation → lifestyle advice, laxatives, review. Faecal impaction → disimpaction regimen, treat in community unless complications. Suspected obstruction → admit for surgical assessment. Cancer red flags → urgent referral/FIT and colonoscopy.

references.label: NICE CKS — Constipation.
NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (lower GI).

oneLiner: Bright-red bleeding is usually benign anorectal disease, but never attribute bleeding to haemorrhoids without excluding colorectal cancer, and resuscitate brisk lower GI haemorrhage. New bleeding in older adults warrants investigation.
framing: Most rectal bleeding seen in primary care is from haemorrhoids or fissures, but rectal bleeding has a meaningful predictive value for colorectal cancer especially with change in bowel habit, weight loss or anaemia. Acute large-volume bleeding (often diverticular or angiodysplasia) can be life-threatening.
keyHistory: Colour (bright red = distal; dark/melaena = upper GI), volume, clots
Mixed with stool vs on paper/dripping (anorectal)
Change in bowel habit, tenesmus, weight loss, anaemia symptoms
NSAIDs, anticoagulants, diverticular history, family history of CRC
keyExam: Abdominal exam and digital rectal examination
Anal inspection — fissure, prolapsing haemorrhoids, mass

differential.pointers: Large-volume fresh bleeding, haemodynamic instability, often painless; older patients.
differential.investigation: Resuscitate; FBC, coagulation, group and crossmatch; CT angiography/colonoscopy; consider upper GI source if unstable.
