differential.pointers: Bleeding with change in bowel habit, weight loss, anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass; older age.
differential.investigation: FIT/2-week-wait referral per NICE NG12; colonoscopy.

differential.pointers: Bright-red blood on paper/coating stool, painless, prolapsing lumps.
differential.investigation: Clinical/proctoscopy; exclude proximal pathology in older patients.

differential.pointers: Severe pain on defecation, bright-red streaking; posterior midline tear.
Bloody diarrhoea, urgency, systemic features, younger patient or travel/contacts.
differential.investigation: Stool culture, faecal calprotectin, inflammatory markers, endoscopy.

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability with large-volume bleeding → resuscitate, crossmatch, admit
Rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit/weight loss/anaemia → urgent colorectal cancer pathway
New rectal bleeding in older adults → investigate, do not attribute to haemorrhoids
Black tarry stool (melaena) → consider upper GI source
initialInvestigations: Observations and assessment of blood loss
Digital rectal examination and anal inspection ± proctoscopy
FBC, U&E, coagulation; group and save/crossmatch if significant
FIT and 2-week-wait referral for cancer red flags; colonoscopy
CT angiography if acute major bleeding
disposition: Minor anorectal bleeding with no red flags → treat cause, safety-net, FIT if uncertain. Cancer red flags → urgent referral and colonoscopy. Acute major bleeding → resuscitate and admit under surgery/gastroenterology for endoscopy/angiography.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (lower GI).
ACPGBI/RCS — Commissioning guide: rectal bleeding.

oneLiner: Hiccups lasting >48 h (persistent) or >1 month (intractable) are not benign — investigate along the hiccup reflex arc. Must-not-miss causes include brainstem/posterior-circulation stroke and CNS lesions, plus thoracic and metabolic pathology.
framing: Transient hiccups are benign. Persistent (>48 h) or intractable (>1 month) hiccups warrant a search along the reflex arc — vagus and phrenic nerves, the brainstem hiccup centre, and the diaphragm. Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) stroke is a classic and dangerous cause; also consider GORD, thoracic and metabolic disease.
keyHistory: Duration (transient <48 h / persistent >48 h / intractable >1 month)
Neurological symptoms — vertigo, dysphagia, dysarthria, limb signs (brainstem stroke)
Reflux, heartburn, recent GI surgery (GORD/diaphragmatic irritation)
Chest symptoms, mediastinal disease, recent surgery (phrenic irritation)
Weight loss, alcohol, uraemia, electrolyte issues; medications
keyExam: Full neurological exam, especially cranial nerves and cerebellar signs (posterior circulation)
ENT/oropharynx (foreign body in ear canal, etc.)

differential.diagnosis: Brainstem / posterior-circulation stroke or CNS lesion
differential.pointers: Persistent hiccups with vertigo, dysphagia, dysarthria, ataxia or sensory crossed signs (lateral medullary syndrome); tumour/MS.
differential.investigation: Urgent neurological assessment; MRI brain (posterior fossa); stroke pathway if acute.

differential.pointers: Reflux symptoms, recent abdominal surgery, subphrenic collection.
differential.investigation: Trial PPI; imaging (CXR, US/CT) if subphrenic pathology suspected.

differential.pointers: Lung/mediastinal mass, pericarditis, recent thoracic surgery.

differential.diagnosis: Metabolic / drug-related causes (uraemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, alcohol, steroids)
differential.pointers: Renal failure, electrolyte derangement, relevant drugs.

redFlags: Persistent hiccups with focal neurology / posterior-circulation symptoms → urgent brain imaging
Hiccups >48 h (persistent) or >1 month (intractable) → investigate underlying cause
Associated weight loss, dysphagia or chest mass → exclude malignancy
Hiccups with metabolic derangement → correct and investigate
initialInvestigations: Targeted history and full neurological examination
MRI brain (especially posterior fossa) if neurological cause suspected
CT chest/abdomen if thoracic or subphrenic pathology suspected
disposition: Transient hiccups → reassure. Persistent/intractable hiccups → investigate cause; urgent neuro-imaging and admission if posterior-circulation stroke/CNS lesion suspected. Treat identified cause (e.g. PPI for reflux) and consider pharmacotherapy for symptom control under specialist advice.

references.label: Steger M et al. Systematic review: the pathogenesis and pharmacological treatment of hiccups.
BMJ Best Practice — Hiccups (assessment of persistent/intractable).

oneLiner: Fever in an infant under 90 days is high-risk for invasive bacterial infection (bacteraemia, meningitis, UTI). Have a low threshold for full septic screen and empirical antibiotics — clinical signs are unreliable in this age group.
framing: Young infants mount poor localising responses, so a temperature 38C or above (especially under 3 months per NICE) is itself a red feature. Risk stratify using clinical appearance, age and inflammatory markers, but maintain a cautious approach with septic screen, parenteral antibiotics and admission for most.
keyHistory: Exact age in days and recorded temperature (>=38C is a red flag under 3 months)
Feeding, wet nappies, alertness, tone, cry
Maternal/perinatal risk (GBS, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever)
keyExam: Appearance using NICE traffic-light system (activity, colour, respiratory effort, hydration)
Full set of observations including temperature, HR, RR, SpO2, capillary refill
Source-seeking exam (chest, abdomen, ENT, joints, skin)

differential.pointers: Poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, bulging fontanelle, seizures; signs often subtle in young infants.
differential.investigation: Lumbar puncture (especially under 28 days or if any concern), blood cultures, empirical IV/IM antibiotics without delay.

differential.pointers: Toxic appearance, tachycardia, poor perfusion, abnormal inflammatory markers.
differential.investigation: Blood culture, FBC, CRP, procalcitonin per local pathway; sepsis-6; empirical antibiotics.

differential.pointers: Commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infants; often no localising signs.
differential.investigation: Clean-catch/catheter urine for microscopy and culture; positive urinalysis raises bacteraemia risk.

differential.pointers: Tachypnoea, recession, hypoxia, focal chest signs.
Neonatal HSV can be devastating; consider in unwell neonate with seizures, vesicles or deranged LFTs.
differential.investigation: HSV PCR (blood/CSF), consider empirical aciclovir if neonatal HSV suspected.

redFlags: Any fever >=38C in an infant under 3 months → high-risk, urgent assessment
Toxic/unwell appearance, poor perfusion, apnoea → sepsis pathway
Non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, seizures → meningococcal/meningitis
Under 28 days → low threshold for LP and empirical antibiotics including HSV cover if suspected
initialInvestigations: Full septic screen — blood culture, FBC, CRP (± procalcitonin), urine, consider LP
Blood glucose, U&E, blood gas if unwell
Empirical parenteral antibiotics per local neonatal/paediatric sepsis policy without delay
disposition: Almost all febrile infants under 90 days warrant hospital assessment; under 3 months with fever generally require septic screen, parenteral antibiotics and admission. Apply NICE NG143 traffic-light and local febrile-infant pathways; never discharge a febrile neonate without senior paediatric review.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management (traffic light).
NICE NG51 — Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management.

oneLiner: Reduced or absent urine output signals acute kidney injury or obstruction. Exclude post-renal obstruction (palpable bladder, hydronephrosis) which is rapidly reversible, treat life-threatening hyperkalaemia, and identify pre-renal and intrinsic causes.
framing: Categorise into pre-renal (hypoperfusion), renal (intrinsic, e.g. ATN, glomerulonephritis) and post-renal (obstruction). Anuria especially suggests obstruction or a vascular catastrophe. The immediate priorities are relieving obstruction, restoring perfusion, and managing hyperkalaemia and fluid overload.
keyHistory: Urine output trend, anuria vs oliguria, lower urinary symptoms/retention
Volume status — vomiting, diarrhoea, bleeding, sepsis (pre-renal)
Known prostate disease, pelvic malignancy, stones (post-renal)
keyExam: Volume status — BP (incl. postural), HR, JVP, mucous membranes, oedema
Signs of fluid overload (pulmonary oedema) and uraemia

differential.pointers: Rising potassium with ECG changes (peaked T waves, broad QRS) is immediately life-threatening.
differential.investigation: U&E, ABG/VBG, ECG; treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, salbutamol); dialysis if refractory.

differential.pointers: Anuria/oliguria with palpable bladder or hydronephrosis; prostatic disease, pelvic malignancy, stones.
differential.investigation: Bladder scan; catheterise if retention; renal tract ultrasound for hydronephrosis; relieve obstruction.

differential.pointers: Volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure; responds to perfusion restoration.
differential.investigation: Assess and correct volume; treat cause; monitor response.

differential.diagnosis: Intrinsic renal disease (ATN, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis)
differential.pointers: Nephrotoxins, ischaemia, haematuria/proteinuria, systemic features.
differential.investigation: Urinalysis, urine microscopy, immunology if GN suspected; nephrology referral.

redFlags: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes → treat immediately, urgent nephrology
Anuria → exclude obstruction and vascular cause urgently
Fluid overload/pulmonary oedema in AKI → may need urgent dialysis
Severe metabolic acidosis or uraemic complications → dialysis
initialInvestigations: U&E and bicarbonate (assess AKI stage and potassium)
Bladder scan and catheterisation if retention; renal tract ultrasound
Urinalysis ± microscopy; FBC, CRP, CK; immunology if GN suspected
disposition: Treat hyperkalaemia and fluid overload immediately. Relieve obstruction (catheter/nephrostomy). Correct pre-renal causes. Admit for intrinsic renal disease, refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, or oligo-anuric AKI; involve nephrology and consider renal replacement therapy.

references.label: NICE NG148 — Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management.
Renal Association / UK Kidney Association — Treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults.

oneLiner: First exclude pregnancy. Then the must-not-miss is gynaecological malignancy — postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Use PALM-COEIN to frame structural vs non-structural causes; resuscitate heavy acute bleeding.
framing: Abnormal uterine bleeding covers heavy menstrual bleeding, intermenstrual, postcoital and postmenopausal bleeding. The PALM-COEIN system separates structural (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy/hyperplasia) from non-structural (coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not classified) causes. Pregnancy must always be excluded first.
keyHistory: Pattern — heavy menstrual, intermenstrual, postcoital, postmenopausal bleeding
Age and menopausal status (postmenopausal bleeding = cancer until excluded)
Endometrial cancer risk — obesity, diabetes, tamoxifen, unopposed oestrogen, family history
keyExam: Speculum — cervix (polyp, lesion, ectropion, source of bleeding)

differential.pointers: Postmenopausal bleeding, persistent intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, suspicious cervix; older age and risk factors.
differential.investigation: Pregnancy test; 2-week-wait referral; transvaginal ultrasound, hysteroscopy + endometrial biopsy; colposcopy if cervical lesion.

differential.diagnosis: Acute heavy uterine bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
differential.pointers: Large volume bleeding, tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia.
differential.investigation: Resuscitate; FBC, coagulation, group and save; tranexamic acid/hormonal control; gynaecology.

differential.pointers: Heavy/prolonged menses, bulky uterus, intermenstrual bleeding.
Irregular cycles, extremes of reproductive age, PCOS, thyroid disease.
differential.investigation: TFTs, hormonal assessment; treat underlying cause.

differential.pointers: Heavy bleeding since menarche, easy bruising, anticoagulant use.
differential.investigation: FBC, coagulation, von Willebrand screen; review anticoagulation.

redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding → urgent suspected gynaecological cancer referral
Persistent intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding / suspicious cervix → urgent referral
Haemodynamic compromise from heavy bleeding → resuscitate and admit
Positive pregnancy test with bleeding → manage as early pregnancy / ectopic pathway
initialInvestigations: FBC (anaemia); coagulation and group and save if heavy bleeding
Transvaginal ultrasound; hysteroscopy + endometrial biopsy as indicated
TFTs/hormonal tests for suspected ovulatory dysfunction
disposition: Postmenopausal or persistent abnormal bleeding → urgent gynaecology referral via cancer pathway. Heavy acute bleeding → resuscitate, medical management (tranexamic acid, hormonal), admit if unstable. Stable benign-pattern bleeding → investigate and treat underlying cause in community/outpatient setting.

references.label: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (gynaecological).
NICE NG88 — Heavy menstrual bleeding: assessment and management; FIGO PALM-COEIN.

oneLiner: A transient focal deficit (sudden face/arm/leg weakness, speech or visual disturbance) that has resolved is a TIA until proven otherwise — a medical emergency and warning of imminent stroke. Distinguish from mimics (hypoglycaemia, seizure, migraine).
framing: TIA confers high short-term stroke risk; urgent assessment, antiplatelet therapy and specialist review reduce recurrence. Always check glucose (hypoglycaemia mimics stroke). For persisting deficit, follow the acute stroke pathway. Identify cardioembolic sources such as AF.
keyHistory: Exact symptoms — unilateral weakness, facial droop, dysphasia, visual loss (amaurosis fugax), ataxia
Onset, duration, complete resolution (TIA) vs persistence (stroke)
Vascular risk factors — AF, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, prior stroke
Mimic features — preceding aura/headache (migraine), tongue-biting/post-ictal (seizure), low glucose
keyExam: Full neurological exam (may be normal if resolved)
Cardiac rhythm (AF), blood pressure, carotid bruits
Use a validated stroke recognition tool (FAST/ROSIER)

differential.diagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack / minor ischaemic stroke
differential.pointers: Sudden focal deficit, vascular risk factors; high early stroke recurrence risk.
differential.investigation: Urgent TIA clinic/specialist assessment; aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated); brain imaging, carotid imaging, ECG for AF.

differential.diagnosis: Acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (persisting deficit)
differential.pointers: Deficit not resolved; candidate for thrombolysis/thrombectomy if ischaemic and in window.
differential.investigation: Immediate stroke pathway, urgent CT/CT angiography; do not give aspirin until haemorrhage excluded.

differential.pointers: Diabetic on treatment; focal deficit resolving with glucose.
Preceding convulsion, post-ictal confusion, tongue-biting.
Younger, gradual spreading symptoms, headache, prior similar episodes.
differential.investigation: Clinical; diagnosis of exclusion after vascular causes considered.

redFlags: Persisting focal deficit → acute stroke pathway, urgent imaging (do not delay)
Resolved focal deficit → treat as TIA, urgent specialist assessment, aspirin 300 mg
Hypoglycaemia → treat immediately before attributing to stroke
Crescendo TIAs / AF → high risk, urgent admission
initialInvestigations: Urgent brain imaging per pathway (CT/MRI); carotid imaging
Validated tool (FAST/ROSIER); ABCD2 used historically but urgent assessment for all
Aspirin 300 mg if TIA suspected and haemorrhage not a concern
disposition: Persisting deficit → emergency stroke admission for imaging and reperfusion assessment. Resolved deficit (TIA) → aspirin 300 mg and urgent specialist TIA assessment (within 24 h for high-risk). Treat hypoglycaemia immediately. Address modifiable risk factors and cardioembolic sources.

references.label: NICE NG128 — Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management.
Royal College of Physicians — National Clinical Guideline for Stroke.

oneLiner: Fever (or sepsis signs) in a patient on chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise — an oncological emergency. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour; do not wait for the neutrophil count.
framing: Neutropenic sepsis is defined as temperature >38C (or signs/symptoms of sepsis) in a patient with neutrophils typically <0.5 x10^9/L (or expected to fall), usually 7-14 days post-chemotherapy. Mortality is high if antibiotics are delayed. Treat empirically immediately, then risk-stratify.
keyHistory: Fever, rigors, or any signs of infection/sepsis
Localising symptoms (chest, urinary, GI, skin, perianal)
keyExam: Full set of observations and NEWS2 / sepsis screen
Examine all potential sources including line sites, mouth, perianal area
Avoid digital rectal examination if neutropenic (risk of bacteraemia)
Signs of shock — hypotension, tachycardia, poor perfusion

differential.pointers: Fever or sepsis signs in a chemotherapy patient; may deteriorate rapidly even when initially well-appearing.
differential.investigation: Blood cultures (peripheral + line), FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, lactate, urinalysis, CXR; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour — do NOT await neutrophil count.

differential.pointers: Hypotension/lactataemia not responding to fluids.
differential.investigation: Sepsis-6, fluids, vasopressors, critical care referral.

differential.pointers: Central venous catheter, erythema/discharge at site, rigors with line use.
differential.investigation: Paired cultures (line and peripheral); consider line removal.

differential.pointers: Localising symptoms guide source control but do not delay empirical antibiotics.

redFlags: Fever/sepsis signs in a chemotherapy patient → treat as neutropenic sepsis, antibiotics within 1 hour
Hypotension, lactataemia, altered consciousness → septic shock, critical care
Do NOT delay antibiotics for the blood count
Avoid PR examination and unnecessary mucosal trauma while neutropenic
initialInvestigations: Blood cultures (peripheral and from any central line) before antibiotics if no delay
FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, lactate, clotting
Empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local neutropenic-sepsis policy within 1 hour
disposition: Treat all suspected neutropenic sepsis with immediate empirical IV antibiotics and admission. High-risk or unstable patients → escalate to critical care. Continue antibiotics and source control; involve oncology. Low-risk patients may step down per local protocol once assessed.

references.label: NICE CG151 — Neutropenic sepsis: prevention and management in people with cancer.
NICE NG51 — Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management.

oneLiner: Marked hyperglycaemia with dehydration: distinguish diabetic ketoacidosis (ketones, acidosis, often type 1) from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (very high glucose/osmolality, minimal ketones, older type 2). Both are emergencies; abdominal pain in DKA may mimic an acute abdomen.
framing: DKA: hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis. HHS: profound hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality with little/no ketosis and marked dehydration, usually in older type 2 patients. Look for the precipitant (infection, missed insulin, MI). Fluids, insulin and potassium management are the priorities.
keyHistory: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, lethargy, confusion
Known diabetes, insulin omission, new diagnosis
Precipitants — infection, MI, stroke, drugs (steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors)
keyExam: Hydration and volume status, BP, HR
Conscious level (GCS) — reduced in HHS/severe DKA

differential.pointers: Hyperglycaemia (may be modest in euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2i), ketonaemia, metabolic acidosis; abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing.
differential.investigation: Capillary/blood ketones, glucose, VBG (acidosis), U&E, bicarbonate; fixed-rate insulin infusion, IV fluids, potassium replacement; treat precipitant.

differential.pointers: Very high glucose, high osmolality, minimal ketones/acidosis, marked dehydration, altered consciousness; older type 2 patients; high VTE risk.
differential.investigation: Glucose, osmolality, U&E, ketones; gradual fluid replacement, cautious insulin, VTE prophylaxis; treat precipitant.

differential.pointers: Infection is a common trigger and may itself be life-threatening.
differential.investigation: Septic screen and treat per sepsis pathway.

differential.pointers: May precipitate crisis, especially in older/diabetic patients; symptoms may be atypical.

redFlags: Reduced consciousness, severe acidosis (pH <7.1) or hypokalaemia → critical care
Hyperosmolality with confusion (HHS) → careful correction, VTE prophylaxis
Severe abdominal pain in DKA → may be the metabolic disturbance, but exclude surgical cause
initialInvestigations: Capillary and laboratory glucose; blood/urine ketones
Venous blood gas (pH, bicarbonate), U&E (potassium critical), osmolality
ECG, troponin if cardiac precipitant suspected; septic screen
Hourly glucose/ketones and electrolyte monitoring during treatment
Manage per DKA/HHS protocol — fluids, fixed-rate insulin (DKA), potassium replacement
disposition: Admit all DKA and HHS for protocol-driven management with close monitoring; severe acidosis, reduced consciousness, hypokalaemia or shock warrant HDU/ICU. Identify and treat the precipitant. Involve diabetes specialist team and arrange education/follow-up.

references.label: Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) — Management of DKA in adults.
Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) — Management of HHS in adults.

oneLiner: Low blood glucose can mimic stroke, seizure or intoxication and is rapidly reversible — check glucose in every collapsed, confused or fitting patient and treat immediately. In non-diabetics, document Whipple's triad and seek a cause.
framing: In treated diabetics, hypoglycaemia is common (insulin/sulfonylureas) and an emergency. Neuroglycopenic features (confusion, focal deficit, seizure, coma) appear at low glucose; adrenergic features (sweating, tremor, palpitations) are warning signs. Always treat first; investigate cause if non-diabetic (Whipple's triad).
keyHistory: Diabetes and treatment (insulin, sulfonylureas), recent dose/missed meals
Symptoms — sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion, behaviour change, seizure, coma
Alcohol, liver disease, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, malnutrition
Drugs causing hypoglycaemia; recent bariatric surgery
keyExam: Conscious level (GCS), focal neurology (may mimic stroke)
Signs of sepsis, liver disease, adrenal insufficiency
Recovery with treatment (part of Whipple's triad)

differential.pointers: Treated diabetic; sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can be prolonged and recurrent.
differential.investigation: Glucose; treat with fast-acting carbohydrate/IV glucose/glucagon; admit/observe sulfonylurea overdose for recurrence.

differential.diagnosis: Hypoglycaemia from critical illness / sepsis / liver failure
differential.pointers: Unwell patient, organ failure, sepsis; hypoglycaemia is a poor prognostic sign.
differential.investigation: Treat hypoglycaemia and underlying illness; septic screen, LFTs.

differential.pointers: Binge alcohol, poor intake, malnutrition.
differential.investigation: Glucose, treat; thiamine before glucose if alcohol-dependent/at risk of Wernicke's.

differential.pointers: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypotension, pigmentation.
differential.investigation: U&E, cortisol; treat suspected Addisonian crisis with steroids.

differential.pointers: Recurrent fasting hypoglycaemia in non-diabetic; relief with food.
differential.investigation: Supervised fast with insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, sulfonylurea screen; endocrine referral.

redFlags: Reduced consciousness, seizure or focal deficit with low glucose → treat immediately
Hypoglycaemia mimicking stroke → check and correct glucose before attributing to stroke
Sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin → risk of prolonged/recurrent hypoglycaemia, admit/observe
At-risk of Wernicke's (alcohol/malnutrition) → give thiamine before/with glucose
initialInvestigations: Treat first — oral fast-acting carbohydrate, or IV glucose/IM glucagon if unable to swallow
If non-diabetic and cause unclear: take a 'hypo screen' (insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, sulfonylurea levels) at the time of hypoglycaemia
U&E, LFTs, septic screen as indicated; thiamine if at risk
Recheck glucose after treatment and monitor for recurrence
disposition: Treat all symptomatic hypoglycaemia immediately and recheck glucose. Diabetics who recover fully and have a clear cause may be discharged with advice and review of medication; sulfonylurea/long-acting insulin hypoglycaemia needs observation/admission. Non-diabetic or recurrent hypoglycaemia → investigate and refer to endocrinology.

references.label: Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) — The hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes.
Endocrine Society — Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycemic disorders (Whipple's triad).

oneLiner: Severe or rapidly developing hyponatraemia causes cerebral oedema — headache, confusion, seizures and coma. Severe symptoms warrant hypertonic saline; correct cautiously to avoid osmotic demyelination. Classify by volume status to find the cause.
framing: Hyponatraemia is a level not a diagnosis; the danger is cerebral oedema in acute/severe cases. Assess volume status (hypovolaemic, euvolaemic — often SIADH, hypervolaemic) and exclude adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism. Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia is an emergency; over-rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
keyHistory: Neurological symptoms — headache, nausea, confusion, seizures, drowsiness
Speed of onset (acute <48 h is higher risk of cerebral oedema)
Fluid losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics) vs gains (heart/liver failure)
Malignancy, chest disease (SIADH); polydipsia; possible adrenal insufficiency
keyExam: Conscious level and any seizure activity
Volume status — JVP, skin turgor, oedema, postural BP
Signs of underlying cause (malignancy, chest disease, hypothyroid, adrenal insufficiency)

differential.diagnosis: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema
differential.pointers: Seizures, marked confusion, coma, especially with acute fall in sodium.
differential.investigation: Urgent sodium; hypertonic (3%) saline boluses per protocol for severe symptoms; senior/critical care input; controlled correction.

differential.pointers: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, pigmentation.
differential.investigation: Cortisol, U&E, glucose; treat with hydrocortisone if suspected.

differential.pointers: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia, concentrated urine (urine osmolality high, urine sodium >20-40), malignancy, chest/CNS disease, drugs.
differential.investigation: Paired serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium; fluid restriction; treat cause.

differential.pointers: Volume depletion, low urine sodium (non-renal loss).
Oedema, ascites, raised JVP.

redFlags: Seizures, marked confusion or coma → severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, give hypertonic saline urgently
Acute fall in sodium (<48 h) → high risk of cerebral oedema
Features of adrenal insufficiency → treat empirically with steroids
Avoid over-rapid correction (generally <10 mmol/L in 24 h) → risk of osmotic demyelination
initialInvestigations: Urgent serum sodium and full U&E; glucose
Paired serum and urine osmolality, urine sodium (classify cause)
TFTs and cortisol if euvolaemic / adrenal insufficiency suspected
disposition: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia → emergency treatment with hypertonic saline and admission with close sodium monitoring; involve critical care. Treat the underlying cause based on volume status. Correct sodium at a controlled rate to avoid osmotic demyelination. Specialist (endocrine/nephrology) input for SIADH and complex cases.

references.label: European (ERBP/ESE/ESICM) Clinical Practice Guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia.
Society for Endocrinology — Emergency management of severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.

oneLiner: A prolonged erection unrelated to stimulation. Ischaemic (low-flow) priapism is a compartment syndrome of the penis and a time-critical emergency — painful, rigid corpora with soft glans; aspiration/intervention within hours preserves function.
framing: Distinguish ischaemic (low-flow) priapism — painful, rigid, dark hypoxic cavernosal blood, a true emergency — from non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism, which is painless, not fully rigid, and usually post-traumatic. Ischaemic priapism beyond a few hours risks irreversible fibrosis and erectile dysfunction.
keyHistory: Duration of erection (>4 h ischaemic is emergency), pain (rigid painful = ischaemic)
Trigger — intracavernosal/oral ED drugs, recreational drugs, antipsychotics, trauma
Sickle cell disease/trait or other haematological disorder
keyExam: Rigidity of corpora cavernosa with soft glans (ischaemic)

differential.pointers: Painful fully rigid corpora with soft glans, >4 hours; dark hypoxic/acidotic cavernosal blood gas.
differential.investigation: Cavernosal blood gas (hypoxic, hypercarbic, acidotic); urgent urology — aspiration ± phenylephrine, then surgical shunt; treat within hours.

differential.diagnosis: Priapism secondary to sickle cell disease
differential.pointers: Known/undiagnosed sickle cell; may be recurrent.
differential.investigation: Treat as ischaemic priapism urgently; hydration, oxygen, analgesia, exchange transfusion per haematology; do not delay local treatment.

differential.pointers: Painless, not fully rigid, follows perineal/penile trauma (arteriovenous fistula).
differential.investigation: Cavernosal blood gas (well-oxygenated); Doppler ultrasound; not an emergency, urology referral, may resolve or need embolisation.

redFlags: Painful rigid erection >4 hours → ischaemic priapism, urgent urology, time-critical
Sickle cell disease with priapism → treat urgently as ischaemic + haematology input
Delay risks permanent erectile dysfunction from cavernosal fibrosis
Recurrent (stuttering) priapism → urological assessment and prevention strategy
initialInvestigations: Cavernosal blood gas to differentiate ischaemic vs non-ischaemic
Urgent urology referral for ischaemic priapism (aspiration ± phenylephrine, shunt)
disposition: Ischaemic priapism → emergency urology for aspiration/intracavernosal phenylephrine and surgical shunt if needed; admit. Sickle-related → urgent urological treatment plus haematology management. Non-ischaemic → urology referral, often conservative or selective embolisation. Treat/avoid precipitants and follow up.

references.label: EAU Guidelines — Priapism (sexual and reproductive health).
AUA/SMSNA Guideline (2022) — Diagnosis and management of priapism.

oneLiner: Determine if facial weakness is lower motor neurone (forehead involved — Bell's palsy/Ramsay Hunt) or upper motor neurone (forehead spared — stroke). UMN facial weakness with other deficits is a stroke until proven otherwise; look for a vesicular rash (Ramsay Hunt).
framing: Forehead-sparing facial weakness (the forehead has bilateral cortical innervation) points to a central (UMN) lesion — treat as stroke if acute with other features. Forehead-involving weakness is a lower motor neurone lesion: most commonly Bell's palsy, but exclude Ramsay Hunt (zoster), otitis, parotid lesions and Lyme disease.
keyHistory: Speed of onset (sudden over minutes suggests stroke; over hours/days suggests Bell's)
Associated limb weakness, slurred speech, sensory loss (stroke)
Ear pain, vesicles, hearing loss, vertigo (Ramsay Hunt)
Tick bite/rash (Lyme), parotid mass, bilateral palsy
keyExam: Can the patient wrinkle the forehead/close the eye on the affected side?
Full neurological exam for other deficits (stroke)
Examine ear canal/pinna for zoster vesicles (Ramsay Hunt) and otitis
Parotid examination; eye closure and corneal protection

differential.pointers: Forehead spared, sudden onset, other neurological signs (limb weakness, dysarthria).
differential.investigation: Stroke pathway; urgent imaging; do NOT label as Bell's if forehead spared or other deficits.

differential.pointers: LMN palsy with painful vesicles in/around the ear, hearing loss, vertigo.
differential.investigation: Clinical; antivirals plus corticosteroids early; ENT/ophthalmology if needed.

differential.pointers: Acute unilateral LMN facial weakness including forehead, no rash, no other neurology.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis of exclusion; corticosteroids within 72 h; eye protection.

differential.pointers: Ear infection signs, chronic ear disease, parotid mass.
Tick exposure, erythema migrans; bilateral palsy raises systemic causes (sarcoid, Lyme, GBS).
differential.investigation: Lyme serology; broader workup for bilateral palsy.

redFlags: Forehead sparing or other neurological deficits → treat as stroke, urgent pathway
Vesicular rash around ear with palsy → Ramsay Hunt, early antivirals + steroids
Inability to close eye → corneal exposure risk, eye protection essential
Bilateral facial palsy → investigate systemic cause (Lyme, sarcoid, GBS)
initialInvestigations: Bedside assessment of forehead movement (UMN vs LMN) and full neuro exam
Stroke imaging if UMN pattern or other deficits
Otoscopy for zoster vesicles/otitis; examine parotid
Blood glucose; Lyme serology if exposure; consider HbA1c
disposition: UMN pattern or other deficits → acute stroke pathway. Bell's palsy → corticosteroids within 72 h, eye care, follow-up; safety-net for atypical features. Ramsay Hunt → antivirals + steroids, ENT. Provide eye protection for any incomplete closure and ensure follow-up for non-recovery.

references.label: NICE CKS — Bell's palsy.
NICE NG128 — Stroke and TIA (for UMN facial weakness).

oneLiner: Acute binocular double vision is a neurological red flag. Must-not-miss causes include a painful third-nerve palsy (posterior communicating artery aneurysm), giant cell arteritis, brainstem stroke and raised intracranial pressure. Monocular diplopia is usually ocular.
framing: First establish monocular (persists with one eye covered — ocular/refractive) vs binocular (resolves when either eye covered — ocular misalignment, usually neurological/neuromuscular). Acute binocular diplopia, especially with pain, pupil involvement or other deficits, needs urgent assessment for aneurysm, GCA, stroke and myasthenia.
keyHistory: Monocular (one eye covered, still double) vs binocular (resolves covering either eye)
Direction of separation (horizontal/vertical), worse on gaze direction
Pain (painful third-nerve palsy — aneurysm), headache, scalp/jaw symptoms (GCA)
Vascular risk factors; trauma; thyroid eye symptoms
keyExam: Cover/uncover test; eye movements in all directions
Pupil size/reactivity (a 'down and out' eye with dilated pupil = surgical third-nerve palsy)
Ptosis and fatigability; visual acuity and fields
Temporal artery tenderness; full neurological exam

differential.diagnosis: Third-nerve palsy with pupil involvement (posterior communicating artery aneurysm)
differential.pointers: Painful, 'down and out' eye, ptosis, dilated/poorly reactive pupil — compressive aneurysm until excluded.
differential.investigation: Urgent CT/CT angiography (or MRA) to exclude aneurysm; neurosurgical referral.

differential.pointers: Age >50, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, transient visual loss; diplopia from ischaemic ophthalmoplegia.
differential.investigation: ESR/CRP, urgent high-dose steroids if suspected to prevent blindness; temporal artery biopsy/ultrasound.

differential.pointers: Diplopia with vertigo, ataxia, dysarthria, crossed signs; vascular risk factors.
differential.investigation: Urgent stroke pathway and brain imaging.

differential.pointers: Fatigable, variable diplopia and ptosis, worse at end of day; no pupil involvement.
differential.investigation: Anti-AChR antibodies, assess bulbar/respiratory function; neurology.

differential.pointers: Pupil-sparing third or sixth-nerve palsy in vasculopath; often resolves.
differential.investigation: Glucose/HbA1c, BP; observe with safety-net; image if atypical or no recovery.

redFlags: Painful third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil → exclude aneurysm urgently
Diplopia with headache/jaw claudication in over 50s → GCA, start steroids and check ESR/CRP
Diplopia with vertigo/ataxia/other deficits → posterior circulation stroke
Fatigable diplopia with bulbar/breathing symptoms → myasthenia, assess respiratory function
initialInvestigations: Establish monocular vs binocular; cover test and ocular motility exam
Assess pupil involvement (critical for third-nerve palsy)
ESR/CRP if GCA suspected (and start steroids)
Urgent CT/CTA or MRI/MRA for aneurysm or stroke as indicated
Glucose/HbA1c, BP; anti-AChR antibodies if myasthenia suspected
disposition: Pupil-involving third-nerve palsy or suspected stroke/aneurysm → emergency imaging and referral. Suspected GCA → immediate steroids and urgent rheumatology/ophthalmology. Myasthenia → neurology and respiratory assessment. Isolated pupil-sparing microvascular palsy in a vasculopath → may observe with prompt follow-up.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — Acute diplopia assessment.
BMJ Best Practice — Assessment of diplopia.

oneLiner: New psychotic symptoms require exclusion of organic causes before assuming a primary psychiatric disorder. Red flags for an organic cause (encephalitis, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, metabolic) include acute onset, fluctuating consciousness, fever, focal neurology and abnormal vitals.
framing: Up to 1 in 5 acute psychotic presentations to the ED have an organic cause. A subacute onset with neuropsychiatric features, movement disorder, seizures or autonomic instability should prompt consideration of autoimmune (e.g. anti-NMDAR) encephalitis. Always assess risk, capacity and safety alongside the medical workup.
keyHistory: Onset and course (acute/fluctuating suggests organic; insidious more typical of primary psychosis)
Drugs/alcohol — intoxication or withdrawal; prescribed medications, steroids
Risk — to self/others, command hallucinations, self-neglect; collateral history
keyExam: Vital signs and conscious level (fever, autonomic instability, fluctuation)
Neurological exam — focal signs, movement disorder, meningism
Mental state examination and risk assessment

differential.diagnosis: Delirium / organic brain disturbance (infection, metabolic, drugs)
differential.pointers: Acute, fluctuating, altered consciousness/attention, abnormal vitals, visual hallucinations.
differential.investigation: Bloods (FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, LFTs, TFTs, CRP), septic screen, drug screen, ECG; treat cause; CT head if focal/reduced GCS.

differential.pointers: Subacute neuropsychiatric change with seizures, movement disorder, dysautonomia, reduced consciousness, fever.
differential.investigation: CT/MRI brain, lumbar puncture, EEG, autoimmune antibodies; neurology; consider empirical aciclovir if HSV suspected.

differential.pointers: Stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal (delirium tremens).
differential.investigation: Drug/alcohol history and screen; treat withdrawal (benzodiazepines, thiamine).

differential.pointers: More insidious onset, preserved consciousness, mood/affective features; diagnosis after organic exclusion.
differential.investigation: Psychiatric assessment; early intervention in psychosis referral.

redFlags: Acute onset with fluctuating consciousness, fever or focal neurology → organic cause/encephalitis, urgent medical workup
Seizures, movement disorder or autonomic instability → consider autoimmune encephalitis
Risk to self or others / command hallucinations → urgent psychiatric and safety assessment
Abnormal vital signs or metabolic derangement → treat as delirium until proven otherwise
initialInvestigations: FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, LFTs, TFTs, CRP; drug/alcohol screen
Septic screen if fever; CT/MRI brain, LP, EEG if encephalitis/organic cause suspected
Risk assessment, capacity assessment and Mental Health Act consideration
disposition: Exclude and treat organic causes first; suspected encephalitis → admit for imaging, LP and neurology, with empirical aciclovir if HSV possible. Primary psychosis with risk → urgent psychiatric assessment, consider Mental Health Act; refer to early intervention in psychosis service. Manage substance-related psychosis and withdrawal appropriately.

references.label: NICE CG178 — Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management.
BMJ Best Practice — Assessment of psychosis / organic causes (autoimmune encephalitis).

chiefComplaint: Adult acute eye trauma / chemical injury
oneLiner: Chemical eye injury is a true emergency — irrigate immediately and copiously before anything else (alkalis are worse than acids). Suspect open-globe injury with high-velocity/penetrating trauma: shield the eye, give antibiotics, and do not manipulate.
framing: Time-critical ocular emergencies: chemical burns (immediate prolonged irrigation, check pH), open-globe injury (shield, no pressure, antibiotics, urgent ophthalmology), and other sight-threatening trauma (hyphaema, retrobulbar haemorrhage). For chemical injury, treatment precedes detailed examination.
keyHistory: Mechanism — chemical (type: alkali worse than acid), high-velocity/penetrating, blunt
Time of injury and any first aid/irrigation already done
Eye protection, possible retained foreign body, hammering/grinding
Pain, visual loss, photophobia, foreign body sensation
keyExam: Chemical injury: check and re-check pH; irrigate until neutral BEFORE detailed exam
Visual acuity (document early), pupil, relative afferent pupillary defect
Signs of open globe — peaked/teardrop pupil, prolapsing tissue, shallow chamber, low IOP; do NOT measure pressure if open globe suspected
Hyphaema (blood in anterior chamber), proptosis/tense orbit (retrobulbar haemorrhage)

differential.pointers: Pain, redness, blurred vision after exposure; alkalis cause penetrating liquefactive necrosis.
differential.investigation: Immediate copious irrigation until pH neutral; then assess; urgent ophthalmology.

differential.pointers: High-velocity/sharp trauma, peaked pupil, prolapsing uveal tissue, low IOP, vision loss.
differential.investigation: Shield the eye (no pressure), NBM, systemic antibiotics, antiemetics, tetanus; CT orbit; urgent ophthalmology/surgery.

differential.diagnosis: Retrobulbar haemorrhage with orbital compartment syndrome
differential.pointers: Proptosis, tense orbit, reduced vision, RAPD after trauma.
differential.investigation: Clinical; emergency lateral canthotomy/cantholysis to save sight; CT after decompression.

differential.pointers: Blood in anterior chamber, raised IOP risk, rebleed risk.
differential.investigation: Ophthalmology assessment; IOP monitoring; rest, head elevation.

differential.pointers: Pain, foreign body sensation, fluorescein uptake.
differential.investigation: Fluorescein exam, evert lids; remove foreign body; topical antibiotic.

redFlags: Chemical injury → irrigate immediately and copiously, check pH, before detailed assessment
Suspected open globe → shield the eye, no pressure or drops that sting, antibiotics, urgent ophthalmology
Tense proptotic orbit with vision loss → retrobulbar haemorrhage, emergency canthotomy
Sudden visual loss or RAPD after trauma → sight-threatening, urgent referral
initialInvestigations: Chemical: immediate irrigation and pH testing (do not delay for history)
Visual acuity, pupils/RAPD, slit-lamp with fluorescein (if no open globe)
Eye shield and CT orbit if open globe / retained foreign body suspected
Tetanus prophylaxis; systemic antibiotics for open globe
disposition: Chemical burns and open-globe/penetrating injuries → emergency ophthalmology referral and admission; irrigate chemical injuries immediately and shield open globes. Retrobulbar haemorrhage → emergency canthotomy. Minor abrasions/foreign bodies → treat and follow-up. Always document visual acuity and give tetanus prophylaxis.

references.label: Royal College of Ophthalmologists — Ophthalmic trauma and chemical injury guidance.
RCEMLearning — Chemical eye injuries and ocular trauma in the ED.

oneLiner: Most acute red, hot, swollen limbs are cellulitis, but necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency that can look deceptively mild early. Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis demand immediate surgical review.
framing: Cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis treated with antibiotics; the critical task is recognising necrotising soft-tissue infection early, when survival depends on rapid surgical debridement. Imaging and the LRINEC score support but never override clinical suspicion — high suspicion mandates surgical consultation.
keyHistory: Speed of spread, severity of pain (out of proportion suggests necrotising infection)
Systemic features — fever, rigors, confusion, hypotension
Portal of entry — wound, ulcer, bite, IV drug use; diabetes, immunosuppression
Limb vs other site; recent trauma or surgery
Suspected DVT (differential for a red swollen leg)
keyExam: Extent of erythema (mark the border), warmth, swelling, tenderness
Red flags — pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis/dusky skin, anaesthesia over the area
Source/portal of entry; lymphangitis; assess for abscess

differential.pointers: Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, crepitus, haemorrhagic bullae, skin necrosis or anaesthesia.
differential.investigation: Immediate surgical referral for debridement; bloods incl. CK, lactate, LRINEC score (adjunct only); broad-spectrum antibiotics; resuscitate. Do NOT delay surgery for imaging.

differential.pointers: Hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, lactataemia.
Spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness; often unilateral lower limb with a portal of entry.
differential.investigation: Clinical; mark border; antibiotics per severity (Eron classification); bloods if systemic.

differential.pointers: Fluctuant, localised collection; may need drainage.
Unilateral calf swelling/tenderness, VTE risk factors, less erythema/warmth.

redFlags: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis → necrotising fasciitis, immediate surgical referral
Systemic toxicity/sepsis → resuscitate, IV antibiotics, escalate
High clinical suspicion of necrotising infection → surgery, do not wait for imaging or LRINEC
Facial/periorbital or rapidly worsening cellulitis → admit and IV antibiotics
initialInvestigations: Observations and sepsis screen; mark erythema border
FBC, U&E, CRP, glucose, CK, lactate, blood cultures
LRINEC score as adjunct only (does not exclude necrotising infection)
Imaging (CT/MRI) only if it will not delay surgery in suspected necrotising infection
Doppler ultrasound if DVT in differential
disposition: Suspected necrotising fasciitis → emergency surgical referral for debridement, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation; do not delay. Cellulitis → antibiotics per severity (oral and outpatient if mild; IV/admit if systemic, comorbid or severe per Eron class). Drain abscesses. Reassess and escalate if not improving.

references.label: NICE NG141 — Cellulitis and erysipelas: antimicrobial prescribing.
BMJ Best Practice — Necrotising fasciitis (LRINEC as adjunct).

oneLiner: A brief, now-resolved episode in an infant (cyanosis/pallor, absent/irregular breathing, altered tone or responsiveness). Classify higher vs lower risk; exclude serious mimics (sepsis, NAI, intussusception, cardiac, metabolic) before reassuring.
framing: BRUE (formerly ALTE) describes a sudden, brief (<1 min) and resolved episode in an infant under 1 year with at least one of: colour change, breathing change, marked tone change, or altered responsiveness — and no explanation after history and exam. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; the task is to find or safely exclude an underlying cause.
keyHistory: Detailed event description — duration, colour, breathing, tone, responsiveness, what stopped it
Relationship to feeding/sleep/position; choking, vomiting (reflux, aspiration)
Prematurity, prior events, family history of sudden death
Social/safeguarding concerns; inconsistent or changing history (NAI)
keyExam: Full set of observations, oxygen saturations and full systems exam (often normal post-event)
Signs of sepsis, respiratory infection, dehydration
Cardiac examination; tone, fontanelle, neurological assessment
Examine for injuries / signs of non-accidental injury (retinal/bruising/torn frenulum)

differential.pointers: Fever or unwell appearance; young infants may present with apnoea.
differential.investigation: Observations, septic screen if any concern; admit unwell infants.

differential.pointers: Inconsistent/changing history, unexplained injuries, repeated events.
differential.investigation: Safeguarding pathway; examine for injuries; involve senior/child protection.

differential.pointers: Family history of sudden death, abnormal cardiac exam, event with pallor/collapse.
differential.investigation: ECG; cardiology if abnormal or high-risk features.

differential.pointers: Episodic pallor/lethargy, drawing up legs, vomiting, redcurrant stool.
Event after feed with arching/regurgitation; well infant, normal exam, no risk features.
differential.investigation: Clinical; lower-risk BRUE may be observed and safety-netted per criteria.

redFlags: Unwell appearance, fever or recurrent events → admit and investigate
Inconsistent history or signs of injury → safeguarding/NAI assessment
Family history of sudden death or abnormal ECG → cardiology
Prematurity, age under 2 months, or multiple events → higher-risk, admit
initialInvestigations: Full observations including SpO2; thorough history and examination
Blood glucose; further bloods/septic screen if unwell or concern
Consider abdominal ultrasound (intussusception), and safeguarding assessment as indicated
Risk stratify into higher vs lower-risk BRUE
disposition: Higher-risk BRUE (e.g. age under 2 months, prematurity, multiple events, abnormal findings) → admit for monitoring and investigation. Lower-risk, well infant with normal assessment → may be observed and discharged with safety-netting and follow-up. Any safeguarding concern → involve child protection and senior paediatrician.

references.label: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline — Brief Resolved Unexplained Events (BRUE) in lower-risk infants.
RCEMLearning — Brief Resolved Unexplained Events (BRUE).

oneLiner: A rash with systemic upset, mucosal involvement, skin pain, blistering or skin detachment after a new drug signals a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP). Stop the culprit drug immediately and treat as an emergency.
framing: Most drug rashes are benign exanthems, but red-flag features distinguish life-threatening reactions: mucosal involvement and skin detachment (SJS/TEN), fever/eosinophilia/organ involvement weeks after starting a drug (DRESS), and rapid pustular eruption (AGEP). Early drug withdrawal and supportive care are critical; mortality in TEN is high.
keyHistory: New drugs in preceding days to weeks (allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, antibiotics, NSAIDs)
Time course (SJS/TEN ~1-3 weeks; DRESS 2-8 weeks after drug)
Skin pain, blistering, peeling; mucosal symptoms (mouth, eyes, genitals)
Systemic features — fever, malaise, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy
Extent of skin involved (body surface area)
keyExam: Mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital) — hallmark of SJS/TEN
Skin pain, blistering, Nikolsky sign, percentage body surface detachment

differential.pointers: Painful skin, target/dusky lesions, blistering, mucosal involvement, positive Nikolsky, skin detachment.
differential.investigation: Stop culprit drug; FBC, U&E, LFTs; SCORTEN severity; urgent dermatology/burns/ophthalmology; fluid and wound care.

differential.diagnosis: DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
differential.pointers: Widespread rash, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hepatitis/nephritis weeks after drug.
differential.investigation: FBC (eosinophilia), LFTs, U&E; stop drug; systemic steroids; monitor organ involvement.

differential.pointers: Rapid urticaria/angioedema with airway/breathing/circulation compromise.
differential.investigation: Treat as anaphylaxis with IM adrenaline if ABC compromise.

differential.pointers: Rapid onset of numerous sterile pustules on erythema, fever, recent drug (often antibiotic).
differential.investigation: Stop drug; FBC; supportive; usually self-limiting after withdrawal.

differential.pointers: Symmetrical maculopapular rash, no mucosal involvement, no systemic upset, no skin pain.
differential.investigation: Clinical; stop likely culprit; antihistamines; monitor for evolution to severe reaction.

redFlags: Mucosal involvement, skin pain, blistering or detachment → SJS/TEN, emergency
Fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia and organ involvement → DRESS
Rash with airway/breathing/circulation compromise → anaphylaxis, give adrenaline
Always stop the suspected culprit drug immediately and document the allergy
initialInvestigations: FBC (eosinophilia), U&E, LFTs, CRP; assess organ involvement
Estimate body surface area involved; SCORTEN for TEN
Urgent dermatology referral; ophthalmology for ocular involvement; burns/ICU for extensive detachment
disposition: Suspected SJS/TEN, DRESS or extensive reaction → admit (burns unit/ICU for severe TEN), stop culprit drug, supportive and specialist care. AGEP → withdraw drug, supportive. Benign exanthem → stop likely culprit, treat symptomatically, safety-net for evolution. Document drug allergy clearly in records.

references.label: UK guidelines for the management of Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis in adults (British Association of Dermatologists).
Primary Care Dermatology Society — Severe adverse cutaneous drug reactions.

oneLiner: Most childhood ingestions are minor, but identify the time-critical hazards — button battery (oesophageal burn within hours), multiple magnets (bowel injury), and toxic agents per TOXBASE. Establish the agent, amount and timing; involve the poisons service early.
framing: Accidental ingestion is common in toddlers. The assessment hinges on what, how much and when. Some agents and objects are emergencies even when the child looks well: a button battery in the oesophagus causes liquefactive necrosis within ~2 hours, and multiple magnets can trap bowel. Always check TOXBASE and consider safeguarding.
keyHistory: Agent/object, formulation and strength, estimated maximum amount, time of ingestion
Symptoms — coughing/choking, drooling, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures
Caustic/corrosive, hydrocarbon, or medication ingestion (which drug)
Plausibility/consistency of history (safeguarding); access to substance
keyExam: ABCDE, conscious level, observations including SpO2 and glucose
Drooling/dysphagia or respiratory distress (oesophageal foreign body/caustic)

differential.pointers: Coin-shaped object; oesophageal lodging causes burns/perforation within hours; may be asymptomatic initially.
differential.investigation: Urgent X-ray (look for double-rim/halo sign); if oesophageal → emergency removal; honey/sucralfate per protocol while awaiting; do NOT delay.

differential.pointers: More than one magnet (or magnet + metal) can attract across bowel walls causing pressure necrosis/perforation.
Agents dangerous in small doses for toddlers (e.g. certain cardiac, hypoglycaemic, opioid drugs); paracetamol; corrosives.
differential.investigation: Consult TOXBASE/National Poisons service; agent-specific bloods/levels and antidotes; observe per agent.

differential.pointers: Oral burns, drooling, dysphagia, refusal to feed.
differential.investigation: Do NOT induce vomiting; ENT/surgical input; endoscopy as advised.

differential.pointers: Substance/quantity below toxic threshold, asymptomatic child.
differential.investigation: Confirm via TOXBASE; observe and safety-net.

redFlags: Button battery (especially oesophageal) → emergency removal, time-critical (burns within hours)
Multiple magnets ingested → urgent surgical review
Reduced consciousness, seizures, respiratory distress or arrhythmia → resuscitate and treat toxidrome
Inconsistent history or recurrent ingestions → safeguarding assessment
initialInvestigations: Consult TOXBASE / National Poisons Information Service early
X-ray if button battery, magnet or radio-opaque object possible
Agent-specific bloods/levels and antidotes (e.g. paracetamol level at 4 h)
Do not induce vomiting; activated charcoal only if advised and airway safe
disposition: Button battery in oesophagus or multiple magnets → emergency removal/surgical referral. Toxic ingestions → manage per TOXBASE with appropriate observation, antidotes and admission. Asymptomatic non-toxic ingestions → discharge with safety-netting after confirmation. Address safeguarding and prevention (storage advice) for all.

references.label: TOXBASE / National Poisons Information Service — agent-specific guidance.
RCEMLearning — Paediatric toxicology; NHS button battery safety guidance.

chiefComplaint: Adult suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
oneLiner: Sudden severe abdominal/back pain with shock in an older patient (especially a male smoker) is a ruptured AAA until proven otherwise. The classic triad (pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass) is present in under half — mortality is extreme, so act fast.
framing: Ruptured AAA is frequently misdiagnosed as renal colic, diverticulitis or musculoskeletal back pain, delaying life-saving surgery. Maintain a high index of suspicion in any older patient with abrupt abdominal/flank/back pain and haemodynamic compromise. Do not allow a tentative alternative diagnosis to delay vascular referral.
keyHistory: Sudden severe abdominal, flank or back pain; collapse/syncope
Known AAA or screening result; cardiovascular risk (male, age >65, smoking, hypertension)
Radiation to back/groin (may mimic renal colic)
keyExam: Vitals — hypotension, tachycardia (may be transiently normal then crash)
Pulsatile/expansile abdominal mass (may be hard to feel)
Signs of shock and poor perfusion

differential.pointers: Sudden abdominal/back pain, shock, pulsatile mass; first presentation of renal colic in an older person should prompt AAA exclusion.
differential.investigation: Immediate vascular surgical referral; bedside ultrasound (aortic diameter); CT angiogram only if stable; do NOT delay theatre if unstable.

differential.pointers: Tearing pain radiating to back, pulse/BP differential, may extend to abdomen.
Loin-to-groin pain, haematuria; but new 'renal colic' in older patients must exclude AAA first.
differential.investigation: Urinalysis, CT KUB after AAA excluded.

differential.diagnosis: Other acute abdomen (perforation, diverticulitis, mesenteric ischaemia)
differential.pointers: Peritonism, sepsis; out-of-proportion pain (mesenteric ischaemia).

redFlags: Sudden abdominal/back pain with hypotension in older patient → ruptured AAA, emergency vascular referral
New 'renal colic' presentation over age 60 → exclude AAA before attributing to stone
Do not delay theatre for imaging in the unstable patient
initialInvestigations: Immediate vascular surgical referral and resuscitation (permissive hypotension)
Large-bore IV access, crossmatch, activate major haemorrhage protocol
CT angiogram only if haemodynamically stable
disposition: Suspected ruptured AAA → emergency vascular surgery for open or endovascular repair; resuscitate with restraint (permissive hypotension), crossmatch and activate major haemorrhage protocol. Symptomatic/tender AAA without rupture → urgent vascular admission. All require immediate senior and vascular involvement.

references.label: NICE NG156 — Abdominal aortic aneurysm: diagnosis and management.
RCEMLearning — Abdominal aortic aneurysm.

oneLiner: Core temperature above ~40C with central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma) is heat stroke — a medical emergency. Cool rapidly and immediately, support organs, and consider drug causes (serotonin syndrome, NMS, malignant hyperthermia).
framing: Distinguish heat exhaustion (preserved mental status, often sweating) from heat stroke (core >40C with CNS dysfunction). Identify drug-induced hyperthermia (serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, anticholinergic, sympathomimetic, malignant hyperthermia) as management differs. Rapid cooling is the priority and time-critical.
keyHistory: Environmental exposure (heatwave, exertion), or new/changed medications/drugs
Neurological symptoms — confusion, agitation, seizures, collapse
Drugs — serotonergic agents, antipsychotics, stimulants, anticholinergics; anaesthesia (malignant hyperthermia)
keyExam: Skin (hot dry vs sweaty), rigidity/clonus (serotonin syndrome/NMS)
Vitals — tachycardia, hypotension; signs of end-organ dysfunction

differential.pointers: Core >40C with CNS dysfunction after heat exposure/exertion; risk of multiorgan failure, rhabdomyolysis, DIC.
differential.investigation: Rapid cooling immediately; bloods incl. U&E, CK, LFTs, coagulation, lactate; monitor organs; ICU.

differential.pointers: Serotonergic drugs, agitation, clonus/hyperreflexia (lower-limb predominant), hyperthermia.
differential.investigation: Stop serotonergic agents; cooling; benzodiazepines; consider cyproheptadine; supportive care.

differential.pointers: Antipsychotic exposure, lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, raised CK.
differential.investigation: Stop antipsychotic; cooling; supportive; consider dantrolene/bromocriptine; ICU.

differential.pointers: Infection source, fever rather than environmental hyperthermia.
differential.investigation: Septic screen; treat per sepsis pathway (note antipyretics ineffective in true hyperthermia).

redFlags: Core temperature >40C with confusion, seizures or coma → heat stroke, cool immediately
Multiorgan dysfunction (renal, hepatic, coagulopathy, rhabdomyolysis) → ICU
Drug history of serotonergic/antipsychotic agents with rigidity → serotonin syndrome / NMS
Do not rely on peripheral temperature — measure core temperature
initialInvestigations: Begin rapid cooling without delay (evaporative/cold water immersion per setting)
Bloods — U&E, CK, LFTs, coagulation, glucose, lactate, ABG; urinalysis (myoglobin)
ECG; medication/drug review for drug-induced hyperthermia
disposition: Heat stroke → rapid cooling, organ support and ICU admission; treat complications (rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC). Drug-induced hyperthermia → stop offending agent, cool, give specific antidote/supportive care, ICU. Heat exhaustion (normal mental status) → rest, cooling, rehydration; observe and safety-net.

references.label: Expert consensus on standardized diagnosis and treatment for heat stroke.
BMJ Best Practice — Heat-related illness / hyperthermia.

oneLiner: Core temperature below 35C. Handle gently (rough movement can precipitate VF), rewarm core before periphery, and remember no one is dead until warm and dead. Identify precipitants (immersion, sepsis, hypothyroidism, alcohol, drugs).
framing: Hypothermia is core temperature <35C (mild 32-35, moderate 28-32, severe <28). The myocardium is irritable below ~32C and prone to malignant arrhythmias, so move the patient gently. Prolonged resuscitation may succeed because hypothermia is neuroprotective. Look for and treat the underlying cause.
keyHistory: Exposure — environmental, immersion, prolonged collapse, found down
Precipitants — alcohol, drugs/sedatives, sepsis, hypothyroidism, hypoglycaemia, stroke
Conscious level and shivering (shivering ceases as hypothermia deepens)
keyExam: Cardiac rhythm and pulse (may be slow/hard to detect — check for a prolonged period)
Conscious level; signs of injury/precipitating illness

differential.diagnosis: Severe hypothermia with arrhythmia / cardiac arrest risk
differential.pointers: Core <28-30C, bradycardia, J (Osborn) waves, risk of VF with rough handling; prolonged resuscitation may be appropriate.
differential.investigation: Gentle handling; core rewarming (warmed fluids, warmed humidified oxygen, ECMO/bypass for severe); continue CPR until rewarmed.

differential.pointers: Infection causing hypothermia (a marker of severe sepsis), especially in elderly.
differential.investigation: Septic screen and treat; do not assume environmental cause only.

differential.pointers: Diabetes, myxoedema, Addison's.
differential.investigation: Glucose, TFTs, cortisol; treat accordingly (e.g. myxoedema coma).

differential.pointers: Intoxication impairing thermoregulation and exposure.

redFlags: Core <30C or arrhythmia → handle gently, core rewarming, prolonged resuscitation may be justified
Cardiac arrest in hypothermia → 'not dead until warm and dead', continue CPR while rewarming
Hypothermia in the elderly → consider sepsis or endocrine cause
Core temperature afterdrop → rewarm trunk before limbs
initialInvestigations: Core (low-reading rectal/oesophageal/bladder) temperature and continuous cardiac monitoring
ECG (J waves, arrhythmia); handle and transfer gently
Bloods — glucose, U&E, FBC, coagulation, TFTs, cortisol, blood gas; septic screen
Begin rewarming (passive for mild; active core for moderate/severe)
disposition: Mild hypothermia → passive rewarming and observe; treat cause. Moderate/severe hypothermia → admit with active core rewarming and cardiac monitoring; severe/arrest → consider extracorporeal rewarming and prolonged resuscitation in a critical care/specialist setting. Treat the underlying precipitant.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Hypothermia (special circumstances).
Accidental hypothermia update (ICAR MEDCOM consensus).

oneLiner: Very high blood pressure: the key is to detect acute end-organ damage (a hypertensive emergency needing controlled immediate reduction) versus asymptomatic severe hypertension (urgency, lowered over hours-days). Avoid over-rapid reduction, which itself causes harm.
framing: A single high reading is rarely an emergency by itself; the question is whether there is acute hypertension-mediated organ damage — encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, acute heart failure/pulmonary oedema, ACS, aortic dissection, AKI, retinopathy, or pre-eclampsia. Emergencies need careful parenteral control; urgencies are managed with oral therapy and follow-up.
keyHistory: Chest pain, breathlessness, orthopnoea (ACS, heart failure, dissection)
Medication non-adherence, drugs (cocaine, sympathomimetics), known hypertension
keyExam: Blood pressure in both arms (repeat/confirm), fundoscopy for retinopathy/papilloedema
Cardiovascular/respiratory exam (heart failure, murmurs, pulse deficit)
Pregnancy assessment in women of childbearing age

differential.pointers: Encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, acute pulmonary oedema, ACS, aortic dissection, AKI, retinal haemorrhages/papilloedema.
differential.investigation: ECG, troponin, U&E, urinalysis, fundoscopy, CT head/CXR/CT aorta as guided; controlled IV antihypertensive in a monitored setting.

differential.pointers: Pregnant/postpartum, headache, visual symptoms, proteinuria, oedema, seizures (eclampsia).
differential.investigation: Urgent obstetric referral; BP control; magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention/treatment.

differential.diagnosis: Aortic dissection / ACS as cause or consequence
differential.pointers: Tearing chest/back pain, pulse deficit (dissection); ischaemic chest pain (ACS).
differential.investigation: ECG, troponin, CT aorta; specific BP/heart-rate control.

differential.pointers: Very high BP without acute organ damage.
differential.investigation: Confirm BP, baseline tests, oral therapy and outpatient follow-up; avoid abrupt reduction.

redFlags: Neurological signs, chest pain, breathlessness or visual loss with severe hypertension → hypertensive emergency
Retinal haemorrhages/papilloedema → end-organ damage, urgent management
Pregnant/postpartum with high BP and symptoms → pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, urgent obstetric care
Avoid over-rapid BP reduction (risk of cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion)
initialInvestigations: ECG and troponin; U&E and urinalysis (proteinuria, AKI)
Targeted imaging — CT head (neuro signs), CXR/CT aorta (dissection)
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age
Assess for organ damage to classify emergency vs urgency
disposition: Hypertensive emergency → admit for controlled parenteral BP reduction in a monitored environment with treatment tailored to the affected organ. Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia → urgent obstetric care. Asymptomatic severe hypertension (urgency) → start/adjust oral antihypertensives, baseline investigations and early follow-up; do not lower BP precipitously.

references.label: NICE NG136 — Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management.
ESC/ESH Guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension (hypertensive emergencies).

oneLiner: Use the timing after surgery and the classic causes (the '5 Ws') to direct assessment. Early fever is often inflammatory, but exclude dangerous causes at any time — anastomotic leak, sepsis, PE, and necrotising surgical-site infection.
framing: Postoperative fever (>38C) is common; the differential is structured by time and the '5 Ws' — Wind (atelectasis/pneumonia), Water (UTI), Walking (DVT/PE), Wound (surgical-site infection), Wonder drugs (drug fever, transfusion). Do not miss anastomotic leak, intra-abdominal collection, sepsis and PE.
keyHistory: Type/timing of surgery and days postoperatively
keyExam: Abdominal exam (peritonism — anastomotic leak/collection); line sites

differential.pointers: Days 5-7 after GI surgery, abdominal pain, peritonism, tachycardia, rising inflammatory markers, deterioration.
differential.investigation: Bloods, lactate, blood cultures, CT abdomen; urgent surgical review; sepsis-6.

differential.pointers: Pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia, calf swelling; postoperative immobility.
differential.investigation: Wells score, CTPA; assess VTE prophylaxis.

differential.pointers: Wound erythema/discharge; pain out of proportion, crepitus, necrosis → necrotising infection.
differential.investigation: Wound assessment, cultures; surgical review; emergency debridement if necrotising.

differential.pointers: Early fever with basal atelectasis; catheter-associated UTI.
Temporal relation to drug/transfusion; diagnosis of exclusion.

redFlags: Sepsis features / haemodynamic instability → sepsis-6 and urgent source control
Peritonism after abdominal surgery → suspected anastomotic leak/collection, urgent surgical review
Pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, hypoxia → exclude PE
Wound with pain out of proportion, crepitus or necrosis → necrotising infection, emergency surgery
initialInvestigations: Observations and sepsis screen; examine wound, chest, calves, abdomen, lines
FBC, U&E, CRP, blood cultures, lactate
CXR, urinalysis/culture; wound swab as indicated
CT abdomen if leak/collection suspected; CTPA if PE suspected
disposition: Stable, benign causes (atelectasis, minor UTI) → treat and monitor on the ward. Suspected anastomotic leak/collection, sepsis, PE, or necrotising infection → urgent investigation, surgical/critical-care involvement and appropriate intervention. Escalate any deteriorating postoperative patient promptly.

references.label: BMJ Best Practice — Evaluation of postoperative fever.
NICE NG51 — Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management.

oneLiner: Severe hyperkalaemia is a cardiac emergency — get an ECG immediately. ECG changes (peaked T waves, broad QRS, sine wave) or potassium above ~6.5 mmol/L warrant emergency treatment to protect the myocardium and shift/remove potassium.
framing: Hyperkalaemia is often asymptomatic until it causes life-threatening arrhythmia. Risk rises with AKI/CKD, drugs (ACE-I/ARB, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim), tissue breakdown and acidosis. Treatment priorities: cardiac protection (calcium), shift potassium intracellularly (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol), then remove it, and stop the cause.
keyHistory: Often found on bloods; symptoms vague (weakness, palpitations) or absent
AKI/CKD, missed dialysis; drugs (ACE-I/ARB, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, potassium supplements)
Tissue breakdown — rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis, crush injury
keyExam: Signs of volume status and underlying cause

differential.pointers: Peaked T waves, flattened P, broad QRS, sine-wave pattern; risk of VF/asystole; K+ typically >6.5 or any ECG change.
differential.investigation: Immediate ECG; IV calcium gluconate/chloride for cardioprotection; insulin-dextrose + nebulised salbutamol to shift K+; treat cause; dialysis if refractory.

differential.diagnosis: Acute kidney injury / CKD with hyperkalaemia
differential.pointers: Reduced excretion; missed dialysis.
differential.investigation: U&E, VBG; treat hyperkalaemia; urgent nephrology/dialysis if refractory or severe.

differential.pointers: ACE-I/ARB, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, supplements.
differential.investigation: Stop offending drugs; recheck; treat per severity.

differential.pointers: Crush/ischaemia, chemotherapy, massive haemolysis.
differential.investigation: CK, urate, phosphate, LDH; treat cause and hyperkalaemia.

differential.pointers: Haemolysed/old sample, very high WCC/platelets, no ECG changes.
differential.investigation: Repeat sample carefully; correlate with ECG.

redFlags: Any ECG change (peaked T, broad QRS, sine wave) → emergency treatment, start with IV calcium
Potassium above ~6.5 mmol/L → emergency management even if asymptomatic
AKI/missed dialysis with high potassium → urgent nephrology/dialysis
initialInvestigations: Immediate 12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring
Treat per severity — IV calcium for cardioprotection; insulin-dextrose ± salbutamol to shift
Identify cause — CK, urate/phosphate (tissue lysis), medication review; repeat sample if spurious suspected
Monitor potassium and glucose after treatment
disposition: Severe hyperkalaemia or ECG changes → emergency treatment and admission with cardiac monitoring; refractory or dialysis-dependent → urgent renal replacement therapy and nephrology. Mild hyperkalaemia → treat cause, stop offending drugs, dietary advice and recheck. Always correlate the level with the ECG.

references.label: UK Kidney Association — Clinical practice guideline: treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults.
Resuscitation Council UK — Hyperkalaemia (life-threatening electrolyte disturbances).

oneLiner: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Immediately exclude tension pneumothorax (a clinical diagnosis needing instant needle decompression) and distinguish primary (no lung disease) from secondary (underlying lung disease) pneumothorax, which need different management.
framing: Tension pneumothorax (haemodynamic compromise, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds) is treated immediately on clinical grounds — do not wait for imaging. For non-tension pneumothorax, management depends on symptoms, size and whether there is underlying lung disease (secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is higher risk).
keyHistory: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness
Tall thin young smoker (primary) vs known COPD/lung disease (secondary)
Previous pneumothorax; family history (e.g. connective tissue disease)
keyExam: Reduced/absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on affected side
Tension signs — hypotension, tracheal deviation away, distended neck veins, severe distress

differential.pointers: Severe respiratory distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation away from side, absent breath sounds, distended neck veins.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis — immediate needle decompression then chest drain; do NOT delay for CXR.

differential.pointers: Underlying lung disease (COPD, asthma, CF, ILD); poorly tolerated even when small.
differential.investigation: CXR; usually needs admission and chest drain; respiratory referral.

differential.pointers: No underlying lung disease; often young, tall, slim smokers.
differential.investigation: CXR (size); management by symptoms/size per BTS pathway (observation, aspiration or drain).

differential.diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism / other acute chest pathology
differential.pointers: Pleuritic pain and dyspnoea overlap; consider if no pneumothorax on imaging.

redFlags: Haemodynamic compromise with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation → tension pneumothorax, immediate decompression
Pneumothorax with underlying lung disease (secondary) → admit and drain
Hypoxia or significant breathlessness → oxygen and urgent management
Bilateral pneumothorax or recurrence → respiratory/surgical referral
initialInvestigations: Erect CXR (or bedside ultrasound) — but treat tension clinically without delay
Assess size and underlying lung disease to guide management
ABG if hypoxic or significant secondary pneumothorax
Respiratory referral for drainage and follow-up
disposition: Tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression and chest drain, admit. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax → admit, usually chest drain, respiratory team. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax → manage per BTS pathway (observation/aspiration/drain) based on size and symptoms; arrange follow-up and smoking cessation, with recurrence prevention advice.

references.label: BTS Guideline for the management of spontaneous pneumothorax.
Resuscitation Council UK — Tension pneumothorax (special circumstances).

oneLiner: A non-blanching (petechial/purpuric) rash in a child is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise — treat a febrile or unwell child with purpura immediately. Differentiate from ITP, HSP and leukaemia by the clinical picture.
framing: Petechiae are <2 mm and purpura >=2 mm non-blanching lesions (confirm with the glass/tumbler test). A child with fever and purpura should be treated as meningococcal disease even if they look well. Other causes (ITP, HSP, leukaemia) are usually distinguishable by systemic features and onset, but never miss invasive meningococcal infection.
keyHistory: Fever, lethargy, irritability, rapid spread of rash (meningococcal sepsis)
Recent viral illness with otherwise well child and bruising/petechiae (ITP)
Palpable purpura on legs/buttocks with joint or abdominal pain (HSP)
Fatigue, pallor, weight loss, bruising, bone pain (leukaemia)
keyExam: Confirm non-blanching with glass/tumbler test; distribution and progression
Full observations and sepsis screen; capillary refill, perfusion

differential.pointers: Fever, unwell/toxic child, rapidly spreading purpura, poor perfusion; may also have meningitis.
differential.investigation: Immediate IV/IM benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone; sepsis-6; blood cultures, meningococcal PCR; do NOT delay antibiotics.

differential.pointers: Insidious onset, pallor, fatigue, bruising, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain.
differential.investigation: FBC and blood film urgently; paediatric haematology/oncology referral.

differential.pointers: Well child, often post-viral, widespread petechiae/bruising, isolated thrombocytopenia.
differential.investigation: FBC (low platelets, otherwise normal), blood film; paediatric review.
