differential.pointers: Palpable purpura on lower limbs/buttocks, arthralgia, abdominal pain, renal involvement; usually well.
differential.investigation: Urinalysis (renal involvement), BP; clinical diagnosis; monitor.

redFlags: Fever or unwell child with non-blanching rash → treat as meningococcal disease, give antibiotics immediately
Rapidly spreading purpura, poor perfusion or reduced consciousness → meningococcal sepsis, sepsis-6
Pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or bone pain → urgent FBC for leukaemia
initialInvestigations: Confirm non-blanching nature; full observations and sepsis assessment
FBC and blood film (platelets, blasts), coagulation, CRP, blood cultures, meningococcal PCR
Lactate, glucose; lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected and safe
Immediate parenteral antibiotics if meningococcal disease suspected
disposition: Febrile/unwell child with non-blanching rash → immediate antibiotics, sepsis management and admission (treat as meningococcal disease). Suspected leukaemia → urgent haematology referral. ITP → paediatric assessment, usually monitored. HSP → assess renal involvement and follow up. Always reassess and admit if any uncertainty.

references.label: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s (petechial rash management).
NICE CG102 / NG240 — Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease.

oneLiner: A continuing or recurrent convulsive seizure is a neurological emergency. Treat seizures lasting 5 minutes (or recurrent without recovery) as status epilepticus: protect the airway, give benzodiazepines promptly, and find treatable causes (hypoglycaemia, eclampsia, toxins, infection).
framing: Convulsive status epilepticus carries significant mortality and time-dependent harm. Manage with a staged protocol: benzodiazepine first-line, then a second-line antiseizure medication if ongoing, escalating to anaesthesia/ICU for refractory cases. Always check glucose and consider eclampsia in pregnancy and reversible toxic/metabolic causes.
keyHistory: Duration, recurrence, recovery between seizures (status if >=5 min or no recovery)
Provoked causes — hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, alcohol withdrawal, drugs/toxins, infection, head injury
keyExam: ABCDE — airway protection, oxygenation, capillary glucose immediately
Seizure type and features; conscious level (post-ictal vs ongoing)
Focal neurology, meningism, fever, signs of head injury

differential.pointers: Seizure lasting >=5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery.
differential.investigation: ABCDE, glucose, IV/IM/buccal benzodiazepine; second-line ASM (levetiracetam/valproate/phenytoin) if ongoing; escalate to anaesthesia/ICU if refractory.

differential.pointers: Diabetic on treatment; rapidly reversible.
Seizure in pregnancy/postpartum with hypertension/proteinuria.
differential.investigation: Magnesium sulfate, urgent obstetric care, BP control.

differential.pointers: Fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness.
differential.investigation: Bloods, imaging, LP; empirical antibiotics/aciclovir if suspected.

differential.pointers: Drugs/overdose, hyponatraemia, alcohol withdrawal.
differential.investigation: U&E, calcium, magnesium, toxicology; treat cause; thiamine if alcohol-related.

redFlags: Seizure lasting >=5 minutes or recurrent without recovery → treat as status epilepticus
Hypoglycaemia → treat immediately before anything else
Seizure in pregnancy/postpartum → eclampsia, give magnesium sulfate and urgent obstetric care
Refractory seizures → anaesthesia/ICU for general anaesthesia
initialInvestigations: Benzodiazepine first-line (IV lorazepam, or IM/buccal midazolam); repeat once
U&E, calcium, magnesium, glucose, FBC, antiseizure drug levels, toxicology
CT head and LP if cause unclear/CNS infection suspected
Pregnancy test; second-line ASM and ICU escalation if ongoing
disposition: Status epilepticus → admit with airway protection and protocolised treatment; refractory status → ICU for anaesthesia and continuous EEG. Treat reversible causes (hypoglycaemia, eclampsia, infection, toxins) immediately. A first seizure that self-terminates with full recovery → investigate and refer to first-fit/neurology services with driving and safety advice.

references.label: NICE NG217 — Epilepsies in children, young people and adults (status epilepticus).
Royal College of Emergency Medicine — Management of status epilepticus in adults.

oneLiner: Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or airway. Assess the airway first. Histaminergic/allergic angioedema (often with urticaria, responds to adrenaline/antihistamines) differs from bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE-inhibitor or hereditary — no urticaria, poor response to standard allergy treatment).
framing: The immediate concern is airway compromise. Allergic angioedema is usually rapid, with urticaria/itch, and part of an allergic reaction or anaphylaxis. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE-inhibitor-induced or hereditary/C1-inhibitor deficiency) has no urticaria, can be delayed, lasts longer and responds poorly to adrenaline/antihistamines/steroids.
keyHistory: Site/extent of swelling — lips, tongue, face, pharynx/larynx (airway risk)
Speed of onset; associated urticaria/itch (allergic) or absent (bradykinin)
ACE-inhibitor or ARB use (can occur years after starting)
Family history of angioedema; recurrent episodes without urticaria (hereditary)
Trigger exposure (food, drug, sting); breathing/voice change
keyExam: Airway — voice change, stridor, tongue/pharyngeal swelling, drooling

differential.pointers: Tongue/pharyngeal/laryngeal swelling, voice change, stridor; with ABC compromise = anaphylaxis.
differential.investigation: ABCDE; if anaphylaxis features → IM adrenaline; early senior anaesthetic/ENT for airway; monitor.

differential.pointers: Lip/tongue/airway swelling without urticaria, often facial; may occur after years of therapy; bradykinin-mediated.
differential.investigation: Stop ACE-inhibitor permanently; airway monitoring/admission; poor response to adrenaline/antihistamines (give adrenaline if any airway/anaphylaxis features); consider bradykinin-targeted therapy.

differential.pointers: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria, family history, abdominal attacks; no response to standard allergy treatment.
differential.investigation: C4 and C1-inhibitor levels/function; specific therapy (C1-inhibitor concentrate, icatibant).

differential.pointers: Rapid swelling with urticaria/itch, identifiable allergen, responds to antihistamines/steroids.
differential.investigation: Identify/avoid trigger; antihistamines, steroids; adrenaline if airway/anaphylaxis.

redFlags: Tongue, pharyngeal or laryngeal swelling, voice change or stridor → airway emergency, senior anaesthetic/ENT help
Angioedema with breathing/circulation compromise → anaphylaxis, give IM adrenaline
ACE-inhibitor angioedema → stop drug permanently, monitor airway (can progress/recur)
Recurrent angioedema without urticaria → investigate for C1-inhibitor deficiency
initialInvestigations: Give IM adrenaline if any airway/breathing/circulation compromise (anaphylaxis)
Identify cause — drug history (ACE-I/ARB), allergen exposure, family history
C4 and C1-inhibitor level/function if bradykinin-mediated/recurrent suspected
Admit for airway monitoring if tongue/airway involvement
disposition: Airway involvement → admit for monitoring with anaesthetic/ENT availability; secure airway early if progressing. Anaphylaxis → adrenaline and standard treatment. ACE-inhibitor angioedema → stop the drug permanently and observe. Hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency → specific bradykinin-targeted therapy and immunology referral. Allergic angioedema → antihistamines/steroids and allergen avoidance.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK — Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (airway/angioedema).
BSACI guideline for the management of chronic urticaria and angioedema.

oneLiner: Back pain with fever and any neurological deficit is a spinal epidural abscess until proven otherwise. The classic triad is often incomplete, so maintain suspicion in at-risk patients (IV drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression) — urgent MRI prevents permanent paralysis.
framing: Spinal epidural abscess is frequently missed because the classic triad of back pain, fever and neurological deficit is present in only a minority. Progression to irreversible cord/cauda equina injury can be rapid. Have a low threshold for whole-spine MRI and urgent referral in at-risk patients with spinal pain and fever or raised inflammatory markers.
keyHistory: Severe localised back/neck pain with percussion tenderness
Fever, rigors, recent infection or bacteraemia
Risk factors — IV drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedure/epidural, indwelling lines
Neurological symptoms — limb weakness, sensory loss, radicular pain
keyExam: Spinal tenderness; fever and signs of sepsis
Full neurological exam — power, sensation, reflexes, level

differential.pointers: Back pain + fever + neurological deficit (triad often incomplete); raised inflammatory markers; at-risk patient.
differential.investigation: Urgent whole-spine MRI with contrast; FBC, CRP/ESR, blood cultures; urgent spinal/neurosurgical and infection referral.

differential.pointers: Known/suspected cancer, progressive back pain, neurological deficit.
differential.investigation: Urgent MRI whole spine; oncology; steroids per protocol.

differential.diagnosis: Cauda equina syndrome (other cause, e.g. disc)
differential.pointers: Bilateral leg symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence.
Back pain, fever, raised inflammatory markers; may coexist with abscess.
No fever, no neurology, no risk factors.

redFlags: Back pain with fever and any neurological deficit → spinal epidural abscess, urgent MRI
New bladder/bowel dysfunction or saddle anaesthesia → cord/cauda equina emergency
At-risk patient (IV drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression) with spinal pain and fever → image early
Progressive neurology → emergency, time-critical to prevent paralysis
initialInvestigations: FBC, CRP/ESR, blood cultures (before antibiotics if no delay)
Full neurological examination and bladder assessment
Identify source of infection (echo if endocarditis suspected)
disposition: Suspected spinal epidural abscess → emergency MRI and urgent neurosurgical/spinal and infection team referral; antibiotics after cultures (or immediately if septic), with surgical decompression for neurological deficit. Admit all suspected cases; do not discharge at-risk patients with back pain, fever and raised inflammatory markers without imaging.

oneLiner: Painful, red, swollen breast in a breastfeeding woman. Manage milk stasis and treat infection; identify abscess (fluctuant mass needing aspiration/drainage) and sepsis. In a non-lactating or atypical case, exclude inflammatory breast cancer.
framing: Lactational mastitis usually responds to continued milk removal and supportive measures; antibiotics if no improvement in ~24 hours, systemically unwell, or infected fissure. A fluctuant area or non-resolving mastitis suggests abscess (ultrasound-guided aspiration first-line). Always keep inflammatory breast cancer in mind for atypical/non-lactational or non-resolving cases.
keyHistory: Breastfeeding status; onset and progression; milk stasis/blocked duct
Non-lactating, peau d'orange, skin changes (inflammatory cancer)
keyExam: Erythema, warmth, tenderness, segmental vs diffuse

differential.pointers: Fluctuant tender mass, non-resolving mastitis, systemic features.
differential.investigation: Ultrasound; needle aspiration (first-line) or incision and drainage; antibiotics; culture.

differential.pointers: Systemic toxicity, tachycardia, hypotension.
Breastfeeding, localised red tender wedge, milk stasis, low-grade fever.
differential.investigation: Continue milk removal/feeding; analgesia; antibiotics if not improving in ~24 h, unwell, or infected fissure.

differential.pointers: Non-lactating or non-resolving 'mastitis', peau d'orange, skin thickening, nipple changes.
differential.investigation: Urgent breast clinic (2-week-wait) referral; imaging and biopsy.

redFlags: Fluctuant mass / non-resolving mastitis → abscess, ultrasound and aspiration/drainage
Systemic toxicity → sepsis, IV antibiotics and admission
Non-lactational or non-resolving 'mastitis', peau d'orange → exclude inflammatory breast cancer (urgent referral)
Mastitis not improving after appropriate antibiotics → reassess and image
initialInvestigations: Breast ultrasound if abscess suspected or mastitis not resolving
Urgent breast clinic referral if malignancy not excluded
disposition: Lactational mastitis → support milk removal, analgesia, and antibiotics if not improving or unwell; continue breastfeeding. Abscess → ultrasound-guided aspiration or drainage plus antibiotics. Sepsis → admit for IV antibiotics. Atypical/non-resolving or non-lactational presentation → urgent breast clinic to exclude inflammatory cancer.

references.label: NICE CKS — Mastitis and breast abscess.
NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (breast).

oneLiner: An invisible, odourless killer presenting with non-specific symptoms (headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion). Suspect it when multiple household members or pets are affected, symptoms improve away from home, or there is a faulty appliance. Pulse oximetry is falsely normal — measure carboxyhaemoglobin.
framing: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with high affinity, causing tissue hypoxia despite a normal SpO2 on standard pulse oximetry. Presentations mimic viral illness or non-specific malaise. Give high-flow oxygen immediately, measure carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb), and consider hyperbaric oxygen for severe poisoning (e.g. neurological signs, pregnancy, very high COHb).
keyHistory: Source — faulty boiler/heater, fire/smoke, fumes, generator, blocked flue
Headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, collapse, chest pain
Multiple people/pets in the same dwelling affected; symptoms better away from home
keyExam: Note: standard pulse oximetry overreads — use co-oximetry
Signs of smoke inhalation/burns if fire-related

differential.pointers: Non-specific symptoms with suggestive exposure; collective/household illness; symptoms improve away from source; raised COHb.
differential.investigation: High-flow oxygen immediately; measure carboxyhaemoglobin (venous/arterial co-oximetry); ECG, troponin; consider hyperbaric oxygen for severe features.

differential.pointers: Fire exposure, soot, airway burns, severe metabolic acidosis (cyanide).
differential.investigation: Airway assessment, lactate; consider cyanide antidote; oxygen.

differential.pointers: Chest pain, ECG changes from CO-induced myocardial hypoxia.

differential.diagnosis: Viral illness / other cause of headache and nausea (mimic)
differential.pointers: Similar non-specific symptoms; CO missed if exposure not considered.
differential.investigation: Ask about exposure and household clustering; check COHb if any suspicion.

redFlags: Loss of consciousness, seizures, focal neurology or cardiac ischaemia → severe poisoning, consider hyperbaric oxygen
Pregnancy with CO exposure → fetus highly vulnerable, low threshold for hyperbaric oxygen
Several household members/pets unwell together → strongly suspect CO
Normal SpO2 does not exclude CO poisoning — measure COHb
initialInvestigations: High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask immediately (do not wait for tests)
Assess for smoke inhalation/cyanide if fire-related
Consult TOXBASE/poisons service; consider hyperbaric oxygen for severe features
disposition: Treat all suspected CO poisoning with immediate high-flow oxygen and admit symptomatic patients. Severe poisoning (neurological signs, loss of consciousness, cardiac involvement, pregnancy, very high COHb) → discuss hyperbaric oxygen with the poisons/HBO service. Ensure the source is addressed and the home made safe before discharge; report as needed.

BMJ Best Practice — Carbon monoxide poisoning.

oneLiner: Sudden Airway/Breathing/Circulation compromise after a trigger (commonly food) with skin/mucosal change. Give weight/age-appropriate IM adrenaline immediately into the anterolateral thigh — it is the only treatment that reduces mortality.
framing: Anaphylaxis in children is a clinical diagnosis: sudden onset, rapid progression of airway, breathing and/or circulation problems, usually with skin/mucosal changes. Food is the commonest trigger. Adrenaline is first-line and dosed by age/weight; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only. Observe after treatment for biphasic reactions.
keyHistory: Trigger — food (nuts, milk, egg), drugs, sting, latex; timing (usually minutes)
Known allergy, asthma (higher fatality risk), previous reactions
Symptoms — throat tightness, cough, wheeze, breathlessness, floppy/drowsy, collapse
keyExam: Breathing — wheeze, recession, tachypnoea, SpO2, cyanosis

differential.pointers: Sudden onset after trigger with ABC compromise ± skin changes; can progress to arrest rapidly.
differential.investigation: Clinical diagnosis; immediate IM adrenaline by age (50-150 micrograms <6 yrs; 150 micrograms 6 mo-6 yr; 300 micrograms 6-12 yr; 500 micrograms >12 yr) into anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 min if needed; mast cell tryptase.

differential.pointers: Wheeze and respiratory distress without skin/mucosal change or hypotension; known asthma/viral trigger.
differential.investigation: Treat as asthma; overlap with anaphylaxis if allergen exposure — give adrenaline if anaphylaxis.

differential.pointers: Sudden choking during eating/play, stridor, no allergic features.
Brief, pallor, rapid recovery, no airway/skin features.

redFlags: Airway swelling, stridor or hoarse cry → airway emergency, call for senior/anaesthetic help
Hypotension, floppiness or collapse → circulatory anaphylaxis, lay flat and raise legs
No improvement after first adrenaline → repeat IM adrenaline at 5 min; treat as refractory if 2 doses fail
Known asthma + anaphylaxis → higher fatality risk; biphasic reactions possible, observe
initialInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis — do NOT delay adrenaline for tests
IM adrenaline by age/weight into anterolateral thigh, repeat after 5 min if needed
High-flow oxygen, IV fluids for hypotension, ABCDE
Mast cell tryptase (serial) to support later diagnosis
Cardiac/SpO2 monitoring; refer to paediatric allergy after recovery
disposition: All paediatric anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline, oxygen and fluids; admit/observe for biphasic reactions per local policy. On discharge: prescribe adrenaline auto-injectors, provide an allergy action plan, train carers/school, and refer to paediatric allergy services. Document the trigger and avoidance advice.
